About this work

Abbreviatura Recessuum Capitularium Patrum Ordinis Divi Benedicti — "An Abridgment of the Chapter Decrees of the Fathers of the Order of St Benedict, for the Province of Mainz and the Diocese of Bamberg" — is Trithemius's digest of the recessus, the closing decrees of the Benedictine reform chapters. It is a working document of the Bursfelde-aligned observant reform rather than a treatise: a codified summary of the chapters' rulings on monastic discipline, the sort of administrative-legislative text an abbot kept to hand. As such it is the documentary counterpart to his reform polemics — the De Statu et Ruina Monastici Ordinis and the Sermones ad Monachos — showing the machinery behind the rhetoric.

This is the 1493 Nuremberg edition (BSB scan), printed on 20 September 1493. The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5. No published English translation is known; as an administrative text its register is terse and formulaic, and the proper names and clause references are the hardest part of the OCR.

English translation

An Abridgment of the Chapter Decrees of the Fathers of the Order of St Benedict for the Province of Mainz and the Diocese of Bamberg

Johannes Trithemius

Abridgement of the chapter recesses of the fathers of the Order of Saint Benedict throughout the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg

Nuremberg, 20 September 1493 Inc. c. a. 158

BSB-Ink T-442 - GW M47597

Inc. c. a. 158 8. N 84.3.

8º Inc. c. a. 158 Heretica Hain 20

Inc. c. a. 8º 158. 1493

Folio II

The Abridgement of the chapter recesses of the fathers of the Order of Saint Benedict throughout the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg, held from the time of the Council of Constance down to the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1493, together with the manner of visiting monasteries of both sexes, and with a summary of the privileges of the aforesaid province, diocese, and order, begins happily.

The preface on the visitations of monks begins. Chapter 1.

“You shall visit your brothers, if they are acting rightly.” 1 Kings 17. In these words it is briefly indicated what sort of visitation of monasteries ought to be made. For the visitation itself ought to be charitable, not hateful: 10, question 3, Cauendum. And this is marked in the phrase “your brothers.” For the visitor, if he is to produce the worthy fruit of his visitation, must show himself brotherly and charitable toward those who are to be visited, and must know that he is the brother of those to be visited, not their lord; he should hate vices but love the brothers: distinction 86, Odio; 23, question 4, Duo; and in the Rule of the holy father Benedict, chapter 2, Qualis debeat esse abbas. For if the visitation is to be fruitful, it must be charitable, since charity is the proper gift of Catholic unity and peace: 1, question 1, Multae autem. And where there is no charity, there can be no justice: 24, question 1, Ubi. Therefore visitation must be made from charity, without hatred and cruelty: 10, question 3, Cauendum.

Second, visitation ought to be an examining visitation, namely concerning the life and morals of those to be visited: 10, question 1, Episcopum; Extra, De statu monachorum, Ea quae. And this is indicated in the word “you shall visit,” that is, “you shall examine.”

Third, visitation should be discreetly deliberative; and this is indicated when it says, “if they are acting rightly.” But these matters will be discussed in their proper places at a suitable time.

Therefore let visitation be such as was instituted by the holy fathers, and it will bring much fruit. For if it is properly carried out, it is the reform of the order, the preservation of discipline, the restoration of peace and concord, and the completion of all honor and beauty. It raises up what has collapsed, gathers what has been scattered, reforms what has been dissolved, restores what has been broken, brings back what wanders, puts together what has been torn apart, and duly preserves the things that are holy and just. It reforms unity and peace between head and members, abbot and brothers, and reconciles inferiors to superiors. If visitation is carried out zealously, charitably, and discreetly, it compels subjects to show the obedience owed to chapters. Let it cease, and the discipline of religion will quickly expire. Finally, if it is neglected, the provincial chapter will soon suffer contempt from its own sons. For it is visitation that preserves the obedience of the good and humbles the insolence of the contumacious. It makes delinquents fear, and embraces those who are making progress in the bosom of charity. Few are those who obey out of love; servile fear restrains many from evils. And blessed is the necessity that compels one toward better things. For as a bristle introduces the thread, so initial fear introduces charity: De poenitentia, distinction 2, section Haec quae, before the end. And woe is there where fear has perished from the earth: Micah 7; 16, question 7, Et haec diximus, after the middle.

Since, therefore, visitation has been instituted for this purpose, that through it gains of souls may be sought: 10, question 3, Cauendum, all visitors must carefully consider what is required of them. And lest they depart from the statutes of the ancients, they should always strive to imitate their forms and examples. Therefore, for the sake of this matter, the present formula for visitation, drawn from the constitutions of the fathers, has been brought together in the following manner, so that new visitors, seeing before their eyes the proper order of their office, may avoid various and dangerous errors.

Who Has Authority to Appoint Visitors of Monks

The presidents of our provincial chapter are to appoint visitors of monks, as in Extra, De statu monachorum, chapter In singulis, where it says as follows:

In the same chapter, let religious and circumspect persons also be appointed, who, in our stead, should be diligent in visiting each abbey of that kingdom or province, not only of monks but also of nuns, according to the form prescribed to them, etc. And in the constitutions of Benedict XII, chapter 2, it says as follows: Let them also provide which abbots, and how many and how often, ought to visit cathedral churches, monastic monasteries, and other places of the same order or religion up to the provincial chapter itself. Long-standing custom also, since it is not contrary to the constitutions, is to be held as law: distinction 11, In his. From this it is clear that the authority of the presidents has the right to appoint visitors; yet if at any time it should seem necessary and useful, they may employ the counsel of the chapter in choosing visitors.

What Sort of Persons the Visitors Ought to Be. Chapter 3.

Moreover, in order that the visitors may be able to visit others fruitfully, let religious men of the same order be chosen, having zeal for God and for souls according to knowledge, as in Extra, De statu monachorum, In singulis. And in the constitution of Benedict XII, chapter 3, it says: Let the visitors be suitable, solicitous, and discreet in carrying out the office of visitation; and let them observe all the things that are known to have been established in the aforesaid constitutions of the same council and in the other constitutions of the said Honorius, our predecessor. Thus there.

They must also be diligent: De statu monachorum, Attendentes; in Clementines, De censibus, chapter Romana, book 6. In the constitution of lord Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal legate, which begins Cum pridem, it says as follows: First of all, therefore, we will and, under attestation of the strict examination of the last judgment, enjoin upon you visitors, namely, that at all times, and especially during your visitation, in all conduct, life, morals, and discipline, you strive to conduct and bear yourselves so religiously, holily, and honorably that to the rest who are to be visited by you, you may provide the form of all perfection not so much by word as by example, proceeding during the time of visitation in fitting habit, with suitable household and horses, and and respectable, not superfluous; each of you should be content with a chaplain and a servant, and with three horses; a moderate meal should suffice for you, without murmuring. These are his words.

Moreover, they ought to be gentle, not cruel: 10, q. 3, Cavendum. For this office mature men should be chosen, and men experienced in many matters, not novices, masters before they have been disciples: 16, q. 1, Si clericatus; dist. 61, Miserum. Yet I do not mean by this that mature young men should not be preferred to dissolute old men, since men are deservedly called priests, that is, elders, by wisdom, not by age: dist. 84, Porro; provided that men gray-haired in character are appointed as visitors. What this gray hair is, Job 28 says: “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to depart from evil is understanding”: 26, q. 2, Qui sine. And prelates, because of their honor, are also called elders: dist. 21, Cleros post me.

Let the visitor be, through humility, a companion to the good; but toward the obstinate and those who despise discipline let him display the severity of his authority, because it is harmful to governance if prelates show excessive humility toward subjects: dist. 86, Quando. Yet this severity must be tempered with kindness: dist. 45, Disciplina, and c. Sunt. Therefore let him always appoint from among the fathers, if it can be done, the better men for this office, who know and are able to give counsel to individuals in their needs and cases, and who first do in their own communities what they attempt in those of others.

For thus our fathers said in chapter 5 of the sixth provincial chapter: “Visitors appointed by the sacred provincial chapter shall first and before all else visit and reform themselves and their own monasteries subject to them, lest, when they direct their eyes to the reform of others, the sick murmur and say, ‘Physician, heal yourself,’ Luke 4. Therefore let them begin first with themselves; then let them visit and reform the other monasteries committed to them, of both monks and nuns, with all the diligence they can.” To this pertains De censibus, Romana, book 6; and 3, q. 7, Iudicet, and the two following chapters; dist. 25, Primum; dist. 61, In sacerdotibus; dist. 83, Nemo recte.

No one rightly assumes the role of an admonisher unless he condemns errors by his own deeds and demonstrates love of innocence by his conduct. These are his words. Therefore let the visitors take care first to visit themselves, and so proceed to the correction of others. For it is written, Job 5: “Visiting your own appearance, you will not sin.” For he who neglects himself cannot amend another, as the Lord says in Luke 6: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit.”

III

Lastly, that visitors should have zeal for God and for souls. Chapter 4.

Finally, the visitors themselves must be zealous, in accordance with knowledge, for the salvation of those to be visited, so that they do not carry out their office negligently and merely in passing, lest, with the lazy servant, they be judged useless by the sentence of damnation. And let them have zeal for regular discipline and for the constitutions of the fathers, knowing without doubt that they will be abundantly rewarded for their labors by the giver of all good things. Let them carry out the office of visitation committed to them as if the care of all whom they visit belonged to them alone.

Yet their zeal should be discreet, lest, God forbid, if they correct sinners indiscreetly, they themselves incur a graver fault: 24, q. 3, Non imperpetuum. And where they find anything worthy of correction, let them correct it not from love of vengeance nor from hatred, but from zeal for justice: 23, q. 4, § last. And the just and holy are indignant against sinners not with hatred but with zeal for discipline: dist. 45, Vera iusticia. Nor should they be remiss where fault has deserved discipline, because if they let the faults of offenders go unpunished, they sin gravely: 11, q. 3, Si is; 23, q. 5, Qui viciis. And a prelate who does not correct crimes is called not a prelate but a shameless dog: dist. 83, Nemo. He bears the guilt of the doer who, when he is able to correct, neglects to amend: dist. 86, Culpam; dist. 83, Error. And not to correct the wicked but to foster them is to kill them: 23, q. 5, Qui viciis; dist. 45, Sed illud. And it is not charity but sickness if evil morals are not corrected: 23, q. 5, Non putes. Yet correction itself

and with admonitors; let no one assume the role unless by his actions he condemns errors and shows love of innocence in his conduct. Thus there. Therefore let visitors strive first to visit themselves, and so proceed to the correction of others. For it is written in Job 5: “Visiting your appearance, you will not sin.” For he who neglects himself cannot amend another, as the Lord says in Luke 6: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit.”

That visitors should have zeal for God and souls. Chapter 4.

Finally, the visitors themselves ought to be zealous, according to knowledge, for the salvation of those to be visited, so that they do not carry out their office negligently and perfunctorily, lest they be judged useless under the sentence of condemnation with the lazy servant. And let them have zeal for regular discipline and for the constitutions of the fathers, knowing that without doubt they will be abundantly rewarded for their labors by the giver of all good things. Let them perform the office of visitation entrusted to them as if the care of all whom they visit belonged to them alone. Yet their zeal itself should be discreet, lest, which God forbid, if they correct offenders indiscreetly, they themselves incur a graver fault. 24, q. 3, Non impetu. And where they find anything worthy of correction, let them correct it not from love of vengeance nor from hatred, but from zeal for justice. 23, q. 4, § last. And the just and holy are indeed indignant at sinners not from hatred, but from zeal for discipline. 45, dist., Vera iusticia. Nor should they be lax where a fault has deserved discipline, because if they let the faults of delinquents go unpunished, they sin gravely. 11, q. 3, Si is; 23, q. 5, Qui vices. And a prelate who does not correct crimes is called not a prelate but a shameless dog. 83, dist., Nemo. He who neglects to amend when he is able to correct has the guilt of the doer. 86, dist., Culpam; 83, dist., Error. And not to correct the wicked but to foster them is to kill them. 23, q. 5, Qui vices; 45, dist., Sed illud. And it is not charity but languor if evil habits are not corrected. 23, q. 5, Non putes. And yet correction itself must not be indiscreet, but, as blessed Gregory says in the Moralia, one judging justly, holding a balance in his hand, should carry justice and mercy in each scale. 45, dist., Omnis. For excessive harshness in rebuking receives neither correction nor salvation. Ibid., Cum beatus; and c. Disciplina. Therefore let zeal not be judged indiscreet, but let it be tempered with mercy and gentleness.

That visitors should be discreet in inquiries. Chapter 5.

Those who are appointed as visitors should also be wisely discreet, imbued with the divine Scriptures, and experienced in this sort of business either in themselves or in others, so that they may not rashly believe things not to be believed, or shamelessly conceal things that ought to be believed. For both are evil. For he who believes quickly is light of heart. Ecclesiasticus 19. And we ought not quickly believe evil things about others. 86, dist., Si quid. And evil things about one’s neighbor must first be proved before they are believed. 2, q. 1, Deus; and 3, q. 8, Iudicet; 11, q. 3, In cunctis and c. Quamvis. For it is written in Ecclesiasticus 19: “Do not believe every word.” 11, q. 3, Non solum per quod. Yet to be willing to believe no one belongs to a shameless man. And indeed the innocent always believes well and judges well of others. Proverbs 14; 22, q. 4, Innocens. Therefore let visitors be discreet and prudent, so that, considering the zeal, life, and merit of those making depositions, they may be able to know whom they ought to believe. For witnesses are to be weighed according to trustworthiness, dignity, and seriousness of conduct. 4, q. 3, § Item in testibus, and throughout there. Therefore, as far as can be done, visitors ought diligently to examine the intentions, motives, and causes of those making depositions, lest perhaps they are moved by no just reason. Finally, our fathers established the following on this matter: Visitors should be especially zealous for religion, mature in morals and discreet, and also very solicitous and circumspect in carrying out the act of their visitation. And a little later it is added: But visitors should not readily believe every spirit, 1 John 4, nor condemn anyone on suspicion alone or on the deposition of one witness. Manifest matters, however, do not require accusation. 2, q. 1, Qualetarius, § In manifestis, and the following c. I judge him not a lover of charity but fraudulent who reveals the hidden crime of a brother for the sake of defamation or revenge. 5, q. 5, Qui ambulat; 6, q. 1, Summa. “Crime” can be understood not only as mortal offense, but also as every venial one. 25, dist., Unum orarium, § Nunc autem. In serious matters, however, and those concerning reputation, diligent inquiry should be made; but before just proof, except in manifest cases, let no one be judged or condemned. 30, q. 5, Nullum ante veram, and the following c. And in such matters two or three testimonies must be brought forward. 2, q. 5, c. 1 and c. Placuit. Therefore visitors should be cautious in judging such secret matters, to avoid scandal, unless the person has been convicted or has confessed freely. 2, q. 1, Nos vero quemquam, and the following c., Nomen presbyteri, and the following c. For if the accuser fails in proof, he ought to be punished with the penalty of retaliation. Extra, De calumniatoribus, c. 1; 2, q. 3, Calumniator, and the following c.; q. 8, Qui crimen; 3, q. 10, Eos and the following c. It must also be guarded against that matters which have been corrected and punished should be brought up again. Extra, De accusationibus, c. De his; and 2, q. 1, Prohibentur; 23, q. 4, Si illic. Thus also the holy fathers established: Let each one beware that he not disturb the minds of the brothers or of their fathers with beginnings. Moreover, if any secrets have been revealed to the visitors themselves, let them beware of bringing them into public. 2, q. 1, Si peccaverit; 6, q. 2, Episcopus si clerico, c. Placuit. And concerning hidden matters one must not inquire too curiously. Extra, De accusationibus, Qualiter iii. Yet concerning manifest matters, as I said above, the clamor of an accuser is not necessary. Same title, c. Evidentia. If they perceive that some matters have not been properly proposed, let them act as prudent men, and, insofar as it can be done while preserving the truth,

They should not readily believe, even if belief is required; yet those things whose intention is unknown should be interpreted in the better sense, since we ought to presume good rather than evil. De regulis iuris, c. Esto te. And in such matters the intention of the one giving testimony is to be weighed rather than the words. For if someone sets forth true things from an evil intention, the intention makes the good act evil. 23, q. 5, Cum minister.

Let the visitors be cautious, and especially discreet, in examining the excesses of prelates, who, since they have to correct the sins of others, frequently incur the hatred of many and suffer plots. Extra, De accusationibus, c. Qualiter, II. In all things let them always act so that they do not lose the form of charity. For correction must be made according to each person’s rank and with the peace of the Church preserved. 23, q. 4, Ecce, and c. Quisquis, c. Quidam, c. Cum quisque, c. Ipsa pietas, c. Quid faciet circa me.

Likewise, correction must be made with the intention of healing, not of raging. 86 dist., Odio; 23, q. 4, Ita plane circa me. And not from hatred but from charity. Extra, De accusationibus, c. Qualiter, II; 24, q. 3, Corripiantur. And sometimes it should have more gentleness than severity. 45 dist., Qui sincera, and c. Licet, because one gently chastised shows reverence for the one who chastises. c. Cum beatus Paulus; 12, q. 2, Fraternitas; 24, q. 3, Corripiantur.

These and other testimonies of discretion, the mother of virtues, the visitors ought not to omit, so that they may proceed worthily and justly.

The Form of the Oath Which Visitors Once Used to Present to the Presidents. Chapter 6.

Formerly the presidents, not only in Mainz but also in other provinces, used to require from the visitors an oath concerning the diligent fulfillment of their office. In our times, however, this is not done, nor do I judge it useful or necessary, because a man whom the spur of his own conscience does not drive to act diligently is scarcely, or only rarely, compelled by another’s command. Yet I wished to insert here the form of the oath, so that when the oath is read, what is to be done may be considered.

The form of such an oath, which I found in old books, follows thus:

I, Brother N., abbot of such-and-such monastery, appointed as visitor of the diocese of N. with respect to the monasteries of our order by the reverend fathers in Christ, the lord presidents of the provincial chapter recently celebrated in the monastery of N., swear by these holy Gospels of God that I will carry out the office of visitation entrusted to me faithfully and diligently, according to my powers, in accordance with the Rule of Saint Benedict and the decrees of the holy fathers, setting aside love, hatred, favor, and every other disordered affection. So help me God and these holy Gospels. Those absent used to give this oath; those present, however, swore in chapter before the lord presidents. But neither now seems necessary.

On the Power and Authority of Visitors. Chapter 7.

They have it from the apostolic see, as in Extra, De statu monachorum, c. In singulis, where it is said: “Let religious and circumspect persons also be appointed in the same chapter, who, according to the form prescribed for them, shall take care to visit, in our stead, the several abbeys of that kingdom or province, not only of monks but also of nuns.” “In our stead,” it says, so that, when the visitor’s authority is considered, none of those to be visited may dare to rebel. Their authority is more fully noted by the Abbot on the same chapter and the final chapter of De statu monachorum.

Yet their power is limited, as in the same c. In singulis, because they cannot depose the rector of a place from his office without a special mandate. Therefore, if they see that he must be removed altogether, let them report this to his own bishop, so that he may see to removing him; but if he does not do so, let the visitors refer this to the judgment of the apostolic see. Those exempt, however, are to be reported directly to the lord pope. The visitors should also have monks corrected by the abbot of the place, as in the same title, c. Ea quae. But those whom they find contumacious and rebellious, according to the measure of the fault, let them strike with regular censure in the place of the lord pope, without [unclear].

without distinction of persons, not sparing rebels because of their obstinacy or the power of their friends, but rather casting the diseased sheep out of the fold, lest it infect the healthy sheep. Nor is there to be an appeal from correction: De officio ordinarii, c. Licet; and De appellatione, Ad nostram; and c. Reprehensibilis, and c. Cum speciali. Understand this unless the one correcting has exceeded due measure. 23, q. 4, Qui peccat.

Visitors, therefore, according to the decree of Honorius III, in c. Ea quae, if they find monks delinquent, should command the abbots of the places to correct them, as is said in the aforesaid constitution in these words: But if abbots are found negligent in making corrections according to the visitors' command and the regular statutes, either in themselves or in their monks, let them be proclaimed and rebuked, and let them be punished publicly in the general chapter, so that their punishment may be an example to others. And note according to what is said there: visitation of this kind ought to be carried out plainly and without the noise of judicial proceedings, De accusationibus, Olim; because regulars are readily removed from their administrations, De simonia, c. Per tuas; and therefore judicial order is not always to be observed in inquisitions of this kind concerning regulars, De accusationibus, c. Qualiter, II, and there at the end. And visitors should diligently inquire into the condition of monasteries and regular observances, and should correct and reform, both in spiritual and in temporal matters, what they see should be corrected.

But it is asked whether the bishop of the place can visit the monasteries of his diocese. The answer is that he can, as in c. In singulis, § Porro. He can visit them, but he ought not bring secular persons in with him, as Hostiensis notes on the same title in the gloss. For the visitation which the visitors carry out does not remove the bishop's jurisdiction, as is noted in the same c. In singulis. Custom, however, holds otherwise, because bishops also quite often commit their own duties to abbots.

Likewise, concerning the authority of visitors, the fathers in provincial chapters also established many things. Hence c. 1 says: Visitors can make statutes imposing penalties more severe than those appointed in the constitution, Ne in agro, against disorderly monks or those forgetful of their profession, etc. Likewise c. 6, § Decretum, says thus: Where they do not find disciplines effective for reform, let them institute new ceremonies according to the canonical sanctions and the statutes of the provincial chapter, which those visited are bound to observe without any contradiction. If it seems necessary to the visitors, they can bind those to be visited by a bodily oath to tell the truth, as in the constitution of Lord Nicholas, Chuf. le., c. 3; and these matters must be discussed in their proper place. In c. 15 all those to be visited are commanded to receive their visitors with all reverence and humility and to treat them charitably, and diligently to heed and observe their admonitions and ordinances. The visitors themselves also have authority to impose penalties greater than those expressly set out in the constitutions, and to compel rebels, by ecclesiastical censure, to obey their commands.

But many impediments sometimes occur in connection with visitations of monasteries. For sometimes the monks themselves and abbots maliciously impede them by themselves; sometimes through the ordinary bishops; sometimes through princes; and frequently through their relatives, friends, and supporters. What should be done in these cases, if they occur, I shall try to show from the statutes of the fathers. In c. 15, which was celebrated second at Seligenstadt, we read the statute:

Lest so salutary an office of visitation be impeded by any contrived device or pretext, we decree that all and individual abbots, provosts, priors, and their professed monks who refuse or contradict their visitors, and those rebels and disobedient persons themselves, and those who impede the office of visitation by nod, word, deed, or writing, or who cause, order, procure, or by any device arrange that it be impeded by their friends, noble or ignoble, or by any persons subordinate to them, whether by themselves or through another or others, directly or indirectly, or who attempt [unclear]

...attempting to prevent their visitors from being able to exercise this office of theirs freely and peacefully: we will that they incur the sentence of excommunication by the very fact; and the visitors themselves are bound to publish that same sentence of excommunication against them and duly commit it to execution.

But if the visitors cannot carry out the foregoing, in chapter 21, celebrated fourth at Nuremberg, it was thus established: that the visitors themselves should denounce the disobedient and contumacious persons to one of the nearer presidents, who should proceed against them with appropriate legal remedies by apostolic authority. And in chapter 23 what follows was established: We also strictly forbid anyone henceforth, by himself or through others, in any way to arrange with diocesan bishops, princes, or any other temporal lords whatsoever, that the visitors should not be admitted; nor may he claim in any way that the visitors themselves are not to be admitted without the permission of the local ordinaries, since, being directed by apostolic authority, they do not need it, under penalty of thirty Rhenish florins, to be paid irrecoverably to the chapter as often as any abbot or any of the other rectors shall have acted to the contrary.

But this penalty seems to be one to be imposed on the rectors of monasteries, without removing the foregoing provision that they are to be compelled to obedience by ecclesiastical censure.

If a bishop wishes to conduct visitation with us. Chapter 9.

It is sometimes customary for it to happen that the ordinary bishops of places wish to visit monasteries with us; whether they are to be admitted in this way or not is often doubted. To resolve this scruple, one must consider that the impulse of bishops to visit monasteries with the visitors of the order has two reasons from which it arises. Either they do this from zeal for discipline, or from a contrivance of malice. If for the first reason, if their zeal is known and there is so great a necessity of visiting the monastery, they can be admitted; but only in their own person, because laymen should by no means be present at a visitation unless it is very necessary.

...can visit even if the bishops have not been negligent.

How visitors are to be received and treated; on the time for visiting monasteries, to be fixed by the presidents. Chapter 11.

The time is to be fixed for the visitors by the presidents themselves, as is said in Constitution 12 of Benedict, chapter 2. Nevertheless, we find it prescribed in the more ancient statutes of the fathers that, within a year from the time of the chapter that has been celebrated, they are to fulfill the office of the visitation committed to them. It belongs to bishops, however, to visit every year: 10, question 1, Relata, and chapter Decrevimus. Concerning the time of visitation, in chapter 7, celebrated at Bamberg, it was enacted as follows: “Let the visitors faithfully complete within a year the office of visitation enjoined upon them.” Thus there.

And how often ought visitation to be made? It seems that every year, as in Extra, De statu monachorum, Attendentes, in the Clementines. On this Franciscus de Zabarella frames the following question: “I ask,” he says, “concerning the point where it says that visitation is to be made every year: is it enough that it be made at the end of the first year and at the beginning of the second?” The gloss on whether that is enough refers to the note on the same title, chapter In singulis, where it is concluded that it is not, because in that way, in the case of chapter In singulis, it could be deferred up to six years, to the prejudice of the monastery, and it would not satisfy the law requiring that it be done from three years to three years. Stephen says the same, because visitation is made for correcting offenses already committed, not for offenses yet to be committed. Therefore, if the first was sufficient, the second will have nothing to correct. Paul says the same, because if this were done at the end of the first year and at the beginning of the second, there would not be one year between the first and the second, but two years. Hence it seems that they ought to stand at equal intervals, by the argument from De consanguinitate, Quod dilectio, as Paul thinks. This is precisely true with respect to chapter In singulis, because the text there says “from three years to three years.” Thus Franciscus de Zabarella on the said chapter.

From these things it seems one must say that the visitation ought to correspond to the chapter, so that as often as the chapter is celebrated, so often too the visitation is celebrated. We also have this in custom, that we regularly visit from three years to three years. This, however, chapter Attendentes, seems to concern only nuns, whom bishops are no less ordered to visit.

Can a visitation be repeated? The answer is yes, if there is a reasonable cause. On this matter, in chapter 17, celebrated at Nuremberg for the third time, the fathers decreed as follows: “We enact that after the visitors have once visited some monastery and received procuration from the same, if they judge, for the richer discipline of regular observance, that it is expedient, they may exercise the office of visitation again, as often as it seems useful to them, by authority of the chapter. They are also to be received as true visitors, yet without exaction of procuration.” Franciscus de Zabarella says the same in the said chapter Attendentes, question 10: that visitation is to be made as often as there is need. From all these things I conclude that the visitation must be completed in the first year from the time of the chapter that has been celebrated, and afterward may be repeated as often as there is need, but that procuration should not be received except within a three-year period.

How visitors are to be received and treated in monasteries. Chapter 12.

When, therefore, they come to some monastery for the sake of visitation, let them be received as visitors and be led to prayer; if they are not neighbors and often received, let their feet be washed, and let them be treated with charity. In conventual places, let the abbot of the house yield place and acknowledge them; let him not take it ill if he has others set over him: 2, question 6, Qui scit. Yet the abbot himself, in his usual manner, is to give the blessing everywhere, not the visitors. For this has been enacted in several chapters: that visitors are to be received with honor and reverence, and treated in all things with charity, as is fitting.

With how many horses visitors ought to come. Chapter 13.

In the first two chapters it was enacted that none of the visitors should bring with him more than twelve mounts...

would dare to bring them, under the penalty contained in the same statutes; therefore at that time the visitors, and also those coming to the chapter, were permitted to bring twelve mounts with them. Then, in the third chapter, which was celebrated at Fulda, it was enacted that no visitor should bring more than six mounts with him. But Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal legate, in his form of visitation, which he handed over to the visitors, orders that each visitor should be content with a chaplain and a servant, with three horses. Nevertheless, in the same constitutions of lord Nicholas, cardinal, he commands the visitors themselves to conduct themselves properly and to have respectable servants, so that they may not be burdensome to those visited. In chapter 15, celebrated second at Seligenstadt, it stands thus: Let the visitors themselves also have an honorable household and retinue, and let each of them be content with a number of four, unless a reasonable cause demands more.

How long visitors should remain in one monastery. Chapter 14.

Therefore, lest visitors become burdensome in expenses to those whom they visit, they should take care to dispatch their business as quickly as they can; and, as the fathers have enacted, they should not stay more than three or four days in one place visited by them, unless there is evident necessity. But if such matters should occur as demand delays of a longer time, they should take care to dispatch their business in such a way that they prove in all things that they seek not themselves, but God and the peace of those visited. Let the visitors also advise their servants to conduct themselves honorably and without murmuring in all things.

Those visited are bound diligently to guard the property and horses of the visitors. Chapter 15.

Since frauds and deceits are sometimes accustomed to occur against the visitors themselves among those especially who hate the one correcting them, with malicious subordinates or wicked persons plotting at the gate, lest the malicious should gain advantage from their own dishonesty, the fathers, in chapter 5, celebrated first at Wurzburg, established as follows. This sacred chapter has decreed and enacted that when visitors come to some monastery for the sake of visitation, the abbot and convent of that monastery shall have the horses and property of the visitors guarded with the greatest diligence. But if anything from their goods or property should happen to be lost or taken away, before all else the abbot and convent of that monastery shall without any contradiction pay the value of the lost goods or property to those visitors without delay. And nevertheless such negligence shall be punished in chapter at the judgment of the presidents. This was also often enacted afterward in other chapters.

On the penalty for visitors negligent in visiting at the proper time. Chapter 16.

Since the increase of holy religion and regular observance arises in no small measure from frequent and diligently conducted visitations, lest so salutary an institution of the fathers be destroyed by the sluggishness of negligent visitors, since where the governance of discipline is despised, it remains that religion suffers shipwreck, as in De statu monachorum, Attendentes, in the Clementines, the fathers in nearly all chapters celebrated up to now have imposed penalties on visitors if they neglected their office. And first, in the constitution of Benedict XII, chapter 3, on visitors, it is said as follows: But if those visitors neglect to execute their office, we will that by the very fact they incur the penalties incurred by those who do not come to the provincial chapter without having a canonical impediment. And in chapters 4 and 5 and certain others it was enacted as follows: This sacred chapter has further decreed that those deputed to visit, if they neglect the time appointed for them, namely within the year, shall pay the penalty like those who neglect to come to chapter, namely thirty Rhenish florins, with moderation and just assessment reserved to the judgment of the presidents in the provincial chapter. And in chapter 19, celebrated second at Bamberg, it was enacted that all visitors who their visitations [unclear]

as it has been enjoined upon them, they shall be bound, as a penalty, to pay three florins to the chapter for each monastery not visited, especially in the case of monasteries of men, unless they have a legitimate cause excusing them. The same was likewise laid down in chapter 20 and in chapter 21. Besides these things, however, the presidents, whenever it seems necessary to them, may also impose other penalties. Concerning these matters also the constitution of Honorius III, Extra, De statu monachorum, chapter Eaque, speaks thus: “Let the succeeding visitors diligently investigate the traces of the previous visitors, and let them report their negligences and excesses to the following general chapter, so that, according to their fault, they may publicly receive the penalty due.”

If it should happen that the visitors are robbed on the way while carrying out their office. Chapter 17.

Finally, if, which God forbid, visitors of this kind, while going to fulfill their office, should happen to be robbed on the way or suffer loss, the provincial chapter shall make satisfaction for such loss as is fitting, as was laid down in the fifth chapter held at Würzburg.

When the visitors first come to some monastery to be visited, how they are to begin. Chapter 18.

Therefore, when the visitors have come to visit some monastery, if it can be done, on that same evening they should summon the abbot and the convent, the monks and professed conversi, to the chapter room; or on the following morning, at the hour they have determined to be suitable. When these have assembled, they themselves should also enter. And when all have taken their seats, one of the visitors should say, “Bless.” When they answer, “The Lord,” he should add these or similar words:

“Venerable father and beloved religious brothers in Christ: if you have read the recess of the last chapter held at N., you have certainly understood that we, though insufficient, have been appointed as visitors for you. But if you have not read the recess, nevertheless we are prepared to fulfill the office enjoined upon us.

Therefore we have come for this reason: that, obedient to the precepts of the chapter according to our ability, we may visit you.

“And we do not doubt that you know that, in the order of visitation, three things are principally to be done. First, the visitors themselves must present themselves to those to be visited in the chapter room, make known their authority to visit, and first offer prayer according to the custom of the order, and an exhortation according to the character of the time and of the persons: De statu monachorum, Attendentes, in the Clementines, and in the constitution of the provincial chapter, and in the constitution Nimis carum.

“Second, there must be a diligent examination of those to be visited, and an inquiry into the conduct and state of both parties: 10, q. 1, Episcopum, and q. 3, Cavendum; De statu monachorum, chapter Eaque.

“Third, there must be a final conclusion and the due correction of the guilty: chapter In singulis.

“Therefore, since even in the smallest matters divine help must always be implored, as blessed Dionysius says in the fourth chapter of On the Divine Names, and since in spiritual matters especially one must begin from prayer, it is fitting that we too observe the commands of such teaching, and not pass over the praiseworthy custom of the order. Let us therefore pray.”

And, rising, let them read alternately the psalm Ad te levavi oculos meos:

“To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens. Behold, as the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant are on the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes on the Lord our God, until he have mercy on us. Have mercy on us, O Lord, have mercy on us, for we are greatly filled with contempt. For our soul is greatly filled: a reproach to the prosperous and contempt to the proud. Glory be to the Father. As it was. Kyrie eleison. Christe eleison. Kyrie eleison. Our Father.”

According to the season, let them kneel. One of the visitors says:

“And lead us not into temptation. Save your servants. Send them help, O Lord, from the holy place. Be to us, O Lord, a tower of strength. O Lord God of hosts, convert us. O Lord, hear my prayer. The Lord be with you. And with your spirit.”

[unclear] of heavenly help, that they may seek you with their whole heart, and and may deserve to obtain what they worthily ask.

Direct our actions, we ask, O Lord, by your inspiration, and further them by your help, so that every work of ours may always begin from you and, once begun, may be completed through you.

O God, who taught the hearts of the faithful by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, grant us, in that same Spirit, to discern what is right and always to rejoice in his consolation. Through Christ our Lord.

After this, the visitor is to give an exhortation. Chapter 19.

Note that the visitation ought not to begin with examination or correction, but with exhortation, as in De statu monachorum, Attendentes, in the Clementines, and as Francis Zabarella also notes on the same chapter, 18, question 2, Visitandi, and chapter Semel. This is also contained in the statutes of the chapter in this form: Then one of the visitors shall give to those being visited an exhortatory address on discipline, on fraternal charity, on peace, on spiritual progress, on perseverance, and on the other virtues, according to the requirements of the persons or of the time.

How necessary depositions are to be made. Chapter 20.

When the exhortation has been completed, the visitor shall then instruct those being visited how and in what manner they ought to conduct themselves in their depositions; and he shall say in order as follows:

Beloved brothers, although you who have often been visited are not ignorant of the form of the visitation itself, nevertheless, for the sake of those who have more rarely been present at a visitation, I shall briefly set forth the method and form in which you ought to conduct yourselves in your depositions. First, we exhort you, all and singly, that, just as visitation was established for this purpose, that vices may be rooted out and virtues introduced, so each person should direct his intention in making proclamations to its proper end. Likewise, each person should make deposition out of charity, if he has seen anything that necessarily must be corrected, and not out of hatred, which God forbid, nor out of aversion, for this would be a grave sin. Likewise, each person should strive to observe due and honorable measure in depositions of this kind. Likewise, no one should bring up again matters that have worthily been punished. Likewise, no one, making much of those small matters that are corrected daily, should depose them as though they had been reserved for us to cause greater confusion, unless they were such that they seemed worthy of correction. Likewise, each of you should keep before his eyes zeal for God and for souls, and should conceal none of those matters that ought to be brought to light.

And when instruction has been given in this way, a place suitable for examination shall be assigned to them; the brothers shall approach it in order, beginning with the prior down to the last one established in holy orders.

On whether an oath should or should not be required from those being visited. Chapter 21.

But it is rightly asked whether those being visited should be bound by oath to speak and to answer the truth concerning the questions put to them. On this point it should be known that, as I have found in the old statutes, including those of other provinces of the order, where it seemed necessary an oath was required from those being visited. This still seems to me quite reasonable, especially if the monks have conspired, or made an agreement, or maliciously concealed the truth. And I judge that this statute, which I approve, should be strengthened.

Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal legate, writes among other things as follows to the visitors of the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg: But because among many people words of exhortation have little effect unless a coercive penal censure is also added, therefore in the monasteries or places that you visit at that time, after the act of salutary exhortation, and after receiving from all a bodily oath to speak the truth in their examination, you shall proceed according to the tenor of the commission delivered to you in other letters.

Likewise, I have found the contrary in the statutes of the chapter. For in the sixth chapter, held at Erfurt, the statute is read as follows: It also pleased the fathers that, without requiring an oath, after the word of God has first been set forth, the visitors themselves should complete their act. This same thing, in the following chapter held at Bamberg,

...it was established. Likewise also in certain other chapters. What then? If he requires an oath contrary to the statutes of the fathers, he commits a fault of disobedience; if it is not to be required, why did the legate of the apostolic see, a cardinal and distinguished doctor, order it to be required? Can it both be required and not required? Clearly, I think so. Where it is necessary and useful, it can be required; nevertheless it ought not to be required lightly. And let him have at hand the form of such an oath, as I have also found in the older institutions of the fathers and have taken care to insert here, so that if it should be necessary there may be no need for a long inquiry.

The form of the oath and the manner of swearing, with the hand placed upon the text of the Gospel, beginning here:

O Brother M., I swear by these holy Gospels of God that concerning all matters about which I shall be questioned by you, or by any one of you, generally or specially, I wish to tell the truth; and also that all things which I know to require reform, and which are necessary for the full reform of this monastery, according to my knowledge, I will faithfully disclose to you. So help me God and these holy Gospels of God.

While saying this he shall place his hands upon the Gospel according to Luke.

At that time, while Jesus was speaking to the crowds, a certain woman, lifting up her voice, said to him: Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you. But he said: Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it. Amen.

Of examination. Chapter 23.

When the visitors are prepared for the examination and inquiry and are seated in the place assigned, let them exercise great diligence in inquiries of this kind, asking into each necessary matter. And if anything worthy of correction has been disclosed, let it be marked down on a schedule by one of the visitors; let him also guard it carefully, lest it ever come into anyone else's hands. And concerning conspiracies, pacts, and oaths

let them inquire first, lest perhaps the abbot has presumed upon any such thing against the visitation. And if they find any, let them annul them, as in Extra, De accusationibus, chapter Olim.

Concerning general matters, the following, or at least some of them, can be asked.

First, let them ask about general matters as it seems good to them.

Whether the abbot has extorted an oath from the monks about keeping the truth silent, or has otherwise forbidden them to report anything.

Item, whether all are professed, and how.

Item, whether any have been received simoniacally. And if so, what has been done with the simoniacal goods.

Item, whether they observe true obedience to the abbot and to their superiors according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Item, whether any or all of them are proprietors.

Item, whether any are fornicators, and who.

Item, whether they are chaste, as befits religious.

Item, whether the healthy eat meat; whether all do, or some; where, when, and how often.

Item, whether they keep silence in the four prohibited places, and whether they do the same during the night hours or not.

Item, whether they observe the fasts of the Church and of the Rule, as they are bound to do.

Item, whether there is always reading at table for those who are eating.

Item, whether all eat together in one refectory.

Item, whether all sleep together in one place, and whether they are regularly clothed and girded.

Item, whether they use garments or bed-linens made of linen.

Item, whether they sleep on feather beds or mats.

Item, concerning habit and tonsure, they can be inspected and questioned.

Item, whether they continually wear the monastic habit.

Item, whether they go about outside the enclosure of the monastery without the permission of their superiors.

Likewise, let inquiry be made about the state of the temporal goods, what it is like and how each item is spent.

These and similar matters may be inquired into generally, as it shall seem expedient to the discreet visitors.

Inquiries concerning the divine office should also be made thus, or in a similar way.

First, at what time do they rise for Matins?

Likewise, whether they sing Matins and all the other Hours, or only some of them?

Likewise, at what time do they rise for Prime?

Likewise, at what time do they perform the other Hours?

Likewise, whether they discharge the Hours deliberately and religiously, as is fitting?

Likewise, how often the chapter of faults is held in the week?

Likewise, how faults are examined there?

Likewise, whether all diligently attend the work of God?

Likewise, whether the sacred vestments, the ecclesiastical ornaments, the books, chalices, and other things are handled cleanly?

Likewise, how many Masses are celebrated daily?

Likewise, whether they sing the high Mass every day?

Likewise, how often the brothers celebrate in the week?

Likewise, whether they always confess before Mass?

Likewise, whether the Rule is read to them and expounded according to the statutes of the fathers?

And many other things in this manner.

Questions concerning abbots, provosts, or priors, if they are the supreme rulers of monasteries. Greater diligence must be applied in inquiring about abbots and their way of life, since by their merit the condition of monasteries is often led in either direction. Many things indeed occur for inquiry, but, with a few of the greater matters indicated, let the visitors themselves investigate the rest.

First, therefore, let inquiry be made whether he has zeal for God and for souls, as befits a pastor?

Likewise, whether he diligently visits the choir, the divine services, and the conventual places?

Likewise, whether he presides in person over the chapter of faults, and how often?

Likewise, whether he corrects offenders without respect of persons?

Likewise, whether he shows himself to the brothers as exemplary and imitable in all good things?

Likewise, whether he often wanders outside the monastery without reasonable cause?

Likewise, whether he takes excessive riding retinues with him?

Likewise, whether he has associates who are suspect or harmful to the monastery?

Likewise, whether he has any suspect familiarities with women?

Likewise, whether he has been in any way marked by a charge of incontinence?

Likewise, whether he admits women into the monastery, and what kind?

Likewise, whether he diligently preserves the temporal goods?

Likewise, whether he is too intent on cares for temporal affairs?

Likewise, whether he provides the brothers with necessities according to the Rule?

Likewise, whether he burdens the monastery with debts?

Likewise, whether he alienates the immovable goods of the monastery?

Likewise, whether he uses the counsel of the convent in matters to be done according to the Rule, or not?

Likewise, if he has monasteries subject to him, whether he visits them?

Likewise, whether he has had the recesses of the chapter published in the convent?

Likewise, whether he has observed the charter of the most recent visitation?

Likewise, whether he duly observes the Rule in all things, as is fitting?

And many things similar to these may be inquired into according as there is need; to express them all here would be tedious.

Likewise, questions concerning the other officials and brothers.

As for the other officials, the questions must be formed according to need, namely:

Whether there is a prior; who he is, what kind of man, and of what importance?

Likewise, whether he is continually in the convent?

Likewise, whether he is for the convent in providing necessities?

Likewise, whether he is zealous for discipline according to the statutes of the fathers?

Likewise, whether he gives the brothers an example of good conduct?

Likewise, whether he corrects offenders according to the Rule?

Likewise, whether he diligently causes the other regular statutes to be observed?

Likewise, whether he is diligent in the office entrusted to him?

Concerning the cellarer: who he is and what kind of man?

Whether he diligently fulfills his office?

Whether he duly visits the divine services and conventual duties when he is otherwise free?

Whether he diligently disposes necessities for the brothers according to the Rule?

Whether he is humble, good, and exemplary before outsiders?

How often he renders an accounting to the abbots for receipts and expenditures?

Likewise, whether he reverently obeys the abbot's commands in all things?

Likewise, whether he is wasteful and a squanderer of the monastery's goods?

Whether he is too anxious about temporal affairs?

Likewise, whether he diligently observes the Rule in fasts, vigils, and so forth?

As for the other brothers, the visitors shall inquire according to what seems opportune to them: concerning mutual charity, peace, obedience, continence, private property, and so forth.

Where, however, the abbot is diligent in correcting, less inquiry will be made about the simple brothers.

Lastly, after all have been examined, let the abbot himself also be examined, in case perhaps he wishes to say anything. And the greater articles concerning which the brothers have made depositions should be put before him; let him be advised seriously to amend. But if there is something of such a kind that it ought not to pass without correction, and he denies it, the testimonies of those making deposition must be examined more carefully, until the truth appears more clearly. Nevertheless, let disturbances and scandals be guarded against.

Concerning the final proclamation of each one, after the examination has been begun according to custom in chapter. Chapter 24.

When it shall seem opportune to the visitors, let all be called together to the chapter place to continue the act of visitation. When they are seated, one of the visitors should say: “Give a blessing.” And when the response has been made, “Lord,” let him add:

Most beloved brothers, there now remains, as you know, the final execution of our visitation; and for carrying it out we ought to give thanks to God.

XV

with God's help, we have come together to carry it out. And we exhort your charity that you also receive charitably the admonitions we make in charity, since we intend to accomplish only what is fitting for our salvation and yours.

And he may add the general depositions or matters seen, for admonition and correction. Then let the conversi, novices, and subdeacons, that is, those not yet constituted in sacred orders, be called to the mat, one after another, or two by two, or certainly those concerning whom such a deposition has been made that they ought deservedly to be proclaimed.

When the one called comes to the mat, let him bow moderately; and let the visitor tell him his faults. He should at once lie prostrate on the ground until he has been ordered to rise.

When those who are not members of chapter have been dealt with and have gone out, let the abbot first be called to the mat, then the prior and the others in order. But while the abbot stands in judgment before the visitors, all the other brothers, out of reverence, ought to stand uncovered until he has again been ordered to sit. And note that the abbot’s faults are to be stated here briefly, and the lesser ones, lest an occasion for contempt be given to the weak. But in private, or before a few of the seniors, let them tell him all necessary things, great together with small, etc.

But they shall impose penances at the discretion of the visitors, with discernment, according to the custom of the daily proclamation. But if anyone there comes to be punished more severely, let the visitors have this done through the abbot, as in Extra, De statu monachorum, Ea quae.

On Making the Final Exhortation. Chapter 25.

After all who are to be proclaimed have been proclaimed, and penance has been enjoined on each, let the visitor make a brief exhortation concerning regular observance, rebuking the general negligences of the brothers; and let him declare how such things are contrary to the rule and harmful to the soul, etc. And the rest in this manner, as seems expedient to them. But at this exhortation other professed monks and conversi who are not members of chapter, who had gone out, may also be recalled and be present, unless something else prevents it.

On the Customary Absolution. Chapter 26.

When these things have been finished according to custom, let all humble themselves for absolution, bending their knees, and let them say, Confiteor, concluding: Pray for me. Let the visitor, standing, say:

May almighty God have mercy on you, through the intercession of blessed Mary and all the saints, and may he forgive you all your sins and lead you to eternal life. Amen.

By the authority of almighty God, and of the ecclesiastical keys granted in this matter to our order, we absolve you from ecclesiastical censures; and we restore you to the communion of the Church and to participation; and we dispense with you and rehabilitate you for the execution of the things to be done. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. And let some psalm to be said be enjoined on each; for conversi, the Lord’s Prayer twice or three times.

When these things have been completed, the visitors may excuse their insufficiency before those visited, and commend themselves to their prayers, as is often done in these or similar words:

Most beloved brothers, we ask you to receive charitably those things that we have said or done here to all, or also in private to individuals; and do not think anything else of us than that we have done all things in charity. Ah, also, I beg you, pardon me for the things said by me; and if I have offended anyone with words, or if I did not speak as I ought, or otherwise than I ought, ascribe it to my lack of skill, not to my will, etc., and such things. And let him add, if there is time: Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.

On Making the Charter of Visitation. Chapter 27.

According to the statutes of the fathers, when the visitation has been completed, the state of the monks visited must be set in order in a charter, in which the necessary articles are to be inserted, in which each one ought to amend himself: first concerning the abbot, then concerning the prior.

XVI

of the prior, the cellarer, and the other officials, and lastly concerning all in general. And he should also command, under penalties and censures if need be, in part or in whole, concerning the observance of the matters inserted. At the end of the charter, moreover, he should command how often in the year it is to be read in the convent, and he should insert the condition of the monasteries in respect to the number of persons and the amount of revenues, or also of debts. Let the charter be sealed with the two seals of the visitors themselves, as testimony for each. And it should be noted that the abbot is bound to make an accounting to his visitors concerning all revenues, according to the statutes of the fathers, as in chapters 1 and 2, and as was established in many other places.

The visitors should have a copy of the charter transcribed by themselves or by the monks visited, not by a layman, who ought not to know the defects of the monks. And they should carry this copy with them, to be sent to the chapter. Let the visitors carefully take heed not to hand over to the abbot the notes of the depositions, lest an occasion for ill-will be given, however zealous he may be; but let them carry them with them, to be revealed to the presiding lords, or certainly, if they do not need them, let them burn them in the fire.

Concerning what should be received from those visited for travel expenses. Chapter 28.

Every abbot and convent visited is bound, according to the decrees of the fathers, to pay his visitors, when they visit, three Rhenish florins for travel expenses, without any contradiction, as in chapter 11 and the three immediately following. Hence in the same place it says as follows: The whole community of the fathers decreed that every abbot visited should be bound to pay the visitors three Rhenish florins for travel expenses, unless the visitors themselves, for some good consideration, wish to act more moderately. Thus there. But let the visitors see that they demand necessities in such a way that they do not hide greed under the appearance of need. For a procuration of this kind ought not to be burdensome, but moderate: 10, q. 3, Cavendum, and 2, c. se. But if they do not visit, they ought to demand nothing, 10, q. 1, Relata.

IVX

That visitors or their attendants should dare to accept any gift or money, offered in any way, from those visited. Chapter 29.

Because gifts make the giver and the receiver turn aside from justice, 11, q. 3, Pauper, and c. Qui rector, it is strictly forbidden to all visitors to accept any gift from those visited, or money offered in any way by anyone, whether by themselves or through their attendants. As is said in Constitution Benedictus XV, chapter De visitatoribus, where it has as follows: Visitors and their attendants should receive no money on an occasion of this kind or in any other way; nor should they themselves, or any one of their people, presume to receive any gift, whatever or of whatever sort it may be, from anyone who offers it, so that they may not seem to seek the things that are their own, but those of Jesus Christ. Hence we establish and ordain that all and each of the visitors of this kind, or their attendants, who, besides the expenses to be provided to them only in food, presume to demand or receive money, even from one willing to give it, or who themselves, or any one of their attendants, presume in any way to receive such gifts, shall be bound within a month to restore twice the amount they received to the church or monastery or other place of that same order or religion from which it was received. Otherwise from that time onward let such visitors, who delay beyond this period in restoring that double amount to them, know that they are suspended from office and benefice until they have made full satisfaction for such double payment to the churches, monasteries, or places thus burdened; no remission, liberality, or grace on the part of those who gave it being of any force for them in this matter. And nevertheless, if it is expedient, let the visitors thus suspended be compelled by the presidents to restore the aforesaid double amount, by apostolic authority, through ecclesiastical censure and by other appropriate remedies, with the obstacle of appeal removed. Thus there.

Therefore let the visitors forbid their chaplains and attendants to accept anything from anyone, on account of visiting, during the time of visitation.

...except for the customary expenses, under a fixed penalty; and if they do not do this, and those persons receive anything, they will not be free from the guilt of prevarication.

That those visited should provide their visitors with safe-conduct. Chapter 30.

If there is need, the abbots and convents that have been visited shall provide their visitors, at their own expense, with safe-conduct from one visited monastery to another to be visited at the visitors’ discretion, as has been established in many provincial chapters.

That visitors should not reveal to anyone the secrets of those visited. Chapter 31.

Let the visitors take care not to presume to reveal to anyone, especially to laypeople, matters entrusted to them, or even discovered by them, in visitations; nor indeed to their brothers or to any familiars whatever. For what each person does not wish to be done to himself, let him not do to another. For he who reveals secrets is fraudulent, 5, question 5, “He who walks.” And in the council of Pope Benedict XII, chapter 3, it says: “And because it proceeds from the virtue of prudence if a way is closed to scandals, we forbid the aforesaid visitors to presume to reveal to others those persons, or their names, who have revealed any secrets to them in visitations, except only when, on account of revelations of this kind, it will be necessary to proceed to the punishment or penalty of someone. But those who reveal such things otherwise are to be punished more or less severely, according as the quality of the deed shall require, at the discretion of the presidents.” This is found there.

This brief form of visitation, drawn from the writings and statutes of the fathers for the direction of myself and those like me when there is need, as best I could, I, brother Johannes, abbot in Sponheim in the diocese of Mainz, have written out and humbly offer to the lord presidents of the provincial chapter, to be examined and corrected. If they approve it as to be observed in visitations, I shall not be deprived of the fruit of my labor; but if they reject it, by subjecting myself patiently and humbly I shall be granted the reward of humility. In the year of the Lord 1490.

C

From the constitutions of Pope Benedict XII concerning visitors. Chapter 3.

Moreover, the visitors who, according to the aforesaid constitution of that general council, shall have been appointed in such provincial chapters, are to be suitable, diligent, and discreet in carrying out the office of their visitation; and they are to observe everything that is known to have been established in the aforesaid constitution of that council and in the other constitution of the said Honorius, our predecessor.

But if those visitors omit to carry these things out, or do so negligently, we will that by that very fact they incur the penalties incurred by those who do not come to the provincial chapter and have no canonical impediment.

And because we desire that the conduct of the aforesaid visitors proceed with complete sincerity, we decree that no one may be the visitor of the visitor appointed to him in the same year.

The aforesaid visitors, or their familiars, shall in no way remain more than two days in a cathedral church, monastic church, monastery, or other place of that order or religion to which they have chosen to turn aside for the sake of visitation, unless evident necessity or some great advantage of the church, monastery, or place of this kind should require a longer stay there by the visitors themselves or by their servants or familiars. But then they shall do this with the counsel of the elders of the aforesaid church, monastery, or place.

Nor shall the visitors or their familiars be burdensome and oppressive to those churches, monasteries, and places visited. They shall not seek sumptuous meals, but with thanksgiving shall receive what has been honestly and suitably provided for them.

And the said visitors and their familiars shall receive no money on this occasion or in any other way; nor shall they themselves, or any of their people, presume to ask for any gift, whatever it may be, or however it may be offered, so that they may not seem to seek the things that are their own, but those of Christ.

We decree and ordain that all and each of such visitors, or their attendants, who, beyond the expenses to be provided to them only in food, presume in any way to demand or receive money, even from one willing to give it, or who themselves, or any of their attendants, similarly presume to receive gifts, shall be bound within one month to restore double what they have received to the church, monastery, or other place of that same order or religion from which it was received. Otherwise, from that time on, such visitors who delay beyond that time in restoring the double amount to them should know that they are suspended from office and benefice, until they have made full satisfaction for this double amount to the churches, monasteries, or places thus burdened, no remission, generosity, or favor from those giving it availing them in this matter. And nevertheless, if it is expedient, those visitors thus suspended shall be compelled by the presidents of the said chapters, and by each of them, to restore the aforesaid double amount, by apostolic authority, through ecclesiastical censure and other suitable remedies, with the obstacle of appeal removed.

And because it proceeds from the virtue of prudence if the way is barred to scandals, we forbid the aforesaid visitors to presume to reveal to others those persons, or their names, who have disclosed any secrets to them in visitations, unless only when, because of such disclosures, it will be necessary to proceed to someone’s punishment or penalty. Otherwise, those who make such revelations are to be punished more or less severely, as the quality of the deed requires, according to the judgment of the same presidents.

There follow, from the decrees, various rubrics concerning the state of monks, which it is sometimes useful to have at hand in visitations.

The conduct of monks ought to be separated from all others, according to the etymology of the name, because he is called “singular.” 16, q. 1, c. 1.

Monks ought not to be in a crowd of the people; for they are called “singular” for this reason, that they ought to avoid the multitude of people. 16, q. 1, Si cupis.

According to the etymology of the name, a monk is to lead a solitary life; let him be content with his own cloister, because just as a fish without water lacks life, so a monk lacks life without the monastery. Therefore let him sit solitary and be silent, because he is dead to the world but lives to God. Let him recognize his name: for monos in Greek is “one” in Latin; achos in Greek is “sad” in Latin. Thus monachus is so called, that is, one and sad. Therefore let him sit sad and attend to his office. 16, q. 1, Placuit communi.

Except in illness, no permission is granted to a monk either to taste or to take meat. But if anyone presumes to act against the rule, let him be subject to confinement and penance for a period of six months. De consecratione, dist. 5, Carnem.

Monks ought to be subject to their abbots with all obedience and devotion. 18, q. 2, Abbates.

No one ought to become a monk in hope of an abbacy. 16, q. 7, Per laicos. See, however, the fine distinction in the gloss in the same place.

A monk cannot make a testament. 19, q. 3, Quia.

When anyone has been made a monk, all the things he had are to be conferred on the monastery; nor can he afterwards hand them over to anyone. 19, q. 3, Praelatum.

A monk is not permitted to make vows without the consent of the abbot; but if he has made a vow, it will have to be broken. 20, q. 4, Monacho.

No one may receive or ordain a monk without the permission of his abbot. 20, q. 4, Monachum.

A monk should never be idle, because every idle person is in desires; rather he should always be engaged either in the offices or in manual labor fitting for his state. Let him love knowledge of the Scriptures, and he will not love the vices of the flesh. Let body and soul tend toward the Lord. Let his senses keep watch; and, not lying open to wandering thoughts, let him do some work, so that the devil may always find him occupied. And many other fine things Jerome says to Rusticus. De consecratione, dist. 5, Nunquam.

XIX

Monks may neither make women their co-mothers, nor have familiarity with women: 18, question 2, Pervenit ad nos.

Monks are not permitted to live with nuns or to dine with them: 18, question 2, Diffiniuimus, and the two following chapters.

Monks are not permitted, at their own pleasure, to expel abbots or appoint others: 18, question 2, Nullam.

Women are forbidden to enter the monasteries of monks: 18, question 2, chapter Pervenit ad nos.

A monk is not permitted to possess property of his own: 12, question 1, Non dicatis, and chapter Quia tua; but all things ought to be common to them: chapter Scimus.

Incontinent monks are to be confined in the prisons of harsh penance: 27, question 1, Impudicas; 12, question 1, Non dicatis.

A monk is not permitted to receive anything without the permission of his prelate.

A congregation of monks, however holy it may seem, is rarely found without some admixture of bad men: distinction 47, Quantumlibet. And this is the saying of Augustine to Vincent the Donatist, where he also says: Just as I have scarcely found better men than those who have made progress in a monastery, so I have not found worse men than those who have failed in a monastery. Hence, I think, comes the saying in the last chapter of the Apocalypse: Let the just man still be justified, and let him who is in filth still become filthy. Thus there.

A monk who seeks to live delicately in religion, though he was poor in the world, is to be detested: 12, question 2, Gloria.

A monk has the office not of one who teaches, but of one who laments, who mourns either himself or the world, and who awaits the coming of the Lord with fear: 16, question 1, Monachus.

Monks who fail in religion are the worst; those who make progress are the best: distinction 47, Quantumlibet.

True monks and good religious men are to be honored before the rest: 16, question 1, Qui vere.

Monks are not to be received into a monastery for a price, nor are they to be permitted to have a private fund: De statu monachorum, chapter Monachi.

c iij

A monk who has property of his own is to be removed from communion at the altar; and if such a man is found at the point of death, he is not to receive burial among the brothers: in the same place, and chapter Super quodam, and chapter Cum ad monasterium.

Monks are bound to observe continual silence in the oratory, dormitory, refectory, and cloister: in the same chapter Cum ad monasterium.

Healthy monks are not to feed on meat: in the same place, section In refectorio.

From the Summa of Brother Angelus, on religious.

Whether religious are bound to be perfect. The answer is that they are not, except with that perfection to which they have obligated themselves; but they are bound to tend toward perfection, according to Thomas, Secunda secundae, question 186. Contempt for perfection is contrary to this. Hence they are not liars, although outwardly they bear the state of perfection, because they do not assume it as professing themselves to be perfect, but as professing themselves to be tending toward perfection. Therefore they would indeed be liars if they recalled their mind from the intention of perfection, according to Astesanus, book 6, title 47.

On obedience, collected from the Decrees.

Obedience alone possesses the merit of faith and is rightly preferred to sacrifices, because through sacrifices another’s flesh is slain, but through obedience one’s own will is slain: 8, question 1, Sciendum.

Obedience ought to be promised in writing; this is from custom and from the precept of the Rule of Saint Benedict. Likewise, he who knows that he has been placed over others should not be vexed that someone has been made his prelate, but should himself render the obedience that he demands: chapter Qui suis.

It is often not expedient to obey commands: 11, question 3, Non semper. It is not always evil not to obey commands; when the lord commands things that are contrary to God, then he must not be obeyed. And the following chapter, and chapter Iulianus, and chapter Si is.

Superiors are to be obeyed promptly: distinction 93, Si inimicus.

God is to be obeyed principally: distinction 8, Quae contra.

XX 11, question 3, Imperatores.

A monk ought to obey his own abbot more than the bishop in matters that pertain to the Rule: 18, question 2, Quam sit, § Nullus, and chapter Abbates; 9, question 3, Conquestus.

The commands of superiors are to be obeyed even if they themselves act otherwise, unless they have erred in the faith: 2, question 7, Sacerdotes.

Evil must never be done through obedience, but some good can sometimes be omitted because of obedience: Quod agit, 11, question 3, Quod generale.

Likewise, collected from the decrees concerning the correction of sinners.
