Correction ought to be made from charity, according to the diversity of faults: 24, question 3, Corripiantur.

Correction ought to be made with the intention of healing, not of raging: distinction 86, Odio; 23, question 4, Ita plane circa me.

Correction ought to be mingled with kindness and severity: distinction 45, Disciplina; 12, question 2, Fraternitas; distinction 45, Omnis.

For excessive severity receives from those rebuked neither correction nor salvation: distinction 45, Cum beatus.

Many things about these matters are found scattered above in the form of visitation.

He who consents to sins is accursed before God: 11, question 3. He who consents to sinners and defends another who is offending will be accursed before God and before men, and he is to be corrected with a very severe rebuke. Hence also a certain most holy father says: If anyone defends a sinner, let him be restrained more sharply than the one who sinned. These are the words there of Isidore, and in the chapter Ita corporis and the two following chapters.

He who does not resist errors consents to them: distinction 83, Error. What he does not resist, he approves; and truth, when it is not defended, is oppressed. For to neglect to disturb the perverse when you can do so is nothing other than to foster them; nor is he free from the scruple of hidden fellowship who ceases to oppose manifest crime. This is the saying of Innocent. And in the following chapter, Pope Pius says:

For what does it profit him not to be polluted by his own error, if he grants consent to one who errs?

And in the following chapter Gregory says:

He seems to consent to one who errs who does not meet and cut away the things that ought to be corrected.

The faults of inferiors are imputed to the negligence of rulers: distinction 86.

The faults of lower orders are to be referred to no one more than to slothful and negligent rulers, who often nourish many plagues while they avoid applying a harsher medicine.

Men are to be loved; sins are to be held in hatred, in the following chapter.

Let them hate sins, not men. Let them correct the proud, tolerate the weak; and what it is necessary to punish more severely, let them strike with the mind not of one raging, but of one healing.

One must have pity on the man and be angry at the sinner: 23, question 4. When we say these two names, man and sinner, they are not said in vain. Because he is a sinner, correct him; because he is a man, have mercy on him. Nor will you wholly free the man unless you have pursued the sinner. This is Augustine on the Psalter.

XXI

The manner and form of celebrating a provincial chapter of the fathers of the order of Saint Benedict in the province of Mainz.

Since, in celebrating provincial chapters, many occupations are accustomed to confront the lord presidents, lest, when those who are experienced and practiced depart or are absent, those less experienced and unaccustomed to celebrating chapters of this kind should happen to be distracted by those very many occupations, I have taken care to send in writing, for the knowledge of those who follow, the present form, which in those very chapters that I have more often attended, when they were being celebrated, I saw and heard. Although in it we do not have all the things that are to be done in chapters, nevertheless many and more necessary things will be found. For I think this will be of profit both to those present, for the exercise of discipline, and to those to come, by the example and consideration of their predecessors.

That the presidents, visitors, and treasurers should arrive before the day of the chapter.

Therefore the past and future presidents, together with the visitors or treasurers, should come some days before the appointed day for celebrating the chapter, in the meantime also being supported by the expenses of the chapter, in order to discuss and advise one another in the matters that occur and must be done, as was ordained in the fifteenth chapter, celebrated for the second time at Seligenstadt in the year of the Lord 1454.

On the Saturday preceding the day of the chapter, let one citation be made of the absent, and of those who have not yet satisfied the assessment of the contribution. The promoter of the order, by command of the lord presidents, shall have this citation posted by the notary of the chapter on the doors of the monastery at vespers or compline. And he shall have the same done in two other churches if there is need. The citation may be made in this form:

By mandate of the reverend lord presidents of the black monks of the order of Saint Benedict of the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg, all and singular abbots, provosts, and priors of the order of the province...

of the province and of the aforesaid diocese, who ought to be present at the chapter to be held on the coming Sunday Jubilate in the monastery of Saint N., to appear in person, or through their lawful proctors, on such-and-such a day at the sixth hour in the morning in the said monastery, before the aforesaid lord presiders, to show that they have obeyed the mandates of the visitors and have really and effectively made satisfaction concerning the imposed contribution, and to hear other matters concerning the foregoing declared and pronounced. But if they do not appear within the fixed time, then the said lord presiders will proceed against those contumacious persons, as the order of equity shall dictate, according to the tenor of the privileges of the often-mentioned order, the absence of those cited notwithstanding. In testimony of all these things the seals of two presiders have been affixed. Given in the year, etc., on such-and-such a day, etc.

The notary should subscribe himself to this citation in the usual way, and have the execution made at vespers or at compline.

The one who is to deliver the sermon on the following day should, on Saturday, present it in writing to the lord presiders, to be examined and corrected if necessary, lest scandal arise.

The past presiders, before the day of the chapter, should give the future presiders a full account of the receipts and expenditures, which the latter should read beforehand in writing if there is need. And therefore both groups are ordered to come to the chapter on Wednesday, as was established in chapter 17 at Nuremberg in the year of the Lord 1459.

On Sunday let the signal for terce be given rather early, according to the arrangement of the presiders; and the abbot appointed to sing the Mass should vest with the ministers and, during the introit, enter the choir, as is the custom. Before the presbytery he should recite the Confiteor with the ministers; and let the Mass of the Holy Spirit be sung solemnly, at which all the fathers must be present. When the Mass has ended, let a lectern be prepared at the head of the choir. Let there be a conference for the fathers and any others who wish to be present, on religion, discipline, humility, the virtues, and perseverance. The preacher, however, before he begins the sermon,

should ask a blessing from one of the presiders, who is the principal presider, if he is present. When the sermon is finished, let them enter the chapter place and let each take his seat: first the abbots, then the provosts and priors, and the proctors of the absent, according to the placement made by the promoter.

XXII

Then the promoter, standing while all listen, should say:

In the name of God, amen. By command of the venerable lords, the presiders, I warn and require all and each of those present here to whom it does not belong to attend this our sacred provincial chapter, under penalty of excommunication and suspension, to go out and withdraw from this chapter place. The notary should remain with the witnesses; nevertheless even they may be ordered to leave while secret matters are being discussed. If those matters must afterwards be written down after their withdrawal, they shall also be recited to the notary.

Then, in the customary way, let readings be made from the martyrology, and let the Precious be added by the prior of the convent, after he has first asked a blessing from the presider, saying: Lord, bid a blessing. And the presider who makes the response should answer: May the almighty and merciful Lord direct us in the way of his commandments. And all should answer: Amen.

And in place of the regular reading, let him read from the second chapter of the Rule, namely what sort of person the abbot ought to be. Chapter 2 of the Rule.

The abbot who is worthy to preside over a monastery must always remember what he is called and fulfill the name of superior by his deeds. He is believed to act in the place of Christ in the monastery, since he is called by his own name, as the Apostle says: You have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, Abba, Father. Therefore the abbot must neither teach, establish, nor order anything outside the Lord’s command, which God forbid; rather, his command or teaching should be sprinkled into the minds of the disciples as the leaven of divine justice. This section is often customarily read as an introduction.

For an examination must be made in the dread judgment of God concerning both matters: his own teaching and the obedience of his disciples. And the abbot should know that whatever lack of profit the father of the household finds among the sheep will be charged as the shepherd’s fault. [unclear] he can find that is of less profit among the sheep of the householder. Yet he will again be free from blame if all the diligence of a shepherd has been applied to a restless and disobedient flock, and every care has been shown for their diseased actions. Their shepherd, absolved in the judgment of God, may say with the prophet to the Lord: “I have not hidden your justice in my heart. I have declared your truth and your salvation; but they, despising them, have rejected me.” And then at last death itself shall be the punishment for the disobedient sheep under his care.

Therefore, when someone receives the name of abbot, he must preside over his disciples with twofold teaching: that is, he should show all good and holy things by deeds more than by words. To receptive disciples he should set forth the Lord’s commands in words; but to those hard of heart and simpler, he should demonstrate the divine precepts by his own deeds. All things, however, that he teaches his disciples to be contrary to his own deeds, he should indicate are not to be done, lest, preaching to others, he himself be found reprobate; lest God someday say to him in his sin: “Why do you recount my justices and take up my covenant in your mouth? But you have hated discipline and have cast my words behind you.” And: “You saw the speck in your brother’s eye, but in your own eye you did not see the beam.”

Let him make no distinction of persons in the monastery; let not one be loved more than another, unless he has found one better in good deeds or obedience. Let not the freeborn be preferred to one converted from servitude, unless some other reasonable cause exists. But if justice so dictates and it seems good to the abbot, let him do this from any rank whatever. Otherwise let them keep their proper places, because whether free or slave, we are all one in Christ, and under one Lord we bear an equal service of military duty; for there is no acceptance of persons with God. We are distinguished before him in this respect alone: if we are found better than others in good works and humble. Therefore let equal charity be shown by him to all; let one discipline be applied by him to all according to their merits.

XXIII

In his teaching, therefore, the abbot must always observe that apostolic form in which it says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke”; that is, mixing times with times, blandishments with terrors. Let him show the stern affection of a master and the loving affection of a father: that is, he should reprove the undisciplined and restless more harshly; the obedient, gentle, and patient he should entreat, so that they may advance toward what is better; but the negligent and contemptuous we admonish him to rebuke and correct. Nor should he dissemble the sins of offenders; rather, as soon as they begin to spring up, he should cut them out by the roots before they gain strength, mindful of the danger of Eli the priest of Shiloh. Those of better character and understanding he should correct with words at the first or second admonition; but the wicked, hard, proud, or disobedient he should restrain at the very beginning of sin with blows or bodily chastisement, knowing that it is written: “A fool is not corrected by words.” And again: “Strike your son with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from death.”

The abbot must always remember what he is, remember what he is called, and know that more is required from the one to whom more is entrusted. Let him know how difficult and arduous a thing he has undertaken: to rule souls and to serve the characters of many. One he must guide by blandishments, another by rebukes and persuasions; and according to each one’s character and understanding, he should so conform and adapt himself to all that he not only suffer no losses in the flock committed to him, but rejoice in the increase of a good flock.

Above all, let him not, by dissembling or making little of the salvation of the souls committed to him, show more concern for transitory, earthly, and perishable things; but let him always consider that he has undertaken to rule souls, concerning whom he will have to render an account. And lest perhaps he complain of too little substance, let him remember that it is written: “First seek the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things shall be added to you.” And again: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear God.” Let him know that whoever undertakes to rule souls should prepare himself to render an account; and however many brothers he knows he has under his care...

number, let him know for certain that on the day of judgment he will render account to God for the souls of all of them, with, beyond doubt, his own soul added as well. And thus, always fearing the future examination, the shepherd, while guarding himself concerning the reckoning for the sheep entrusted to him, becomes solicitous concerning his own.

When these things have been completed, or as much as shall please the presidents has been read, the names of the dead, if any occur, shall immediately be recited from the book of the monastery. Then, from the slips brought by the priors, the names of the brothers of the order who have died since the last chapter was celebrated shall be recited by the same reader of the martyrology. When these are finished, the president shall add: May the souls of the brothers, familiars, and benefactors of our order rest in peace. And when the others have said Amen, let them read, as is customary, the psalm De profundis to the end, concluding with Requiem eternam. And after each has said the Pater noster silently, the official shall add Et ne nos, and the other things contained in the acts of the daily chapter.

When these things have been completed, one of the presidents shall enjoin the abbot of the house that after vespers the brothers shall perform vigils in choir for those dead. And he shall appoint one of the priors who on the next day shall solemnly sing the high mass for the same dead. After this the promoter of the order shall read the chapter In singulis from the Decretals, as follows: Innocent III, in the general council.

In each kingdom or province, every three years, with the right of the diocesan bishops preserved, there shall be held a common chapter of abbots and of priors who do not have their own abbots and who have not been accustomed to celebrate such a chapter. All who do not have a canonical impediment shall come together for it at one of the monasteries suited for this purpose, with this moderation observed: that none of them bring more than six mounts and seven persons. At the beginnings of this new practice, however, they shall summon two neighboring abbots of the Cistercian order to provide them suitable counsel and assistance, since they are, by long custom, more fully instructed in celebrating chapters of this kind.

XXIII

These, without contradiction, shall associate with themselves two from among them whom they think suitable. And those four shall preside over the whole chapter, in such a way that from this none of them assumes for himself the authority of prelacy; hence, when it is expedient, he may be changed by prudent deliberation. They shall celebrate this kind of chapter continuously for several fixed days according to the custom of the Cistercian order, and in it they shall hold a careful discussion concerning the reform of the order and regular observance. And what has been established with the approval of those four shall be observed inviolably, all excuse, contradiction, and appeal being removed; provision nevertheless having been made where the chapter should be celebrated at the next term. And those who have assembled shall lead a common life and shall all together meet the common expenses proportionally, so that, if not all can stay in the same house, at least several may stay together in different houses.

They shall also appoint in the same chapter religious and circumspect persons who, according to the form prescribed to them, shall in our stead endeavor to visit every abbey of the same kingdom or province, not only of monks but also of nuns, correcting and reforming what they see to be in need of the office of correction and reform. Thus, if they recognize that the rector of a place must be wholly removed from administration, they shall denounce him to his own bishop, so that he may see to removing him. And if he does not do so, the visitors shall refer this to the examination of the apostolic see.

The things that follow in that chapter are not customarily read in sequence. The following chapter will continue it: Honorius III, to the abbots and monks established in Lombardy and the March of Treviso.

From Quae pro religionis honestate, etc. Moreover, when the visitors appointed according to the statute of the general council by the general chapter of abbots have proceeded to carry out the office of visitation, they shall diligently inquire into the state of the monks and their regular observances; and they shall correct and reform, both in spiritual and in temporal matters, what they see should be corrected.

so, however, that he should have delinquent monks corrected by the abbot of the place, and that a salutary penance be imposed upon them according to the Rule of blessed Benedict and the apostolic statutes, not according to the standard of a depraved custom that has taken root in some churches almost as law. The visitors themselves, moreover, should, in our stead, strike with regular censure those monks whom they find contumacious and rebellious, according to the measure of their fault and without preference of persons; they should not spare rebels because of their stubbornness or because of the power of their friends, but should cast out the diseased sheep lest it infect the healthy sheep.

But if abbots are found negligent in correcting, according to the visitors' mandate and the regular statutes, either themselves or their monks, let them be denounced and rebuked, and let them be punished publicly in the general chapter in such a way that their penalty may be an example to others. But if an abbot who is not exempt is found by the visitors to be excessively negligent and lax, they should report this without delay to the diocesan of the place; and through him let a faithful and prudent coadjutor be given to him until the general chapter. But if he is found to be a squanderer, or otherwise deserving removal, after this has been reported to the diocesan by the visitors, let him be removed from the governance of the abbey without the noise of legal proceedings; and in the meantime let a suitable administrator be provided for the monastery, to take care of temporal affairs until an abbot has been provided for that monastery.

But if perhaps the bishop is unwilling or neglects to fulfill these things, the visitors or the presidents of the general chapter should not delay reporting the bishop's default to the apostolic see. We order these same things to be done concerning exempt abbots by the visitors or the presidents of the general chapter, with their deposition reserved to the apostolic see: so that, once the abbot who appears fit to be removed has meanwhile been suspended from administration by the visitors or by the presidents in chapter, a suitable administrator may be appointed for the monastery. Their offenses, however, and the other matters that seem proper to be reported to the chapter, the presidents shall report to us through faithful and prudent messengers,

to whom expenses shall be sufficiently supplied from the common contribution of the abbots, according to each one's means.

The following visitors, moreover, shall carefully trace the footsteps of the former visitors, and shall report their negligences and offenses to the next general chapter, so that they may publicly bear the penalty due according to their fault. We command the same to be observed also concerning abbots presiding over the general chapter. And after a few words: We command all these things to be observed also in monasteries that do not have their own abbots but priors, and likewise in monasteries of nuns, insofar as the articles are suitable to abbesses and nuns.

Then, if the presidents order it, also the following.

From the constitutions of lord Pope Benedict XII, concerning provincial chapters, chapter 2.

We also decree and ordain that, in the order or religion of the said Black Monks, in each of the provinces assigned by us below, there shall be held, in a place to be assigned for this purpose, every three years, saving the right of the diocesan bishops, a common or provincial chapter of abbots and of priors who do not have their own abbots; and of other priors of cathedral churches of that order or religion, or of others greater in those churches after their bishops, by whatever name they are called; and of the other prelates who, as stated above, do not have their own abbots, whether exempt or not exempt, of the same order or religion. To this chapter, unless a just impediment prevents them, all the aforesaid abbots, priors, and other prelates shall assemble; and concerning the reformation of this order or religion and regular observance, they shall strive to carry out what is set forth in this constitution.

Those, however, who are unable to come personally to the chapter shall, to allege the cause of a just impediment, send a fellow monk of their own church or monastery, if this can conveniently be done; otherwise another suitable person with sufficient mandate, containing an adequate cause of excuse and also authority

with authority to swear on their behalf that such a cause is true, they shall be bound to send him to the said chapter. The discretion of the presidents of such provincial chapters is reserved, and their power shall continue from one provincial chapter to another, so that they may decide whether a cause of excuse, or causes of excuse when several have been alleged, are sufficient or insufficient; and no one shall be permitted frivolously to appeal from their decree on this matter, or to protest in any other way.

Those, however, who do not come when no lawful impediment exists, or who do not send to it, as stated above, their fellow monk or another suitable person as excuser and procurator with sufficient mandate, shall be bound, within a term set by those presidents, to pay double what they would have spent in coming to the said chapter, remaining in it, and returning from it, as estimated by the judgment of those presidents or the greater part of them, the sum to be turned to the benefit of that provincial chapter. The presidents themselves may compel them to pay such double amount by ecclesiastical censure, by apostolic authority, and may publish, or have published, in places of the same order or religion, the proceedings to be carried out against them in this matter and the sentences to be issued. No favor may be granted to anyone concerning that double amount, whether in whole or in part, nor may any remission be allowed. Nevertheless proceedings shall be taken against the aforesaid non-attendees, especially if they maliciously withdraw themselves either to avoid correction or so that the condition of their church or monastery may not be known, or otherwise as shall seem good to the said presidents or to the greater part of them, notwithstanding their absence.

With respect to the presidents and visitors to be appointed in the same chapters, and all other matters to be carried out in them, those things shall be observed which are contained in the constitutions of the said general council and of Honorius III, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, while still preserving our statutes, ordinances, and additions written above

and below, as it is modified and limited in them.

And because this is a salutary institution and observance for the prelates and monks of that order or religion, we decree that the priors of cathedral churches of the same order or religion, or the chief persons in those churches after their bishops, who after those bishops have regular care of the monks, by whatever name they are called, are to assemble in those provincial chapters under the modes and penalties designated above. We also decree that those same priors or chief persons, the chapters, and all monks of those churches or monasteries, even if they have priories, offices, or administrations, or have their residence, in the churches or monasteries themselves or outside them wherever they may be, both exempt and non-exempt, even if the non-exempt are subject to certain exempt prelates, are included and comprehended under the coercive authority and ordinances of the said provincial chapters. They are to be compelled to those ordinances, under the penalties that the said presidents shall think should be imposed on them, by the presidents themselves; and any of the aforesaid monks of the said bodies who hold monastic benefices belonging to those churches are also to be compelled by the aforesaid priors or chief persons, by apostolic authority, through ecclesiastical censure and other suitable remedies, with the obstacle of appeal removed, to contribute to the moderate and reasonable expenses that the said priors or chief persons incur in coming to those chapters, staying in them, and returning from them.

Wherefore all local ordinaries, exempt and non-exempt, shall place no impediment against the aforesaid matters, either collectively or individually, nor permit one to be placed; but, when requested at the lawful times, they shall cause each and all of them to be ordered into execution and inviolably observed.

Since, indeed, we intend to take precautions lest an impediment arising with respect to the meeting of any provincial chapter be able to harm it, it is to be understood we understand and will that, if monastic cathedral churches should happen to be vacant, or to lack their pastors, that is, priors or others who, after their bishops, are the greater officials in them, as stated above, or if monasteries or places of the same order or religion should be vacant or lack their pastors, who would be bound to come to the aforesaid provincial chapter at the time when the holding of that provincial chapter is imminent, then the chapters of the churches and the convents of the monasteries and of the other aforesaid conventual places shall be bound to send to the said chapter a suitable person from the body of those churches, monasteries, and places, if this can conveniently be done, or else some suitable person from elsewhere, to do and fulfill all the things that the aforesaid abbots, priors, or superiors presiding in those cathedral churches or other same conventual places could do, if they had come to the same chapter and were present there in person.

But what is set forth above concerning a provincial chapter to be held every three years, in order to remove every scruple of hesitation, we wish to be referred to a sound understanding: namely, that when a provincial chapter has been held in one year, it may be omitted in the next following year, and in every case shall be held in the third year following.

Indeed, since it would be useless to issue sanctions if their execution were neglected and there were no one to uphold them, we ordain and will that the said common or provincial chapter ought to be celebrated at one of the monasteries of the same order or religion suitable for this purpose, if such a monastery exists in the same province; otherwise, let it be celebrated in another fitting and secure place. Concerning this, and concerning the day for holding the first chapter of this kind, and the other matters to be done opportunely about it, those who have been appointed for this by the apostolic see shall make provision on the first occasion.

And so that thereafter and forever there may be a reasonable ordinance concerning the same chapter and through it, we decree that in the said chapter to be held first, and always thereafter successively, those presiding at each chapter to be held, or the greater part of them, shall provide and see to it that it is ordained by whom, in the following chapter, the sermon is to be delivered and the mass celebrated; and they shall choose the place for holding the aforesaid chapter on the next following occasion, and who ought to preside in it. And so let it be done thereafter in successive provincial chapters.

Let them also provide which abbots, how many, and how often, until the next provincial chapter itself, ought to visit the monastic cathedral churches, monasteries, and other places of the same order or religion. If it seems necessary to the presiding lords, the following chapter from the same constitutions of Benedict XII, concerning subventions and collections, can also be read. Likewise from the Benedictine constitution, chapter 5.

Since in the often-mentioned constitution of the general council, among other things, it is expressed that those who have assembled in the triennial chapter are to lead a common life and proportionally meet common expenses as sons in common, we, considering that besides expenses of this kind other expenses are required as necessary not only for the aforesaid provincial chapter but also for the annual chapters, decree and ordain that in the same chapters, notwithstanding anyone’s contradiction or absence, for liberties, necessities, utilities, common expenses, and other customary matters, since a burden divided into parts is more lightly borne, collections, subventions, or contributions are to be made, imposed, and assessed by apostolic authority, according to the judgment of those presiding or of the definitors with respect to such a provincial chapter, or of the abbot or other president of the annual chapter itself and of the definitors with respect to the aforesaid annual chapter.

But so that, in the preservation of collections, subventions, or contributions of this kind, the safeguard of security may be faithfully maintained, we will and ordain that the collections that shall be made in the provincial chapter by three upright and faithful abbots or other prelates of that order or religion of the province in which the same chapter has been celebrated, in some secure monastery

or in another suitable place. Those, however, which are made in individual churches, monasteries, or other places of the same order or religion shall be made by three upright and faithful monks of each church, monastery, or place in which, as stated above, they are made. Of these, the abbot or other prelate of that place shall appoint one, the prior or priors and administrators or officials another, and the chapter of the church or the convent of the monastery or place of this kind the third. The money collected shall be faithfully and diligently kept in one chest, locked with three different locks and keys, and shall be applied only to the use of those for whom the collections were made, and shall not be diverted to any other uses. For faithfully observing and fulfilling these things, the said three abbots shall take a bodily oath in the presence of those presiding, and the aforesaid monks in the presence of the abbot and chapter, and also of the convent of the church or monastery, or of the prelate of the other principal place where the said annual chapter shall have been held. Nor may another contribution be made so long as any sufficient amount of the first contribution happens to remain.

The aforesaid presiding officers, and each of them, who are for such provincial chapters, as well as the abbots and greater men or others already mentioned, shall have power, by the apostolic authority stated above, to demand, collect, and levy collections, subsidies, and contributions of this kind from all and each of the subject abbots, if they have or shall have any, and from priors, prelates, administrators, officials, and beneficiaries of every kind who shall be subject to that annual chapter, or to the church, monastery, or other principal place; and to compel all and each of the aforesaid persons, by the same authority, through ecclesiastical censure, without appeal, and by other remedies of law and of that order or religion, to pay in full the aforesaid collections, subsidies, and contributions, as shall have been ordained in such provincial and annual chapters, with deadlines assigned for this; and freely to publish and execute the aforesaid things, and processes and

sentences in cathedral churches, monasteries, and other places of the same order or religion, when and as often as it shall seem expedient to them; and also to absolve from the said sentences, after suitable satisfaction has first been made; and to relax and remove all processes and sentences of suspension and interdict; and to dispense with them concerning any irregularity which they, while thus bound, may have incurred by profaning divine services or otherwise involving themselves in them, provided this was not in contempt of the keys.

After these things have been read by the promoter of the order, other items from the constitutions of earlier chapters may also be read at the pleasure of the lords presiding. When all these have been completed, one of those presiding, beginning the provincial chapter, shall say: “Bless.” Let the Lord respond. And again let him add:

“Let us now speak. Behold, venerable fathers, from the sacred canons on the orders and from the constitutions of the supreme pontiffs, you have heard the authority of this sacred provincial chapter, to celebrate which God has gathered us together into one. Supported by this authority, we begin this provincial chapter itself in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

Then let him add:

“Therefore we first protest that we wish this place and the other places of this monastery necessary for us for celebrating this chapter of ours to be deputed, and we depute them, as the chapter-place. And we wish this protestation to be considered repeated as often as, being assembled capitularly in those places or in any of them, we shall ordain, establish, or discuss anything.”

Then the same presiding officer shall receive from the notary a manual promise concerning keeping the acts of the chapter secret and not revealing them publicly. And the promoter shall say:

“We protest further that, if there is anyone here who is excommunicated, suspended, or under interdict, we do not intend to celebrate such a chapter in his presence. Therefore, if anyone knows himself to be such, let him leave this chapter-place, and let him not presume to be present unless absolved.”

And, turning to the notary, the same promoter shall add:

And you, lord scribe, I duly and urgently require to record this act and those that follow with diligence, and to mark it among the acts of the chapter, with trustworthy witnesses brought in for these matters.

Immediately the notary shall require witnesses, two or three of whom are to be present at all acts, except at the final proclamation of the fathers. Likewise, the promoter of the order, with all hearing, by the authority of the lords president, shall say by way of mandate to all and singular, both those now present here and those arriving at whatever hour, in virtue of holy obedience, that no one in any way reveal the secrets of this provincial chapter to any secular person or to any person not subject to our aforesaid chapter, to the detriment, disgrace, or burden of the order and of its professed members.

By the same authority, too, it is commanded to all and singular that no one presume to speak in the chapter places and proceedings before the lords president or the officials of the chapter, appointed or to be appointed, unless license has been requested and obtained, and this while standing and with head uncovered, with humility, reverence, and submission. Or, if he wishes, let him present it in writing.

Likewise, by the same authority, it is enjoined on all and singular who are bound to attend this chapter that no one withdraw from the place of the chapter without license, but that he remain until its end, under the penalty for contumacy and for those not coming to the chapter.

Then the register of the monasteries shall be read by the promoter or the notary, and the absentees shall be noted with the pen by one of them, as is customary. When these have been noted, the promoter shall accuse the contumacy of the absentees in these or similar words, saying:

Reverend fathers, lords president, I accuse the contumacy of the absent prelates, who are bound by law to attend this sacred provincial chapter; and I request that a monition be decreed, to be executed on the doors of this monastery against those same contumacious persons, and against rebels toward the visitors, so that they may appear to show that they have obeyed the mandates of the chapter and have actually presented themselves to it; otherwise, that they may see themselves declared to have incurred the penalties written below.

When he has said this, let one of the presidents see to it.

We, the presidents, wishing to act more graciously and not to condemn anyone too quickly, shall await the absentees until the following day, and longer if need be; so that meanwhile the procuratorial mandates of the absentees may also be examined, to determine whether their absence ought deservedly to be excused, and whether their procurators themselves ought to be reckoned present. Moreover, we decree a monition against rebels.

After these things, if there is time, let them choose definitors from among the abbots, who can give counsel and help to the presidents in the business of the chapter. Likewise, let three or four from among the same abbots be deputed to examine the procuratorial mandates of the absentees after dinner, or at a set time, in the place deputed to which the procurators are to come. This proviso is added: that if any procuratorial mandates are found ambiguous, they shall refer their examination to the lords president. The form of a sufficient procuratorial mandate is set out in the acts of the chapter.

Then the president may admonish the visitors beforehand that, at the set time or hour which they shall have determined, they are to be ready to present to the lords president the accounts and summaries of their visitations, according to the constitutions of the preceding fathers.

And if the hour is late and nothing difficult now remains, they shall be licensed to go to table, one of the presidents saying in these or similar words:

Venerable fathers, since the hour has already grown rather late and it is time for dining, lest we delay you, weary as you are, any longer from refreshment, we now wish to put an end to these proceedings. Therefore let each man dispose himself for table according to the promoter’s ordering, with discipline; in silence and with thanksgiving he shall eat what is set before him.

The promoter of the order shall seat the fathers in the refectory according to the time of each man’s prelacy, so far as this can be done. First, indeed, the abbots shall sit, then the priors and provosts, after that the procurators of the absentees, and afterward the other simple brethren. Yet this order of sitting can rarely be arranged in this way, on account of the multitude of those sitting and each individual [unclear].

[... because of] the unknown ages of the individual persons. And if the presidents wish to give any further admonition, let them do so, especially if there are any whose tonsure differs from the others, so that after lunch they may see to it that they are properly shaved. Then let the president conclude: “Our help is in the name of the Lord.” Let the others answer: “Who made heaven and earth.” And so let them go. But before they are dismissed, let all be admonished that at the first or second signal of the bell they are all to be present again in the chapter place; and, if it seems good to the presidents, let some penalty be imposed on those who arrive late.

After lunch.

When the bell has been rung and the fathers have assembled together, let them make the customary prayer, with the president beginning it, which ought to be done on bended knees before every capitular act, as follows:

“Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love, you who through diversity, etc. Alleluia, alleluia. Kyrie eleison. Kyrie eleison. Our Father.”

Let one of the presidents, adding to this, say: “And lead us not into temptation.” Let the others answer: “But deliver us.”

Versicle: “Save your servants.” Response: “My God, who hope in you.”

Versicle: “Send them, O Lord, help from the sanctuary.” Response: “And from Sion protect them.”

Versicle: “Be for us, O Lord, a tower of strength.” Response: “Before the face of the enemy.”

Versicle: “O Lord God of hosts, convert us.” Response: “And show us your face, and we shall be saved.”

Versicle: “O Lord, hear my prayer.” Response: “And let my cry come to you.”

Versicle: “The Lord be with you.”

Let us pray.

“Stretch out, O Lord, over your faithful the right hand of heavenly help, that they may seek you with their whole heart, and may deserve to obtain the things they worthily ask.

“O Lord, we ask you to go before our petitions by inspiring them, and to follow them by helping them, so that all our action may always begin from you and, once begun, may be brought to completion through you.

“O God, who taught the hearts of the faithful by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, grant us in the same Spirit to know what is right, and always to rejoice in his consolation. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.”

These things are to be said by the president who gives the address, with the others answering. After this let the same president say: “Give the blessing.” Let the others answer: “The Lord.” And let him add:

“If any one of you, reverend fathers, wishes to put forward anything for the common good of the chapter, of the order, and of its persons, let him confidently set it forth with fear of the Lord, reverence, and humility, and we will give him a hearing with all patience. But if anything necessary has been proposed, let the presidents, together with the definitors, have mature deliberation as to what is to be done in each matter.”

The presidents are also sometimes accustomed to ask all the fathers in order, according to the requirement of the cases that arise: “If any fathers have complaints to put forward against anyone, which could be met by us, let them put them forward humbly and without disturbance, and in like manner we will patiently hear them.”

And then let him add afterward:

“Likewise, if there are any brothers sent on behalf of their communities with testimonial letters to put forward something against anyone, let them present the letters and explain the causes; we will also hear them patiently and kindly.”

After this, if there are any matters to be treated capitularly, let them be treated. And let one of the fathers be appointed to sing Mass on the next day for the brothers. Then a brief exhortation may be made to the fathers on how they ought to conduct themselves in lodgings and in every place, in this or a similar manner:

“Venerable fathers, as you heard when it was read today from the Rule of Saint Benedict, according to which we are bound to live: he who is appointed abbot over brothers ought to instruct them in holy doctrine and to go before them with examples of good works. Unless he shows both to his disciples, he will undoubtedly receive a fearful sentence in the strict examination of God’s judgment. For he is believed to act in Christ’s place in the monastery; therefore he must follow Christ himself. For he himself says: ‘He who ministers to me, let him follow me.’ Just as Christ fed his disciples by word and example, so too we, who are his ministers, must feed our sheep

through the teaching of holy instructions, let us minister nourishment to our sheep, and through examples of good works let us display incentives to virtue for the weaker. For the pastor’s teaching is useful to all, but examples of virtue profit the weak and the untrained more. Examples are stronger than words, and it is better to teach by deed than by speech. We say these things, therefore, so that, shining forth in good morals, we may provide in all things a good example to those who see us. And to come briefly to the point, we exhort your fatherhoods that in every place and time, but especially in lodgings, you do good, scandalizing no one; for the suspicion of the weak is so readily turned toward worse things that the reputation of many is damaged by the scandal of one or a few, and even the praises of many scarcely know how to repair the infamy of a few.

If nothing more remains, let the fathers be dismissed to their lodgings, first advising them that on the following day all are to assemble for the Mass of the Dead. And let the notary, with the promoter of the order cooperating, write a warning against the absent in the manner of a citation, to be posted tomorrow, for greater abundance of caution, on the doors of the monastery. “Our help is in the name of the Lord.” “Who made heaven and earth.” And when these things have been said, let each go out to his lodging, except those who must remain.

Monday.

On the following day, at the appointed hour, let all assemble, and let them attend the Masses of the Dead, and whoever wishes may celebrate. When Mass has ended, let them assemble at the chapter place, and let him again read “Come, Holy Spirit,” with the prayers stated above. And let the president say, “Bless ye.” Let them answer, “The Lord.” Then, if anything was begun yesterday, let it be continued. And let the presidents entrust to the notary the writing of the chapter proceedings. After this, when the hour is suitable, let the presidents withdraw to some more private place and hear the visitors one by one concerning the office enjoined upon them, and concerning the condition of the monasteries that they visited, both in spiritual and in temporal matters, and whether in any places they were not admitted. And let them present copies of the letters

that they left in the monasteries visited by them. But if any visitors are not present, let them make a report of this kind to the fathers either in writing or through their proctors. If any abbots have been notably accused in any matter by their visitors before the presidents, let them be summoned, if it seems useful to the presidents, and let them be admonished to amend themselves henceforth in the matters charged.

Likewise, if the lord presidents cannot hear them personally, let them appoint three or four fathers to hear and receive from the treasurers themselves, in writing, an account of receipts and distributions; and when this has been reduced to writing, let them send it to be placed in the chapter chest. Then, when it is opportune, let the promoter again accuse the contumacy of those absent, and ask that they be condemned in expenses according to the constitutions of the order, under this form of words:

“Reverend fathers, today, for greater abundance of caution, I have caused another citation to be posted at the doors of the monastery against the abbots and other absent persons who are bound to attend this provincial chapter, so that they might still appear before your fatherhoods; otherwise they should know that they are bound to certain penalties. None of them has appeared or is appearing. Therefore, lest they derive advantage from their disobedience, and so that their penalty may become an example to the rest, I require and ask you, reverend lord presidents, that according to the force and form of the constitutions of Benedict XII, you deign to proceed against those absent persons, as contumacious, disobedient, and rebellious, according to the order of law, and to condemn them in expenses according to the named constitutions of the aforesaid Benedict.”

Then one of the presidents, after the counsel of the others has been communicated to him for this purpose, shall proceed against them in this way, seated, under this form:

“In the name of the Lord, by this our sentence, which we, residing in the place of presidency, with the counsel and assent of those learned in the law, pronounce, decree, and declare in these writings: we condemn the lords N. and N., contumaciously absent, on account of their contumacy, in so great a sum of money as, upon finding

...which they would have been about to spend in staying at the chapter and returning, if they had come, are to be condemned in double, according to the constitution of lord Pope Benedict XII. We therefore condemn them thus in these writings, and declare that they are to be compelled to pay by ecclesiastical censures, and we do compel them. We have assessed the amount of these monies at two Rhenish florins, to be paid irrevocably to our treasurers within this time and N., under penalty of excommunication, which, once that term has elapsed, they shall incur in these writings unless they have made satisfaction truly and effectively before the day fixed.

From these words let the proper form for the process be taken. Or, if the lord presidents wish to proceed more gently, then let the final clause be changed to this or a similar one: “We reserve to ourselves, or to our visitors, the assessment of these sums or shares of money.” The presidents can, however, first cite them to hear the assessment made, though this does not seem necessary, since the Benedictine constitution commits the matter simply to the lord presidents.

Then the promoter of the order shall accuse the rebels and say:

Reverend fathers, in the second place I accuse the contumacy of abbots A, B, and C, who do not appear, neither in person nor through lawful proctors, although they have been sufficiently awaited, and who do not show that they have obeyed the concluded reformation and withdrawn from their contumacy and rebellion. I ask that they be held, as indeed they are, contumacious; and, in their contumacy, I ask that the same men be declared to have incurred the sentence of excommunication contained in the processes of the past provincial chapters, and that appropriate letters be decreed upon this, with further penalties, censures, and sentences, even to the invocation of the aid of the secular arm.

Then the same president shall add: “We hold the aforesaid absentees to be contumacious, as indeed they are.” And he shall add this sentence:

The name of Christ having been invoked, keeping God alone before our eyes, by this our sentence, which we, residing in this place of presidency, issue in these writings with the counsel and assent of men learned in the law, we pronounce, decree, and declare:

that lords A, B, and C, abbots, and A, B, and C, conventuals, being contumaciously absent, because of their contumacy and manifest rebellion, in that they damnably refused in their chapters to receive and effectively enter upon the concluded, holy, and due regular observance, and, not withdrawing from this rebellion of theirs, did not appear, nor did they take care to allege lawful or reasonable causes why they were by no means bound to this, have incurred the sentence of excommunication according to the tenor of our processes in the preceding chapters, or in the last chapter celebrated at N.; and that, as such, they are to be publicly denounced, and are denounced. We decree by these presents that our necessary letters concerning this are to be issued, also under other censures and sentences, up to and including the invocation of the aid of the secular arm.

It should be noted that the lord presidents can proceed otherwise, if they please, against contumacious absentees: namely, in the recess they may state that within a fixed time they are to make terms with them, or with the visitors, or with others to whom they have given authority, a term being given for canonical monition. If they neglect this, once the fixed term has elapsed they shall be excommunicated by the fact itself, to be absolved by no one except by the presidents themselves or by the visitors. If this is done, then they should take care to bring such a process to their certain knowledge.

After the sentence has been issued, let the absentees be cited anew to hear and see the expenses assessed on the next day, in this or a similar form, and let it be posted under vespers:

By mandate of the reverend and venerable fathers, the lord presidents of the black monks of the order of Saint Benedict of the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg, all and singular abbots, provosts, priors, and all others who are bound, or think themselves bound, to have an interest in the same province and diocese are cited to appear on Wednesday after the Sunday Jubilate, at the sixth hour in the morning, in person or through their lawful proctors, in the monastery of N., before the aforesaid...

to the said presidents, to see and hear a taxation made of all and each of the expenses, in which, by the aforesaid lord presidents, according to the constitution of lord Benedict, pope XII, because of their repeated contumacy and for other reasons to be stated at the appointed time, they are held to have been condemned by sentence; and to have the other appropriate matters concerning the premises declared and pronounced, and the decrees and procedures necessary in this matter determined and granted, with the customary intimation. And whether they appear or not, the same lord presidents will nevertheless proceed in the premises, without doubt, as the order of reason shall dictate, notwithstanding the absence of those cited. In witness whereof the seals of two presidents have been affixed to the presents. Given in the year of the Lord, etc. Let the registrar subscribe himself. This citation, as has been said above, shall be affixed under vespers or compline to the doors of the monastery or church.

After dinner on Monday.

If the matters written above can be completed before dinner, well and good. If not, let them complete them in the vacant time, as shall seem appropriate to all the presidents. Likewise, let the recesses of the last chapter be read, and if any commissions were made to anyone, let the execution of them be examined. Then, if nothing remains, let the fathers be dismissed to their lodgings, to return tomorrow at the sixth hour at the ringing.

The third day.

On Tuesday morning let the bell be rung, and let a Mass of the blessed Virgin Mary be sung solemnly by one of the fathers appointed for it on the preceding evening, at which all the others are to be present. When it is finished, let them go to the chapter, and let the customary prayer be said, “Come, Holy Spirit,” etc. And let one of the presidents say, “Bless.” And when the answer has been given, “The Lord,” let him continue if anything was omitted yesterday. Likewise, afterward let attention be turned to the order, and if anything else is newly to be established, let it be inserted this day in the recess. Likewise, if any answers are to be given or written to princes or to others, let them be made and dispatched with the counsel of the fathers. Let some be appointed, if the treasurers are not present, who shall collect the expenses, namely three Rhenish florins from each abbot, on this day, marking down what has been collected on a schedule, lest someone perhaps, which God forbid, pretend that he has given what he has not given.

Likewise, let some be assigned to assist the notary, who know how to arrange the recess, so that by the evening after dinner it may be complete. Likewise, if the necessity of the order requires it, let a proportionate contribution be imposed on all monasteries, and let the cause and form be inserted in the recess, which all are bound to pay under the penalties to be expressed in the same, according to the constitutions of Benedict, pope XII. And it should be noted that the lord presidents, with the definitors, can impose a contribution on others according to the Benedictine constitution without their consent; nor, however, are they themselves free from such a contribution. For what they impose on others they themselves ought first to bear. That it is theirs to impose a contribution is shown clearly in the same constitutions, in these words in chapter five:

“We decree and ordain that in the same chapters, notwithstanding any contradiction or absence, for liberties, necessities, utilities, common expenses, and other customary matters, since a burden divided into parts is more lightly borne, collections, subsidies, or contributions are to be made, imposed, and assessed by apostolic authority, according to the judgment of the presidents or definitors, for such a provincial chapter.”

Meanwhile also, if it has seemed good to the lord presidents, let the common expenses of the chapter be assessed with the father of the house, as is customary.

After dinner.

When dinner has been completed, at the signal of the bell let them assemble at once, as above; and when the president has said, “Bless,” and the answer has been given, “The Lord,” let the chapter be continued. Then, at the command of the presidents, let the recess be read, which ought now to be complete. At its end it should contain the place and day of the future chapter, and the other things that ought customarily to be done. And it should be noted that no more than two years ought to elapse between the chapter that has been celebrated and the one to be celebrated, according to the constitution of Benedict.

whose words on this matter are as follows: “But what is permitted concerning the provincial chapter to be celebrated every three years, in order to remove any scruple of hesitation, we wish to be referred to a sound understanding, namely, that when the provincial chapter has been celebrated in one year, it may be omitted in the next following year, and be held in the third year immediately thereafter.” Yet this must be observed: that the lord presidents, if need requires, may anticipate the term, and likewise prolong it.

When all these things have been completed, after the notary and witnesses have gone out, let the fathers proclaim themselves before the presidents, six or seven at a time, beginning with the juniors up to and including the presidents themselves, and let them receive the salutary penances imposed on them. Then let all read, except one president:

I confess to God, to blessed Mary, to all the saints, and to you, father, that I have sinned exceedingly, through my fault, by pride, thought, speech, deed, and omission. I beg you, pray for me.

And that president shall read the absolution as follows:

May almighty God, through the intercession of blessed Mary and of all the saints, have mercy on you, and forgive you all your sins, and bring you to eternal life. Amen.

By the authority of almighty God and of the ecclesiastical keys granted in this matter to our order, we absolve you from ecclesiastical censures, and restore you to the communion of the Church and to participation in the sacraments; and we dispense with you and rehabilitate you for the execution of acts to be done, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

And when some psalm has been imposed for satisfaction, let all rise; and the same president, kneeling before the other presidents, shall read, “I confess to God.” One of the presidents shall read over him the absolution as above, with the psalm.

And note that this absolution is one of jurisdiction, and that clause which many thought should be added ought not to be placed in it: “and from your sins.” For sacramental absolution, which must be preceded by a special confession of sins, has this clause. But it must be known that this absolution avails only this much: namely, by absolving from censures, if any had been incurred through neglect of the statutes of the order and of the chapter. And just as sacramental absolution absolves from fault, so that of jurisdiction absolves from temporal and spiritual punishment.

When these things have been completed, an end shall be made for each. Yet it must be known that if some advantage or necessity is pressing, the lord presidents may prolong the chapter further, until everything is well and maturely determined. At the end, one of the presidents, if time permits, shall give the fathers a brief exhortation before the blessing, concerning these or similar matters.

Venerable fathers, since now, with God’s favor, we have celebrated this our provincial chapter, lest, as we depart from one another, we forget because of their multitude the things that we have heard, listen patiently to the brief admonition that I make. We exhort you first of all that each of you remember within himself what the Rule says: “Let the abbot know that the fault of the shepherd falls upon him, whatever lack of profit the father of the household shall have been able to find in his sheep,” etc. And let him add, exhorting as the Lord gives him, concerning the preservation of pure religion, the faithful carrying out of profession, peace and charity and goodwill toward all, etc. Finally, let them depart from their lodgings honorably, after paying what is owed, with the knowledge of the host, not secretly but openly, etc. And let the abbots publish the statutes of this chapter to each of their subjects, and have two Masses sung conventually, one for the living and the other for the deceased brothers of our order; and let them see that the other prayers enjoined are fulfilled, and that the recess is publicly read in their monasteries to the brothers in necessary matters.

When these things have been completed, let the blessing be given by the president, as is customary, while all bow moderately.

Save your servants, O my God, who hope in you.

The Lord be with you.

And with your spirit.

Be present, O Lord, to our supplications, and direct the way of your servants in the prosperity of your salvation, so that amid all through the changes of this way and this life, may they always be protected by your aid. Through Christ our Lord.

When these things have been completed, all should go to their own places, except the presidents and officials, if they have anything to arrange, reckon, or pay. These things I have written only concerning the manner and order of celebrating a provincial chapter; although not everything to be done is contained in it, nevertheless it contains many things useful here for such matters, each of which does not refuse to undergo the examination of the lord presidents.

Bull of the Council of Basel on the reform of the Order of Saint Benedict throughout the province of Mainz.

The sacrosanct general synod of Basel, lawfully assembled in the Holy Spirit and representing the universal Church, to the beloved sons of the Church, all and singular presidents and visitors deputed everywhere, and to be deputed in the future, for future provincial chapters of the black monks: greeting and the blessing of almighty God.

Among the many cares by which we are distracted amid the varied affairs and business of the universal Church, that care especially stirs and moves our minds by which regular orders and places dedicated to the yoke of holiness may flourish again in spiritual matters. Therefore we willingly devote effective solicitude to this end, so that those orders and places which have incurred the reproach of deformity may be brought back to the paths of due reform, and, with the Lord continually directing them, may receive increase in these same spiritual matters and also in temporal ones.

Indeed, a petition lately presented to us by the beloved sons of the Church, the religious men of the Order of the black monks of this nation, contained that, although previously the fathers had included certain salutary articles concerning the reform of that order, nevertheless some of the subjects of this order and nation, when the visitors or provincial reformers come to them, do not allow themselves to be reformed according to the form of those articles, taking as their pretext that such articles did not proceed from us, and that, if we should ordain some reform, they would receive it.

Therefore, on behalf of the religious men of this nation, humble supplication was made to us that we would deign to command that reform be carried out in all monasteries of the nation and order in which stricter regular observance does not prevail, according to the content and form of the aforesaid articles.

We, therefore, whose principal concern this is, and who have been gathered into one by divine providence for this purpose, that the saving reform of the Church of God may steadfastly take place and persevere in head and members, considering that articles of this kind are in conformity with written law and the Rule of blessed Benedict, and that they ought to have place and to be observed not only in the aforesaid nation but in all and singular other nations, monasteries, and places of the said order to which such reform applies, and wishing also to provide opportunely concerning the premises, command your discretion by these writings that you and each of you, as pertains and for the time will pertain to the office of each, as often as it shall seem expedient to your consciences, which we burden in this regard, faithfully and diligently exercise the office of visitation and reform in all monasteries and places of the often-mentioned order in which stricter regular observance does not prevail, according to the content and form of the said articles, the tenor of which we have caused to be noted below word for word, by the authority of the universal Church.

For we, so that the desired fruits may follow from the zeal of such visitation and reform, grant and bestow upon you full and free faculty and authority to correct and reform, by salutary remedies, all and singular abbots and other presidents, and persons of whatever state, rank, order, and condition they may be, of the monasteries and places which it shall fall to you to visit, according to the quality and gravity of the offenses perpetrated by them from time to time, and according to the canonical sanctions and the regular statutes of the said order, as you shall see to be fitting for the salvation of souls and for the condition and indemnities of the monasteries and places themselves.

to absolve the abbots and other presidents and persons of this kind, and any of them, if they humbly seek it, from all and each sentences, censures, and penalties of excommunication, suspension, and interdict by which they shall be found bound for the time, or which perhaps shall happen to be promulgated against them in any way in the execution of this office, in the customary form of the Church, after a salutary penance and the other things that by law are to be enjoined have been imposed on them according to the measure of their fault; also to publish and announce the aforesaid articles, and to have them received and observed by all subjects; and to dispose, ordain, establish, and execute all and each other matter necessary or opportune in the premises and concerning them in any way; and to restrain contradictors and rebels by ecclesiastical censure and the other remedies of law, calling in for this, if need be, the aid of the secular arm.

No apostolic constitutions, statutes, or customs of the aforesaid monasteries, places, and order, strengthened by oath, apostolic confirmation, or any other firmness, nor any other contrary things whatsoever, shall stand in the way. Nor shall it stand in the way if to the monasteries, places, and order, to the abbots and other presidents and persons, or to any others, jointly or individually, an indult has been granted by the Apostolic See that they are in no way bound to admit others to visit or otherwise act beyond and contrary to the privileges or indults granted to them, and that they cannot be compelled to this, or excommunicated, or that they themselves or monasteries and places of this kind cannot be placed under interdict or suspension, by letters that do not make full and express, word-for-word mention of such an indult; nor shall any apostolic privileges, exemptions, or indulgences, general or special, of whatever tenor they may be, by which, because they are not expressly or fully inserted in the presents, the exercise of your jurisdiction in this matter could in any way be impeded, stand in the way, since, as regards this, we do not wish them to avail them in any way.

XXXVI

On Absolution.

We will, moreover, that each of the presidents and persons mentioned whom you shall judge should be absolved from such sentences, censures, and penalties, or from any of them, ought and shall be bound, when the impediment has ceased, canonically to render satisfaction within a competent peremptory term to be fixed by you to each person to whom satisfaction may perhaps have to be rendered on that account. Otherwise, when the term has elapsed, they shall by that very fact fall back into their former sentences, censures, and penalties.

The tenor of the aforesaid articles, as they have been set forth, follows and is this:

Articles for Reform.

Because regular discipline and the beauty of religion have almost wholly fallen, and have miserably collapsed, to the grave scandal of the whole order of black monks and to the dishonor, reproach, and contempt of all the professors of that order, and, what is more horrible, to the deadly harm of souls: for, alas, every comeliness has been taken away from religion. She who formerly could glory in the Lord, saying, “I am black in the lowliness of my habit, and beautiful in the holiness of morals and observance,” now, alas, by a certain monastic coarseness, has been perverted into wantonness and insolence, so that neither in reality nor even in appearance does any image of her former beauty now seem to remain.

Therefore we, the abbots and other religious of the said order gathered in the sacred Council of Basel, wishing with such great and most earnest desires and with one zeal to provide against such great and enormous scandals, and for the reform of the same order, lest it hereafter suffer a more grievous ruin, which may God avert, have come and gathered together into one. Devoutly and wholesomely attending with daily labors to the aforesaid reform, we have set forth certain beginnings and foundations of religion, so that, beginning from these, deformed monasteries may be able to advance toward the fruit of monastic profession; and out of abundant caution, from the Rule from the Rule of our most blessed father Benedict and from the constitutions of lord Pope Benedict XII, of happy memory, which we have judged ought to be observed in all monasteries and places of the said order in which the stricter regular observance is not in force.

Yet for this reason we do not intend, as indeed we cannot, to derogate in any way from the other things contained in the aforesaid Rule, even if they are not now explained by us, or from the praiseworthy constitutions of the fathers and the stricter observances, so that the religious of the said order are bound to them as before.

First, just as the said Rule of Saint Benedict took very solicitous care concerning the divine work, we, following it, ordain that the divine office, both by day and by night, be celebrated devoutly, deliberately, with pauses, not racing through it, not cutting it short, at the proper hours, as is contained in the Rule of our most blessed father. And as soon as the signal has been heard, leaving everything that may be in their hands, they shall hasten to it with the greatest speed, yet with gravity, lest frivolity find encouragement, so that nothing is preferred to the work of God.

And so that they may not be able to excuse themselves on the pretext of ignorance because they did not hear the signal, we will that the recitation of matins, which is to begin at midnight or thereabout, of prime, and of vespers last at least more than a quarter of an hour.

But whoever has not come to the aforesaid office shall be punished without remission, as is contained in the Rule.

On Confession and the Celebration of Masses. Article 2.

We also will and ordain that the abbots and the other aforesaid members of the order confess, celebrate, and communicate as is contained in the constitutions of Pope Benedict XII concerning the celebration of masses.

And all those who, according to the law and the Benedictine sanctions, ought to have been established in sacred orders or in the order of priesthood shall be promoted to these within a year; and against those who are negligent the visitors shall proceed as they can by law.

XXXVII

On the Daily Chapter of Faults. Article 3.

We further will and ordain that every day, in places where there are six monks, and in other places where it is customary, after prime if only one mass is said, but if two are said, after the first-mentioned mass or at another customary hour, the daily chapter shall be held. In it, after the martyrology and the reading of the Rule, which is to be explained in the vernacular by the one presiding over that chapter, or by another whom he has ordered, before they proceed to other matters, the faults and excesses of the negligent or delinquent shall be punished.

On the Books and Ornaments of the Church. Article 4.

We will that every abbot or presiding officer, when he has come to his monastery, immediately within a month provide for a clean and proper vessel and place where the sacred Eucharist is to be kept; and also that the books, with the other ornaments concerning the divine office and the monastery, be preserved with diligent custody.

On the Form and Decency of Clothing and Tonsure. Article 5.

Since, through the decency of outward habit, the professed and novices of the said order ought to show moral integrity and the dignity of religion, we establish and ordain that all wear large and broad tonsures, so that the circle of them does not exceed the space or thickness of two transverse fingers. And let them carry themselves decently in garments, habits, and footwear, according to the Clementine Ne in agro and the constitution of the aforesaid Pope Benedict XII on the form and decency of garments: namely, that they wear tunics and garments nearest to the outer habit, of black or brown color according to the custom usually observed among them, round and reaching to the ankles, not slit nor marked by any other deformity, having broad sleeves extending as far as the wrist, in no way buttoned or tied; yet not so broad that their width extends beyond the wrist with the thumb raised, nor around the mouth of the elbow, as the abuse of certain persons has it, beyond what is proper.

so that the arm can easily be turned and inserted. Let them be content with almuces of skins in place of hoods. Yet, with the abbot’s permission, they may use decent hoods in the proper places where they are accustomed to wear them, split over the shoulders to a length of at least four transverse fingers.

They are not to wear sendal in their garments for linings, or miniver, vair, or any other costly material; but for the said linings let them use only the skins of lambs or young sheep, or at least other cloths that are not costly. Nor are the linings to appear in any way above the collar, or at the hems of the garments or sleeves.

Concerning the Clothing of Those Traveling. Article 6.

Further, when it happens that they set out outside the monastery, they are to wear a frock, or a cowl, or a cloak; and beneath the cloak, if they wear it, they are to have a cowl or scapular.

Concerning the Clothing of Novices and Conversi. Article 7.

Novices, however, are to use a cowl, inside and outside the monastery, open on both sides. Conversi are to use a scapular with a hood attached to it and closed, inside and outside the monastery.

Concerning the Length and Width of Garments. Article 8.

But because in the aforesaid habits some use garments more ample and longer, and others less so than is fitting, for this reason we have thought it necessary to insert here the length and width of the aforesaid garments, which we wish to be observed generally. And first, beginning with the hood of the frock, we ordain that its width is not to reach the elbow by the thickness of two transverse fingers; nor may it be narrower, or so short, that it does not extend as far as the middle of the elbow and of the upper bone near the shoulder. At the back, however, it is to extend at least as far as the belt, and is not to extend beyond it by more than four fingers.

The length of the sleeves is to extend one cubit beyond the hand and no more; and their width is not to exceed one and a half cubits. The frock below is to be so wide that steps can easily be taken within it.

And what has been said about the frock we wish to be understood of the cowl also, except for the sleeves, since cowls have none. Within the monastery, however, in places where there are twelve monks, all are to use frocks or large cowls. In other places, however, where there is not so large a congregation, they are to use cowls, not frocks, except for the president of the monastery and the one second after him, whom we wish to wear the frock in every case. Yet during work and the divine office beneath the alb, and while riding beneath the cloak, they may wear a scapular at least half a cubit wide.

And they are to wear boots or high strapped shoes, so that their width covers a space of four fingers on the leg above the ankle. But if in any of the foregoing matters they have not worn the habits as set out above, beyond the penalties inflicted by law we wish them to be punished by their superiors in their religious house, or, if they have no superior, by the visitors of the provincial chapter, in such a way that it may serve as an example to the rest.

That Monks Should Live in Common in the Refectory Without Eating Meat. Article 9.

Likewise, the brothers are to live and eat in common in the refectory, in which no one at all is to eat meat. And the visitors are to be diligent in seeing that they cause the constitution of Benedict concerning the eating of and abstinence from meats to be observed inviolably.
