Concerning the Reading to Be Done at the Brothers’ Table. Article 10.

At the brothers’ table, too, sacred reading is not to be lacking; and the one who is to read for the whole week is to enter on Sunday after the blessing, as is stated in the Rule, chapter 38, concerning the weekly reader.

How Monks Should Sleep. Article 11.

Each monk is to sleep clothed in his own bed, in the same place if this can be done, or at least in groups of ten or twenty; but not in separate rooms, especially if they are not suitably partitioned, so that the bedding in them can be plainly and clearly seen, according to the manner of their way of life.

according to the abbot’s arrangement; and they shall not use feather mattresses.

If, however, chambers are found in the dormitory, we order that they be destroyed by the visitors or by their command, or suitably barred off.

Concerning silence in four places. Article 12.

Silence shall be observed in the oratory, dormitory, refectory, and cloister. And after Compline no one may say anything, except as is contained in the Rule. And before the said Compline, let there be read the Collation of the Fathers or some other edifying work.

Concerning the porter of the monastery. Article 13.

At the gate of each monastery let one porter or doorkeeper, provident and discreet, be appointed, so that without the permission of the abbot or of another president no one may be granted freedom to leave that monastery. But if anyone goes out without such permission, let him be subjected to fitting and due penalties, as is contained in the constitutions of Benedict XII concerning permission to go outside the monastery.

Furthermore, he shall be attentive that he in no way permit women to enter the monastery.

That no one from the order of mendicants be received into our order. Article 14.

Moreover, since we have heard that certain abbots and other presidents in monasteries have received mendicant religious as monks without the permission of their own superiors, and afterward, what is worse, permit them to wander about to the detriment of their souls and the scandal of religion, we forbid them to presume such things henceforth. And those whom they have already received, unless by authority and mandate of the Apostolic See or by sufficient permission, they shall be bound to recall as quickly as they can, together with others wandering outside the monastery, or at least within a year, to the monastery; otherwise they shall be punished by the visitors of the provincial chapter with grave penalties.

Concerning nuns. Article 15.

But the things that have been said concerning monasteries of men we wish also to be observed in monasteries of nuns, as regards the articles applicable to them. Wishing nevertheless, and ordaining,

that they be kept under due and perpetual enclosure, as is contained in the constitution of Boniface that begins Periculoso, concerning the state of monks, and as this sacred Council of Basel commands to be observed, we instruct the visitors of the chapter, in virtue of holy obedience, to apply diligence in this matter.

Concerning the master of novices. Article 16.

Likewise we ordain that abbots and other presidents in their monasteries shall have suitable and sufficient masters, who shall introduce their novices to the elementary branches of learning; and afterward, once they have been instructed, shall suitably send them, according to the form of the statutes of the aforesaid Benedict XII, to the general studies, assigning them a pension.

Concerning the number of monks. Article 17.

We wish and ordain that in every monastery where the resources and revenues suffice, the number of monks established from the foundation shall be maintained; or, if they do not suffice, let as many be maintained as can conveniently be supported. Thus, under pretext of any privilege, pact, transaction, or custom which is called corruption, no one shall be excused, especially since we reject that corrupt practice by which some say that they can receive no one unless he is noble. For although nobles, other things being equal, are preferred in reception, nevertheless others are not excluded on this account, nor ought they to be excluded.

That the goods of monasteries are not to be divided, but provision is to be made for all in common. Article 18.

Since all the goods of a monastery are ordained for the support of the monks and for bearing other necessities, from which provision must be made for each according to the requirement of all, as is contained in the Rule, chapter 33, it is utterly absurd that abbots and officials should belch forth superfluity from the revenues of the monastery, while poor cloistered monks lack clothing, food, or other necessities, especially in bodily sickness, so that they are often compelled to turn back to the assistance of their parents. We wish and ordain that, notwithstanding the divisions of burdens among the abbot and officials among themselves, all

let the necessary things be provided to the monks from the goods of the monastery generally. And for doing this, let there be an allocation extending even to the revenues of whatever officials and of the abbot alike. Nor may that division, nor any other custom, avail in opposition for the abbot himself or for any officials. We wish the visitors of the chapter to attend especially to this matter.

On Places Not to Be Leased Out. Article 19.

Let them not lease out places of the order except with observance of Benedict’s constitution concerning places not to be leased out, which we wish to be firmly observed, both with respect to the persons to whom they are leased and also with respect to the other circumstances.

On Loans. Article 20.

We also will that, when loans have to be made, likewise the constitution of the aforesaid Pope Benedict XII concerning loans and sales be provided for; and we most strictly command that it likewise be observed, under the penalties added there and others to be imposed by the aforesaid visitors of the chapter.

On Inventories of Monasteries. Article 21.

So that it may more clearly be seen and known who are dissipators of the monastery’s goods or restorers of them, we will that, at the assumption of office of any abbot or other president, inventories be made, as is contained in the constitutions of the aforesaid Pope Benedict XII concerning inventories.

On Monks Who Own Property. Article 22.

Against the vice of ownership, let what is contained in chapter 33 of the Rule be observed, together with what is contained on this matter under the same title in the constitution of the lord Pope Benedict XII, and according to the form of common law.

On the Resignation of Officials. Article 23.

We will that all benefices or offices which are assigned for supporting the burdens, both in food and in clothing, of the monks, if, at the abbot’s command, after having been warned three times, they refuse to pay or provide to the religious what they owe, the said abbot may and must, with the counsel of three or four senior monks of the monastery, remove them from the said offices or benefices and establish others in their place, notwithstanding any appeal

--- Page 084 --- presidents, to make their residence and customary dwelling within the bounds of the monastery, and not to make their stay in remote castles, except rarely and at times only for the sake of moderate recreation or to secure some public advantage.

That abbots and presidents of monasteries celebrate there on solemnities. Article 28. We also will that the said abbots celebrate there on the principal solemnities and on others, according to the custom and practice hitherto laudably observed in the said monasteries.

That monks not live with their parents. Article 29. We forbid abbots to permit their religious to make a long stay and residence with their parents or other laypersons, or to be entangled in the services of such people. Indeed, if one prior could not live honorably and fittingly in his priory with at least one religious, let him be brought back to the monastery, according to the constitution of Pope Benedict XII and of the Council of Vienne which begins Ne in agro.

Of beneficed monks to be sent to general studies. But if any priors or beneficed monks wish to go to study, let the greatest care be taken that, under the appearance and shadow of study, they do not wish to wander about in cities. For this reason, when they are seen to be useless and neglectful of study, let them be sent back to the cloister or to their benefice, if, as has been said, they can live there. And the general prior of the monks in study should take diligent care over this matter; and we will that this prior be diligently visited and corrected by the provincial chapter within whose boundaries such a study is located.

Of the chapter of faults of monks who are students. Article 31. We will that the prior of the monks who are students of the said order hold his chapter every fifteen days, and there correct and punish, according to the form of the Rule, any student monks whenever they have behaved scandalously in life or dress. Moreover, he must inquire diligently into this and appoint trustworthy investigators from the order itself in the same study.

According to the form of the constitution of lord Benedict, Pope XII, no general prior shall continue in study except for one year. And we will and decree that the same prior be a formed bachelor in theology, or licensed in decrees, or a man of advanced and proven religious life. This prior shall also have authority to punish the contumacious and rebellious by bodily imprisonment, but with the consent of four or five notable religious present in the study, to be chosen by the religious of the said order studying there. Furthermore, with the consent of the aforesaid persons, when he sees any to be incorrigible and excessively scandalous, he may send them back to the cloister or to their own priory.

Item, we will and ordain that all religious coming to the study present themselves to the said prior within five days, and that he have all of them written down in one book. Nor shall they leave the study unless the cause of their return has first been made known to the said prior. If this prior sees that the cause is unjust on the abbot’s part, then let him take care diligently to inform the visitors of the provincial chapter, so that they may make provision concerning this.

That monks not go on pilgrimage. Article 32. We forbid that abbots permit their monks, under the pretext of some devotion to some saint, or of indulgences to be sought in some place, to go out from their places, especially beyond the boundaries of their diocese, unless perhaps to visit certain regions by whose example they can be edified, or which they can edify; but this rarely and with great caution. And no prior or beneficed monk shall remain outside his own diocese for five days unless he has obtained permission from his abbot. Otherwise the guilty shall be punished most sharply by the visitors of the provincial chapter.

Of the increase of penalties. Article 33. The aforesaid visitors shall impose the more serious penalties of the constitution Ne in agro against any religious so disorderly or forgetful of their profession.

who do not shrink from carrying hunting birds on their fist after the manner of secular nobles, or having them carried before them by their attendants.

That provisions are not to be given in money. Article 34. We forbid provisions, clothing, and other necessities to be supplied to monks in money or revenues in any way, notwithstanding any constitution or ordinance whatsoever. And in this matter the constitution of the aforesaid Pope Benedict XII is to be observed. We also will that the aforesaid clothing and provisions be supplied decently to Benedictine religious at the appointed times.

On the vice of incontinence. Article 35. The visitors of the chapter also are to exercise exact diligence by inquiring whether in any place there are any persons marked by incontinence. And where they find this to be so, especially among superiors, or find persons conniving at the incontinence of others, they are to take every care to purge out that vice with due punishment. And if perhaps they cannot do this because of favor shown to persons, they are to report it to the provincial chapter. The said visitors are to inquire whether abbots are too fleshly in distributing the offices and benefices of their monastery, so that they pay more regard to the advancement of their relatives and blood-kin, and whether on account of them the monastery suffers ruin or loss in spiritual matters and is damaged in temporal matters; and they are to rebuke the guilty very severely and report them to the provincial chapter. They are also to inquire whether an abbot, in pride of heart, treats his monks not in brotherhood, as though he were not one of them; and whether he does not permit them to speak anything, even charitably, for the good of the monastery and of morals; whether he himself, by his own fury, is overturning his house; and whomever they find guilty they are to take care to correct diligently, or else denounce them to the provincial chapter.

On the obligation of these constitutions with respect to penalty. Article 36. By these things we do not understand that the aforesaid provisions bind more to fault than they formerly bound, but only to penalty.

On the constitutions of the supreme pontiffs. Article 37.

XLII

We also will that the declarations of the Roman pontiffs issued concerning the aforesaid Benedictine constitutions have force in the foregoing matters.

That visitors be diligent in all things. Article 38. In all the foregoing articles it is committed to the visitation of the visitors that they be solicitous for the profit of souls and, according to the disposition alike of persons and of places, act prudently in all things.

That laymen are not to be appointed over the needs of the monastery. Article 39. Laymen are not to be appointed over offices, nor monks to receive and collect the goods of the monastery and distribute them, except insofar as they are subject to and servants of the officials themselves of the monasteries, and are bound to render an account to them of what has been received and distributed. Given at Basel, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the year from the birth of the Lord 1439. Here ends the bull of the Council of Basel for the reform of the order, transmitted to the chapter.

Here begins the constitution of Lord Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, legate, concerning visitation.

Nicholas, by divine mercy cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, legate of the Apostolic See throughout Germany, to the visitors of the province, etc.

On the life and morals of the visitors, especially while they are visiting. Since formerly, and below. Therefore, first of all, we will and, under appeal to the promise made to us and to the strict examination of the Last Judgment, enjoin upon you that at all times, and especially during your visitation, in all conduct, life, morals, and discipline, you take care to bear and conduct yourselves so religiously, holily, and honorably that to the others to be visited by you, not only by word but also by example, you may offer a model of complete perfection. During the time of visitation you are to proceed in suitable dress, with a household and mounts appropriate and honorable, not excessive, so that each of you is content with a chapel and household and with three horses.

Moderate

Let refreshment without grumbling suffice you. The eating of meat, except in the case of illness according to the permission of the Rule, and also the acceptance of any offered gift, even one not suspect, shall in no way be lawful for you.

The form of visitation and the manner of proceeding.

With gentleness preserve the censure of discipline, correcting crimes and excesses without any acceptance of persons; strive to extend the offices of charity and kindness to all. Take care to recall those at discord to concord, diligently exhorting prelates to solicitude and vigilance concerning the souls entrusted to them, and to consider how much more perfect they ought to be than others, to whom they have promised that they would teach the way of perfection; how grave a danger hangs over them, since in the strict examination of the last judgment they will be bound to render an exact account for each and all of those entrusted to them; and that all, both prelates and subjects, should fulfill their profession, solemnly made in the person of the prelate before God, who does not deceive, and the vows that their lips have uttered, without which it is impossible for them to be saved; likewise, how sweet is the yoke of the Lord and light his burden to all of good will.

But because among very many the conversations of exhortation make little progress unless the censure of coercion also comes in, therefore in the monasteries or places that you shall visit for the time being, after the customary conference of salutary exhortation has first been given, in order to complete the act of visitation, once a corporal oath has been received from all that they will speak the truth in their examination, you shall proceed according to the tenor of the commission delivered to you by our other letters, even through the coercion of the censures and penalties expressed therein, establishing, ordaining, and carrying out whatever will be opportune there for introducing and continuing regular observance and discipline.

Take particular care that the prelates of the monasteries that you shall visit are so instructed and imbued by the ministry of this visitation of yours that, in decent habit and tonsure, in honesty of life, gravity of morals, the word of doctrine, and the example of holiness, they may preside over their subjects laudably and fruitfully, and correct the excesses of their subjects according to canonical and regular statutes. Let them recall all their fugitive and absent monks to their own monastery as soon as they are able, within a suitable term fixed for them by us for this purpose, except only those absent monks who are bound to the care of annexed parish churches, so that they may live there under regular discipline and observance.

Let all things be common to abbots, priors, and provosts, and indeed to one another, in fraternal charity.

Let no monk be permitted to use the damnable private ownership of things or goods acquired in any way whatever, but let all things be brought back to common use.

Concerning the vice of incontinence.

Against the incontinent, both prelates and subjects, let the strictness of a graver censure proceed, so that not only are public vices of incontinence punished or coerced by vengeance, but also every matter or occasion from which a suspicion of incontinence could arise is removed from the midst.

Concerning the three substantial elements of religion to be observed.

Let the three principal substantial elements of religion be observed most fully by all, so that no dispensation or contrary custom may avail anyone against them.

That monks should keep silence.

Let silence be observed in these places: in the oratory, dormitory, refectory, and cloister, and in the other places and at the customary times.

How the monks are to take refreshment.

Let the brothers take refreshment together under table reading, to be continued until the end of the meal. The eating of meat is to be most strictly forbidden to all, at every time and place, except only in a case permitted by the Rule.

How the brothers are to sleep.

Let all sleep together in one dormitory, as far as possibility permits, girded with cords or belts.

with cords or belts, upon mats or mattresses, or blankets, in no way using linen sheets or linen shirts. Monks are not to sleep in places with boys.

Concerning the enclosure of monasteries.

They are to apply careful and due concern for the enclosure of the monasteries themselves; nor is it permitted for any religious, except certain officials, to go beyond the bounds of the immunity of his cloister without the special permission of his superior. Let all observe the fasts appointed both by the Church and by the rule.

Concerning the divine office.

Monks are to perform the divine office, by day and by night alike, reverently, as is fitting, and distinctly, at the proper hours. When it has been completed, they are to devote themselves to reading or to manual labors, according to the demands of the time and of their duties and under the direction of the rule of blessed Benedict. Books are to be distributed to the brothers at the appointed time. The beds of the brothers are to be inspected from time to time because of particular work.

Concerning holding the daily chapter of faults.

A chapter of faults is to be held daily; in it, after the readings of the martyrology and the rule have first been completed, they are to proceed to the exposition of the rule and to the examination and correction of faults.

Concerning the celebration of masses, confession, and communion of monks.

Let the abbot celebrate or hear mass every day. Monks who are priests and reside in monasteries are to prepare themselves to celebrate at least once each week. Those below the priesthood are to confess at least once each week and receive communion on the first Sunday of each month.

How the brothers are to provide for the sick and for guests.

They are to provide suitably for monks in food, drink, clothing, and other necessities, according to the determination of the rule. Suitable places are also to be assigned in the monasteries themselves, both for the sick and for guests arriving for a time; care and humanity are to be shown to them according to the disposition of the same rule. They are to bring guests to prayer, and a sacred reading is to be read to them for edification, and they are to wash their feet.

Page 092

With due moderation, let the highest care be taken that the monasteries not be burdened with unbearable loads of debts; that their goods not be scattered or alienated uselessly and without cause; and that any alienated goods, if there are any, be diligently recovered.

Concerning the preservation of goods and privileges.

Abbots, presidents, or rectors are diligently to defend and preserve the rights of their monasteries. The fruits, revenues, and income of the same monasteries are to be converted to common uses and benefits. Books, vestments, crosses, chalices, and other vessels and ornaments of the treasury, privileges, rights, letters, and the common seals of the convent are to be kept under lock and in safe places.

Rectors of monasteries are ordered to render accounts to their visitors every year.

Prelates or rectors are to give full certification to their visitors, by whom they have been visited, concerning the state of their temporal affairs. But the prelates themselves and each of their officials are also to render a lawful account of their administrations to the convents every year. Abbots are to abstain altogether from superfluous horses, hounds, and birds, from hounds and hunting birds, and from other animals and beasts by which the inner man is defiled; both they themselves and their religious and household are to do so.

It is not permitted for monks to have weapons within the precincts of the monastery, nor for any religious to become co-fathers.

No religious person within the precincts of the monastery is to presume to have weapons, or to contract any co-fatherhood or co-motherhood in any way.

Concerning nuns and their enclosure.

Nevertheless, we will that the foregoing, insofar as it can concern abbesses and nuns, be extended to their monasteries that stand within the limits of your visitation, with perpetual enclosure to be established by you with apostolic authority, according to the decree Periculoso, book 6.

Concerning those who wish to pass from unreformed monasteries to the reform.

Nicholas, by divine mercy cardinal legate of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Peter ad Vincula. To all the faithful of Christ throughout the province of Mainz, etc. Concerning the enclosures of nuns.

Quoniam multorum, etc., section 1. We strictly command and order that no man, of whatever status, dignity, or preeminence, even if he is exempt, under penalty of excommunication latae sententiae, which we pronounce in these writings, shall henceforth, after the execution of this our mandate, presume in any way to enter any monastery of nuns in the city and province of Mainz, unless he has license from the ordinary, or from the person to whom this belongs, according to the provision of common law, and otherwise in cases permitted by law. But if anyone attempts to do the contrary, we will that he, by that very fact and without any further declaration, be avoided by all as excommunicate, both in divine services and outside them; and wherever he may be, for as long as he remains there, the strictest interdict shall be observed in that place.

Likewise, nuns are forbidden to leave their monasteries under penalty of excommunication. Under penalty of excommunication latae sententiae and of interdict, we command each and every nun of the aforesaid monasteries that, after notice of the present letters, they shall by no means presume to leave their monastery, even with permission granted by the abbess and prioress or by any other woman, except as common law permits; nor shall any one of them presume to do so. Rather, we will that anyone doing the contrary be excommunicate, and that the place wherever she may be be under interdict, without any further declaration.

And we command, under a like penalty latae sententiae, all chaplains and priests who have certain knowledge of this to publish that nun as excommunicate and that place where she may be as under interdict.

XLV

Constitutions of the provincial chapters of the Order of Saint Benedict throughout the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg.

Preface.

Since, for one who wishes to know the individual statutes of the order, namely what and of what kind they are that have been issued by our most devout predecessors, the fathers, in provincial chapters, it would be laborious to run through all the acts and recesses of those chapters because of their length; and yet, lest so great a labor impede the pious desire of knowing, since it is also full of tedium for each person to carry with him the larger volumes of the aforesaid recesses when chapters are to be celebrated according to custom, I undertake to gather those same statutes together, abbreviated into one work. And this is the order of this labor: I shall pass over the sanctions of the supreme pontiffs, and also the decrees of general councils made for the celebration of chapters of this sort, so that what must be done or judged in the remaining statutes may be recognized more easily. Then, with as much brevity and diligence as I can, I shall summarize the times, places, and statutes of the individual provincial chapters celebrated in our province from the time of the Council of Constance. I believe this labor will be useful enough for posterity, if they decide to add to these things what must be established. But if it pleases no one, which I rather fear, I nevertheless pray that I be pardoned, since I have sought to satisfy not my own will, but that of the fathers, who desired and requested this.

Innocent III, in the general council. That a provincial chapter is to be held every three years.

In each kingdom or province, preserving the right of the diocesan bishops, a common chapter of abbots and of priors who do not have their own abbots, and who have not been accustomed to celebrate such a chapter, shall be held every three years. All who have no canonical impediment shall come to it at one designated monastery.

with this moderation observed: that none of them bring more than six mounts and eight persons.

In the beginnings of this new practice, however, let them summon two neighboring abbots of the Cistercian Order to provide them suitable counsel and assistance, since through long custom they are more fully instructed in celebrating chapters of this kind. These abbots, without contradiction, shall associate with themselves two from among the others whom they think expedient; and those four shall preside over the whole chapter, so that from this no one of them assumes for himself the authority of a prelate, since, when expedient, it can be changed by prudent deliberation. Let a chapter of this kind be celebrated continuously for several fixed days according to the custom of the Cistercian Order. In it let there be diligent discussion concerning the reform of the order and regular observance. And what shall have been established, with those four approving, shall be inviolably observed, every excuse, contradiction, and appeal removed; nevertheless provision shall be made where the chapter ought to be celebrated at the following term.

And those who have assembled shall lead a common life and pay proportionally all common expenses, so that if not all can stay in the same house, at least several may stay in different houses and eat in the same manner. In the same chapter let religious and circumspect persons also be appointed, who, according to the form prescribed to them, shall strive in our stead to visit each abbey of the same kingdom or province, not only of monks but also of nuns, correcting and reforming whatever they see to need the office of correction and reform. Thus, if they learn that the rector of a place must be entirely removed from administration, let them denounce it to the proper bishop, so that he may see to removing him. If he does not do this, let the visitors refer the matter to the examination of the Apostolic See. We will and command that this same thing be observed for regular canons according to their order.

But if in this new practice any difficulty should arise which cannot be resolved by the aforesaid persons, let it be referred without scandal to the judgment of the Apostolic See, while the other things which have been provided by common deliberation are to be observed without opposition.

Furthermore, diocesan bishops shall take care to reform the monasteries subject to them in such a way that, when the aforesaid visitors come to them, they find in them more that is worthy of commendation than of correction, taking the greatest care that through them the said monasteries are not burdened in due obligations; for we wish the rights of superiors to be observed in such a way that we do not wish injuries to inferiors to be endured.

Moreover, we strictly command both diocesan bishops and the persons who preside over chapters to be celebrated that, by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal removed, they restrain advocates, patrons, vice-lords, rectors, consuls, magnates, knights, or any others, lest they presume to injure monasteries in persons or property. And if perhaps they have injured them, they shall not neglect to compel them to satisfaction, so that the monks may be able to serve God more freely and peacefully.

Clement V, in the Council of Vienne, De statu monachorum, Ne in agro, in the Clementines, last section. For this, there is text in the Clementines, Frequens, De excessibus praelatorum, at the end. The same constitutions confirm this.

What Innocent IV, pope of happy memory, our predecessor, established concerning the condition of these monks, for a fuller cultivation of regular observance, concerning the use of shirts, the renunciation of private property, silence, the eating of meat, and the holding of their chapters every three years, and also concerning any other matters whatsoever: all these things we renew and approve, and expressly will and firmly decree that they be observed.

Benedict XII, in his constitutions: Concerning the penalty of those who do not come to the chapter.

We establish and ordain that in the provincial order or religion of the said black monks, as above, folio 25.

Pope Martin V to the abbots of the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg. If it happens that one of the presidents is absent or refuses to accept his office, let the others, with the counsel of the fathers, choose another.

Inclined by your honorable supplications and the supplications of the city, that in the celebration...

...the celebration of the provincial chapters of your order: if at any time it should happen that one or more of the presidents in those same chapters are unwilling to accept their office, or cannot conveniently be present at them, the other presidents, with the consent of the greater part of those then constituting the chapter, or, if none of the presidents is present, the others assembling for the celebration of the chapter, may appoint other suitable persons as presidents for these occasions only. By apostolic authority, by the tenor of these presents, we grant this.

So also that the aforesaid presidents may change the place chosen for celebrating a chapter of this kind and afterward found inconvenient for certain reasons, and may choose another place nearer to the former one, with postponement, as shall be expedient, of the fixed time for celebrating the chapter: by the same authority we grant this.

Benedict XII, in his constitutions.

Concerning subsidies and collections to be imposed in chapters.

Since in the often-mentioned constitution of the general council, among other things, it is expressed, etc., as above, fol. xxvii.

The same, in the same constitutions. Those coming to the chapters themselves shall have respectable servants with them, and, under penalty of excommunication latae sententiae, they shall beware of stirring up or causing, by themselves or through others, disturbances or impediments to chapters of this kind.

Again, we decree that each and every person coming to the same chapters shall not bring, cause to be brought, or permit mounts or attendants superfluous in number or excessive in any way; rather, we will and command them to be content with a number of mounts and attendants suitable to the status of each of them.

Moreover, those attendants themselves, and others whom they bring, cause to be brought, or keep, shall be humble and respectable, such that it can in no way be presumed that, by themselves or through other secular or regular persons, they would inflict harm upon any abbot, prior, administrator, official, monk, or anyone else coming with them or otherwise to the chapters themselves, or staying at them, or returning from them, or upon churches, monasteries, priories, or their other places...

--- Page 098 --- of whatever preeminence, dignity, status, or condition, who by himself or through another maliciously hinders, or knowingly and deliberately causes to be hindered, the free celebration of the aforesaid chapters; and whoever presumes to seize, or cause to be seized, those going to them, staying in them, or returning from them, or to detain or hinder them once seized, or to inflict losses, injuries, or offenses on them or on their attendants, in their persons or goods, on an occasion of this kind, namely so that the celebration of any of those chapters may be disturbed or impeded; likewise anyone of that order or religion who, under pretext of visitation, maliciously and deliberately commits the aforesaid acts, or any of them, by himself or through another, against the persons of abbots, priors, or other aforesaid superiors visiting their own subjects, or against the persons of visitors appointed in provincial chapters, or appointed by abbots, other prelates, principals, or priors of monks, or against their attendants, or against their goods; and anyone of the aforesaid order who maliciously hinders them in visitations, corrections, or executions of their process, or opposes them stubbornly and perversely, or consents to those doing the aforesaid things, by himself or through another, by procuring prayers, threats, letters, the help of powerful secular persons or laymen, or any other impediments maliciously; and anyone hindering the same order or the religion itself in making lawful contributions.

But the presidents in the aforesaid provincial and annual chapters, and any one of them, when it has been established to them simply and plainly that anyone from those aforesaid has incurred the aforesaid sentence of excommunication, shall solemnly publish that person throughout all nearby places of the same order or religion where it seems good to them, and shall have him published by others on apostolic authority; compelling by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside, those who do not obey them in this matter, until he has made fitting satisfaction and has been absolved by those presidents alone, or by at least two of them, on the aforesaid authority.

XLVIII

From the Council of Constance. When and why the provincial chapter was reestablished, and at what time.

Ancient authority teaches, and experience makes clear, that it is a small thing to establish laws, however renowned, unless they are duly committed to execution. In former times, at various dates, both the general council and Honorius, and also Benedict XII, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, are read to have issued, with much mature deliberation, salutary statutes concerning provincial chapters to be celebrated every three years in this religion and order, and concerning their general chapters to be held every year. These provincial chapters, and also general chapters, are reported to have been put into execution only rarely, and for a long time, in very many regions. From their omission many inconveniences in spiritual and temporal matters, and almost irrecoverable losses, have come upon this religion.

Therefore, since from the celebration of chapters of this kind there are no doubt accustomed to arise the correction of the depraved, the reform of morals, the avoidance of many evils, and the promotion of manifold good, we, who carry in the depths of charity the reform of this sacred religion and order, whose knowledge and veneration the teachings of the fathers display, have resolved to restore what has been omitted in this matter, and especially, before the holy council is dissolved, to appoint new executors of the said constitutions in the regions where the old ones are not being ruled according to their tenors. And now, beginning in the province of Mainz, in which at present we are staying, we will and ordain that the provincial chapter of abbots and priors, or provosts not having their own abbots, dwelling in the said province of Mainz and in the diocese of Bamberg, united to that province in the aforesaid constitutions of Benedict XII, be celebrated in this city of Constance, or in its suburb, namely in the monastery called Petershausen, of the said Order of Saint Benedict, beyond the bridge of this city, where the sacred general council is sitting; and in that council there are many abbots and superiors of this order from various regions, who will be able to provide fitting counsel and assistance in these matters for the aforesaid provincial chapters of the province of Mainz, and to direct them, since by long custom they are more fully informed in holding chapters of this kind.

In the same bull of the aforesaid council all the abbots and prelates of the whole province of Mainz and of the diocese of Bamberg of this order were summoned, so that on the day before the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord 1417, they should appear in person in the city of Constance, in the monastery of Petershausen, to hold such a provincial chapter. This was in fact done in this way. And from that time up to the present, in the aforesaid province, a chapter has been held every three years according to the constitutions of the supreme pontiffs.

The first provincial chapter was held at Constance in the year of the Lord 1417.

In the year of the Lord 1417, on the last day of February, in the tenth indiction, while the apostolic see was vacant, in the third year of the Council of Constance, the first provincial chapter of our order, of the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg, was held at Constance in the monastery of Petershausen. Presiding in it were the venerable fathers Ludovicus, abbot of the monastery of Tournus in the diocese of Chalon; Thomas, abbot of Ebrach; Sifridus, abbot of Ellwangen in the diocese of Augsburg; and Johannes, abbot of the monastery of St. George in the diocese of Constance.

Concerning the statutes issued in the same chapter.

In this provincial chapter many fathers were present, having been summoned by the general Council of Constance; and those who could not attend in person sent mandates through their proctors. And indeed in the same chapter several statutes for regular observance were issued, which, divided into individual rubrics,

I have inserted in the present pages.

With what reverence and discipline the work of God is to be performed.

Directing the eyes of our mind toward the reform of the order, we ordain that the day office and likewise the night office be celebrated devoutly, slowly, with pauses, not hurried through, not syncopated, and at suitable hours, as is contained in the Rule of our most holy father Benedict. To this, as soon as the signal has been heard, they shall leave everything that is in their hands and hasten together with all speed, yet with gravity, lest frivolity find fuel; and thus nothing is to be preferred to the work of God. And lest they be able to excuse themselves under the pretext of ignorance, saying that the signal was not heard, we will that the course of Matins, which we wish to begin in the middle of the night, and that of Prime and Vespers, last at least more than a quarter of an hour. Whoever does not come to the aforesaid divine office is to be punished without remission, as is contained in the Rule.

Concerning the chapter of faults.

We further will and ordain that each day, in places where there are six monks, and in other places where this is customary, after Prime, if only one Mass is said, but if there are two, after the first of them or at another customary hour, the daily chapter is to be held. In it, concerning regular discipline, after the martyrology and the reading of the Rule, before they proceed to other matters, the faults and excesses of the negligent or delinquent are to be punished.

The ornaments pertaining to divine worship are to be clean.

We will that each abbot or presiding superior, when he comes to his monastery, provide within a month for clean and suitable vessels and for the place where the Eucharist is kept there. And the books, together with the other ornaments concerning the divine office of the monastery, are to be preserved with careful custody.

Because through the propriety of the outward habit...

Concerning the form and propriety of garments and tonsures. g

...of the outward habit, the professed and novices of the said order ought to show uprightness of conduct. We establish and ordain that all shall wear large and broad tonsures, so that the circle of them does not exceed the space or thickness of two transverse fingers; and that they shall dress decently in clothing, habits, and footwear, according to the Clementine constitution Ne in agro and the constitution of Benedict XII, On the Form and Decency of Dress. That is, they shall wear tunics and garments closest to the outer habit of black, brown, or white color, according to the custom usually observed among them: round and ankle-length, not split, nor marked by any other deformity, with wide sleeves extending to the fist, in no way buttoned or tied, yet not so wide that their breadth above the fist can be stretched out with the thumb raised. Nor shall they extend around the elbow-opening, as the abuse of certain persons has it, beyond the point where the arm could easily be turned and inserted.

Let them be content with fur almuces in place of hoods. Yet in proper places where they are accustomed to wear hoods, they may, with the abbot’s permission, use respectable hoods, split over the shoulders for at least the length of four transverse fingers.

They shall not wear sendal for linings in their garments, nor miniver, nor other costly materials; but they shall use lambskins or sheepskins for the said linings, or at least other non-costly cloths. The lining shall not appear in any way above the neck or on the hems of the garments or sleeves.

Concerning the habit of those travelling.

Furthermore, when they must go outside the monastery, they shall wear a frock, cowl, or cloak, and under the cloak, if they wear one, a cowl or scapular.

Concerning the habit of novices.

Novices, however, shall wear a cowl, inside and outside the monastery, fitted on both sides. And lay brothers shall use a scapular with a hood joined to it, closed, inside and outside the monastery.

Concerning the length of garments and the use of the hood of the frock.

We ordain that the breadth of the frocks themselves...

...shall not reach the elbow-opening by the thickness of two transverse fingers, nor may it be narrower or so short that it does not extend as far as the middle of the elbow and of the upper bone near the shoulder-blade. The said hood, however, shall extend behind at least as far as the belt, and may not extend beyond it by more than four fingers. The length of the sleeves shall extend one cubit beyond the hand and no more. Their breadth shall not exceed another cubit and a half. Below, however, it shall be so broad that steps may easily be taken within it. And what has been said about the frock we wish to be understood of the cowl as well, except for the sleeves, since it has none.

Within the monastery, however, in places where there are twelve monks, all shall use the frock, except only the president in the monastery and the first after him, whom we wish always to wear the frock.

Yet during work and the divine office under the alb, and when riding under the cloak, they may wear only the scapular, which we wish to contain a breadth of at least half a cubit.

Likewise, they shall not use linen or hemp shirts, but shall wear either a woolen undergarment or a woolen garment in place of the said shirts. And they shall wear boots or shoes with straps, high enough that their width covers a space of four fingers of the shin above the ankle.

Monks living in common shall abstain from eating meat when healthy.

The brothers shall live in common and eat in the refectory, in which no one at all shall eat meat. And the visitors shall be diligent to see that the constitution of Pope Benedict XII on the eating of and abstinence from meats is inviolably observed. Sacred reading shall not be lacking at the table of the brothers while they eat; and the one who is to read for the whole week shall enter on Sunday with a blessing, as is contained in chapter 38 of the Rule.

All shall sleep in one dormitory, in partitioned cells...

Let each monk sleep clothed in a separate bed, in the same place, if this can be done, or at least in groups of ten or twenty.

But they are not to sleep in private rooms, especially if these have not been suitably latticed, so that the bedding in them can be properly and clearly seen, according to the manner of conversion and according to the abbot’s disposition. And those who have feather mattresses are not to use them.

But if private rooms are found in the dormitory, we command that they be destroyed by the visitors, or by their order, or at least suitably latticed. In what places and at what times silence is to be kept, let it be commanded according to the Rule. We further will that silence be observed at all times in the oratory, dormitory, refectory, and cloister; nor after Compline may anyone speak at all, except as is contained in the Rule. But before the said Compline, let the Collations of the Fathers, or some other edifying work, be read concerning the conference.

Concerning the porter of the monastery. At the gate of each monastery one porter or doorkeeper, provident and discreet, is to be appointed, lest without the permission of the abbot or another presiding officer in the monastery there be granted freedom to leave it. But if anyone goes out without such permission, let him be subjected to the penalties of the constitution of Benedict XII concerning permission not to be given for going outside the monastery without reasonable cause.

The porter is also to be attentive that he permit women in no way to enter. But concerning a sufficient master of novices in the monastery: we ordain that abbots shall place in their monasteries sufficient masters, who shall introduce their novices into the elementary sciences; and, once introduced, they shall send them to the general studies, assigning them a pension according to the form of the statutes of the aforesaid Benedict, Pope XII.

Let an inventory be made at the assumption of each abbacy by each abbot, as is contained in the Benedictina. And so that the condition of the aforesaid monasteries may be known, we command, in virtue of holy obedience and under penalty of excommunication to be imposed by the visitors, that every abbot be bound to hand over to the visitors in writing, distinctly, the ancient and modern condition of his monastery.

Concerning grants and leases to farm, and concerning sales and loans. Let the places of the aforesaid order not be leased to farm unless the Benedictina has first been consulted, concerning places not to be leased to farm; and we will that it be firmly observed. We also will that, when loans must be made under urgent necessity, the constitution concerning loans and sales shall likewise be considered, and likewise observed.

Let there be maintained in the monasteries as many monks as can be suitably supported. We will and ordain that the anciently established number of monks be maintained, if resources suffice for it; but if not, then as many as can suitably be maintained. Nor may anyone defend himself in any way by privilege or custom, which should rather be called corrupt usage, by which they say that they ought to receive no one unless he is noble, especially if they do not have nobles who may be received or who wish to enter the aforesaid monasteries; but if such are found, other things being equal, let them be preferred.

Necessaries are not to be supplied to monks in money. Food and other necessaries to be supplied to monks are in no way to be supplied in money or revenues, notwithstanding any constitution or ordinance whatsoever. And in this matter let the constitution of the aforesaid Benedict, beginning Ne vicarii in pecunia, be observed. But we will that the aforesaid religious be supplied with the said food and clothing in the three ways ordained in the Benedictina, De censibus et redditibus solvendis, chapter 21.

Concerning nuns. The things that have been said concerning monasteries of men we will likewise to be observed in monasteries of nuns, as to the articles pertaining to them; nevertheless willing and ordaining that they be held under perpetual enclosure, as is contained in the constitution of Boniface that begins Periculoso, De statu monachorum, book 6. We command the visitors in virtue of holy obedience, as above, diligently...

...after exact diligence, they are to see to it and apply it.

Visitors and those coming to the provincial chapter shall not have more than twelve mounts. We further will that no visitor shall dare to bring more than twelve mounts with him; and we will the same to be observed regarding those coming to the chapter. But if they do the contrary, they shall be bound to pay as much as they have spent in excess, to be deposited within a month in the common chest for the use of the aforesaid chapter. If they do not do this, they are to be condemned by the presidents in the next chapter to double the amount to be assessed, with no remission to avail them in this matter.

Concerning the appointment of presidents, if any one of them should happen to die before the chapter to be celebrated in the future.

We therefore refrain from naming the presidents for the chapter to be celebrated, so that if any one or more of them should happen to close his last day, his successor in the dignity of the abbacy shall likewise succeed to the presidency. We will the same to be understood concerning the preacher, the one who is to celebrate Mass, and each of the visitors of the whole aforesaid province and diocese.

Mendicants are not to be received into our order without apostolic authority or sufficient license.

It has come to our hearing that certain abbots, or other presidents in monasteries of the said order, have received and incorporated mendicants as monks, even without the license of their superiors; and, what is worse, afterward permit them to wander, to the detriment of their souls and to the scandal of very many. We forbid them to presume such things hereafter. Those whom they have already received they shall be bound, as soon as they can, either to have under apostolic authority or sufficient license, and others wandering outside the monasteries they shall recall to the monastery, at least within a year; otherwise, if they do not exercise diligence in this matter, they shall incur sentences of suspension.

That these statutes be published to all subject to the provincial chapter, and twice a year together with the constitutions of Benedict XII.

But that the aforesaid statutes may be better observed throughout all places of the order in the province and dioceses aforesaid, we ordain that within a year, or at least a month before the future chapter, every abbot shall be bound to hold and complete a general chapter, if he has any subjects outside his own monastery, in which the aforesaid statutes are to be published. We nevertheless will them to be read distinctly twice a year in the daily chapter, so that no one may be able to put forward the excuse of ignorance, together with the constitution of Benedict.

The second chapter was held at Mainz among the Augustinians, in the year of the Lord 1418.

In the year of the Lord 1418, in the eleventh indiction, on the first day of the month of September, in the pontificate of the lord Martin, pope, the fifth of that name, the second provincial chapter of Mainz was held in the monastery of the brothers, hermits of Saint Augustine; for it could not be held at Saint Alban's, where it had been appointed the preceding year, because of the transfer from the order that was then being carried out. In it the venerable fathers and lords, the abbots of Fulda, Kempten, Saint Ulrich at Augsburg, and Reinhardsbrunn, presided.

Concerning the statutes.

In this second provincial chapter few new statutes were issued among those issued in it; but all and each of the old statutes of the preceding chapter were approved and repeated word for word. It is not necessary to set them down here again, since they have once been set down above. Nevertheless, after these I shall briefly mention those things that were not noted or established above. For I judge that the new material should come first in this place.

Concerning the spoils of benefices.

We further ordain that abbots and others to whom, by custom, statute, or privilege, it belongs to receive the spoils of benefices subject to them shall, when receiving them, observe constitution 11. But if they exceed in this matter, they are to be gravely punished by the visitors, even apart from the penalties contained in that constitution, which the visitors may impose.

Concerning the statutes of the preceding chapter, repeated here.

Finally, as I said before, all the statutes issued in the preceding chapter were here renewed and repeated word for word, namely: [unclear] that the divine office is to be performed, and that at their proper times the monks are to confess, celebrate, and receive communion. Likewise, that the chapter of faults is to be observed daily. Likewise, that sacred relics, ornaments, and vessels pertaining to divine worship are to be kept clean. On the form and propriety of clothing, and on the habit of those travelling and of novices. On the common life of monks, and that they are to eat together in the refectory, where sacred reading must never be lacking for those eating. Where monks are to sleep: each in a separate bed, as above. On the silence to be observed in the four regular places. Likewise, on the porter. On the collation before compline. On having a sufficient master of novices in every monastery. And that the places of the order are not to be leased out. Likewise, on inventories to be made at the appointment of a new abbot of any monastery. And that the required number of monks is to be maintained in every monastery. That provisions are not to be supplied to monks in money. On nuns, as to the articles concerning them. Likewise, that visitors coming to the chapter are not to bring more than twelve mounts with them. That mendicants are not to be received into our order without apostolic authority or sufficient license. And that the statutes of the present chapter are to be published and read in every way expressed above.

And all the other statutes above were inserted word for word into this record.

How prelates should correct their subjects.

Finally, in the bowels of Jesus Christ, and under the adjuration of his strict and final judgment, we exhort and beseech all and every abbot, provost, dean, conventual prior, and cloister prior of the said order, that each of them so correct, amend, and reform his subjects and monasteries, and bring their conduct into regular discipline, that when the visitors come to their monasteries for the purpose of visitation, they may find rather what edifies them than anything that stands in need of correction.

The third provincial chapter was celebrated at Fulda, in the diocese of Wurzburg, in the year 1420.

In the year of the Lord 1420, in the thirteenth indiction, in the third year of the pontificate of lord Martin, pope the fifth, on the fifth day of the month of May, the third provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Saint Boniface at Fulda. At it presided the venerable fathers Lambert, abbot of Mons Monachorum near Bamberg, Frederick, abbot of Hirsau, and Henry, abbot of the monastery of Saint Godehard in Hildesheim.

On its statutes.

In this chapter also, many statutes that had been issued in the first chapter celebrated at Constance were repeated and inserted word for word, as they are given above. In it it was ordained that visitors must not have more than six mounts, unless necessity requires otherwise; and whatever they have beyond that must be assigned to the use of the chapter.

On the discipline of praying.

For the reform of the order. First, we ordain and decree that both the day and night office be celebrated devoutly, deliberately, and with pauses, without rushing through, without syncopating, and without one person anticipating another, and at the appropriate hours, as is contained in the Rule of our most blessed father Benedict. For this, as soon as the signal has been heard, all are to leave whatever is in their hands and come together with the greatest haste, yet with gravity, lest frivolity find occasion. And lest under the pretext of ignorance, etc., as is contained above in the first chapter. Thus nothing is to be preferred to the work of God, for cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently.

On the establishment of monks.

But lest anyone be able to excuse himself from celebrating divine offices of this kind because of a lack of persons, we wish that in each monastery as many monks be maintained and received as can conveniently be supported without want from its goods and revenues.

That monks are not to be received for a price or simoniacally.

We most strictly forbid anyone who hereafter wishes to enter this religious order to promise any money for his reception, either by himself or through others, or otherwise to pledge that he will give anything, except those things that are offered at the altar by parents of their free will, without any agreement with the boy. And those received in this way, when the year of probation has elapsed, shall promise to live according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, and to fulfill and observe it according to the tenor of the vow of profession and promise.

On the celebration of Masses.

On the daily chapter of faults.

Furthermore, we will that, in accordance with the constitution of Pope Benedict XII, the daily chapter be observed, in which discipline and regular correction are to be treated; and there too they are to carry out all things just as the aforesaid Pope Benedict established.

That collapsed conventual buildings be repaired.

We also will, and most strictly command by virtue of holy obedience, that in monasteries in which perhaps refectories, infirmaries, or dormitories have collapsed or otherwise been destroyed, they be repaired; and those negligent persons to whom such repair belongs are to be gravely punished by the visitors.

That women not have entry into monasteries of monks.

We altogether forbid entry to the monasteries, choirs, and cloisters to the female sex, commanding that all doors of those monasteries of the said order be closed as the visitors shall have arranged.

We likewise establish concerning the same matter that in monasteries, or within their precincts, in the houses in which monks live, no one shall presume to keep women, even if they are mothers or sisters. Those who do the contrary are to be duly punished according to the fault.

That mendicants not be received into our order, and that those already received who wander be recalled to their monasteries.

We forbid mendicants hereafter to be received into our order; and those already received are to be recalled to their cloisters and instructed and reformed according to the Rule and the statutes of our order.

On the cloister prior.

We will and strictly command, by virtue of holy obedience, that in each monastery there be appointed a provident and discreet prior, as suitable a man as can be found in the congregation of the monastery. Let him be such a man as is capable in work and useful in speech, able to exercise care of the cloister and governance in spiritual matters, who diligently observes all the aforesaid articles insofar as they concern him, causes them to be observed by all, and has vigilant and faithful care in spiritual matters concerning the discipline of the choir, dormitory, refectory, and the other things as described above. And if difficulty arises in any matter, let him refer it to the abbot, who is to examine and judge it.

On baths.

Because the use of baths is sometimes necessary for monks, we will that every abbot, or the one to whom it belongs by office, shall make and build a bathhouse in his monastery, so that the way of wandering away may be closed off to the monks.

On conspiracies, games of dice, and betrayals of the secrets of chapter.

Furthermore, we forbid all conspiracies against abbots and also against private persons, defamations of brothers, every betrayal of a secret of chapter or council, and every game of dice, knucklebones, chess, and other games and disorders by whatever name they are called.

That monks not become godfathers.

Furthermore, according to the ancient decrees of the holy fathers, we establish and forbid monks to become godfathers, as in De consecratione, distinction 4, Non licet abbati, and chapter 16, question 1, Placuit communi.

That the ornaments and books of divine worship be kept clean.

Furthermore, with this sacred chapter approving, it has been decreed and established that churches, oratories, altars, vessels, corporals, vestments, and other ecclesiastical ornaments be kept clean and bright. And provision is to be made in every way for breviaries, missals, and other books, vestments, chalices, and any ornaments necessary for divine worship.

On the quality of garments.

Those things that have been written and defined concerning the quality and quantity of habit, clothing, and footwear in the chapters celebrated at Constance and Mainz, we will to be observed inviolably by all.

Concerning monks living in common and sleeping in one place.

We will that the brothers live in common according to the Rule, and likewise eat together in one refectory, in which no one at all shall eat meat. They shall maintain an infirmary according to the Rule and the abbot's disposition. All private little houses, moreover, shall be destroyed at the abbot's command, or assigned to some offices for the utility of the monastery. All shall sleep in one dormitory, in screened chambers, each in separate beds, according to the abbot's disposition.

Concerning the other statutes of the preceding chapters repeated in this chapter.

Furthermore, the constitutions and statutes decreed in the previous chapters were repeated precisely, word for word, in this one, as they are set forth above: namely, concerning the divine office; concerning the ringing for matins, prime, and vespers; likewise, that monasteries and conventual places that have fallen down and been destroyed be restored; and that a prudent old man be placed at the gate of each monastery. Likewise, that abbots and the other officials of monasteries make to the visitors a full and faithful accounting of receipts and expenditures. Likewise, that silence be kept most strictly in the four conventual places belonging to them. And that, concerning loans, leases, spoils, fiefs, and those to be sent to studies, and also concerning the preservation of the Eucharist and relics, the Benedictine constitution be observed. And that each abbot publish all the statutes of the present chapter to his subjects and cause them to be observed, and the other matters which are contained above in the first chapter.

The matters stated concerning nuns.

What has been said concerning monasteries of men we will also to be understood concerning monasteries of nuns, so far as concerns the articles applicable to them; and we command that they also remain under perpetual enclosure.

Concerning the observance of the mandates.

We will, ordain, and command that all these our mandates written above be observed inviolably by all who are subject to our chapter, as each matter concerns each person. Nor by this do we restrict the statutes of our order or of the preceding chapters; rather, we will that they likewise be diligently and firmly fulfilled and observed by all, without any contradiction. Therefore let the visitors provide that all and each of the things mentioned above be diligently observed, as they are bound to render account on the day of their death and of the last judgment.

The fourth provincial chapter was celebrated in Selgenstadt in the year of the Lord 1422.

In the year of the Lord 1422, in the fifteenth indiction, on the third day of the month of May, in the fifth year of Pope Martin V, the fourth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, martyrs, in Selgenstadt. In it sat the venerable fathers Albertus Hirsfeldensis, Georgius Castellensis, and Theodericus Amerbacensis, abbots of monasteries.

Concerning the statutes of this chapter.

Before reviewing the statutes issued in this sacred chapter, it is fitting briefly to set first those things decreed in previous chapters which were inserted here word for word by way of review. For the repetition of statutes inserted so often serves this purpose: that the more chapters in which something has been decreed, the greater authority it has.

First, this sacred assembly of fathers repeated the statute of the first chapter concerning deceased presidents: that one who succeeds someone in an abbacy also succeeds him in the presidency.

Likewise, that the visitors shall not bring more than six mounts with them, under the penalty contained above.

Likewise, concerning the ringing for matins, prime, and vespers, to be done for the space of one quarter of an hour, as above, c. 1.

And that the chapter of faults be kept daily, as in the same place.

Likewise, that the brothers live in common and eat in one refectory, in which no one shall eat meat.

That all shall sleep in

LVI

one locked dormitory, with enclosed chambers and individual beds. Private little dwellings are to be destroyed; the conventual places also that have fallen into ruin are to be restored. Likewise, provisions are not to be supplied to monks in money. And concerning a prudent old porter. Likewise, monks are not to be received for a price. Women are not to enter the cloister of men. And abbots and each of the officials are to render an account to their visitors. And silence is to be observed at its proper times by all and in all places. And concerning nuns, as above. And the other things issued in the preceding chapters were also here enacted as though newly decreed.

Concerning the claustral prior, what sort he ought to be.

This sacred chapter has decreed that a prudent and discreet prior be appointed in every monastery, as the more suitable one can be found in the congregation, who is capable in deed and speech, diligent concerning regular discipline, and observes the articles of the order that concern him or the brothers. But if he is found to be a transgressor of the aforesaid matters, or blameworthy in anything, let him be admonished once and again. If he does not amend, let him be removed by the abbot from the office of the priorate, and let another who is suitable be substituted in his place. This must be understood not only of the prior, but also of all officials of the monastery.

The lord presidents, visitors, and treasurers are to come before the day of the chapter.

We further enact and ordain that the presidents of the chapter, both past and future, shall henceforth come before the appointed day, together with the treasurers and visitors: so that the treasurers are there on the penultimate Saturday before the Sunday on which the chapter is to be held; the presidents, however, on the Monday preceding that Sunday; and the visitors on the following Tuesday, so that they may make a timely report to the presidents concerning their visitations. Therefore these same presidents and treasurers also are ordered, as has been said, to come before the day on which the chapter is to be held, so that they may inform one another about each matter and render account to the new presidents and to the chapter concerning receipts and expenditures. This statute had also been issued in the earlier chapters, namely in the first and the following ones.

Concerning visitors.

We further decree and ordain that the visitors appointed in chapter, immediately after the chapter has been held, if it can conveniently be done, or as soon as possible, shall begin and complete the act of their visitation, having God alone before their eyes. We also will that these visitors, appointed and to be appointed, should not omit to visit also the monasteries of nuns in the dioceses in which they are to conduct visitation.

Concerning the penalty of visitors who neglect to visit at the proper time.

If the visitors neglect to visit within the time appointed for them, namely within the year, they shall pay the penalty, as do those who come to the chapter neither in person nor through suitable proctors, namely thirty Rhenish florins, saving moderation and just assessment at the discretion of the presidents in the provincial chapter.

Concerning the procurations of the visitors.

We also command and will that every abbot and convent, when their visitors have come to them for the purpose of visitation, shall satisfy them within three days with the sum of three Rhenish florins.

Concerning the confessions of monks.

We prohibit and forbid all monks, conversi, and brothers subject to us that anyone henceforth should dare to confess to anyone, inside or outside the monastery, without the permission of his superior.

Concerning the celebration of masses.

As for celebrations, let them observe those things that are contained in the constitutions of lord Pope Benedict XII and in the statutes of the preceding chapters. We also perpetually forbid monks to become godfathers, and forbid them every game and dishonorable exercise.

Concerning habit, clothing, and footwear; concerning inventories and accounts to be made to the visitors.

We will and ordain that, concerning habit, clothing, footwear, inventories, and accounts to be made, those things be observed inviolably which are found decreed on these matters in the preceding chapters, see chapter 1, 2, 2. Concerning ha-

Concerning the habit of those riding or walking on a journey.

We have decreed that it be ordered in this way: namely, that the outer habit shall be a mantle hanging down to the middle of the calves, cut with one opening on each side; and beneath it a scapular, which shall exceed the mantle by the length of three transverse fingers, and whose appendage shall appear outside. Because of the fear of excommunication laid upon such persons, those who conceal or alter the habit without reasonable cause [unclear].

Privileges of the monasteries. Concerning the custody of privileges.

We command that privileges and the other jewels, relics, and treasures be preserved under faithful custody and firm enclosure.

Concerning conspiracy and defamation.

We strictly forbid every conspiracy against abbots and other prelates and rectors, as well as against private persons; also defamation of abbots and brothers, and every betrayal of the secret of the chapter. We command that transgressors of such things be corrected by their superiors, so that the others may take fear.

That beggars are henceforth not to be received into our order.

We also forbid, in virtue of holy obedience, all prelates subject to our chapter to receive beggars henceforth into our order. Those, however, who have already been received and wander here and there shall be recalled as quickly as possible to their monasteries.

Concerning deceased brothers.

“Mercy alone is the companion of the dead.” We establish and ordain concerning the dead that each abbot, or their proctors, shall henceforth bring and present in each chapter brief notices of the names of deceased brothers, and of the days of their deaths, who have died between the chapter already celebrated and the chapter to be celebrated, so that prayers and suffrages may be made for them. And this is the form of the brief: “Such-and-such a priest or levite, etc., died on such a day in such a place,” etc.

Concerning nuns.

Those things that have been said concerning monasteries of men we will also to be inviolably observed in monasteries of nuns, insofar as they pertain to the articles applicable to them.

Concerning the general chapter and the publication of the statutes.

The statute concerning the publication of the processes of the whole present chapter and of the statutes of this chapter, often set down above, and concerning the general chapter to be observed within the year, is here again set down and renewed in all respects as above, chapter 1, at the end, where it may be read.

Conclusion.

Many other things also were here established, ordained, and treated, which partly are contained above and partly, as less necessary, I have passed over; but all are contained in the book of recesses.

The fifth provincial chapter was celebrated at Saint Stephen’s in Würzburg, in the year of the Lord 1424.

In the year of the Lord 1424, in the second indiction, on the fourteenth day of the month of May, which was Jubilate Sunday, in the seventh year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Martin V, the fifth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Saint Stephen at Würzburg. In it there presided the venerable fathers Balduin in Lüneburg, Theoderic in Northeim, Appello in Sülzheim, and Helfric of Saint John’s in Rheingau, abbots of monasteries.

Concerning the old statutes.

In this chapter almost all the statutes of the preceding chapters were approved and inserted into the recess word for word, though a few things were added; of these I have taken care briefly to mark some here, for greater authority.

First, the ordinances concerning the divine office; concerning ringing; concerning the chapter of faults to be observed daily; concerning the creation of monks; that monks are not to be received for a price; concerning the celebration of masses; concerning the common life of all the brothers; that provisions are not to be given in money; concerning the dormitory; concerning silence; concerning collapsed places to be reformed; concerning the account to be made to the visitors; concerning the old porter; concerning the propriety of vestments; concerning conspiracies; concerning games; concerning beggars not to be received into the order; concerning the publication of the statutes; concerning nuns; concerning visitors.

that they are not to bring more than six mounts with them. Concerning the penalty for visitors who neglect to visit within the year. And many other things that are set out above and are contained in the book of recesses of the chapters. Now let us append the particular statutes of this chapter.

Those being visited are to guard diligently the goods and horses of the visitors.

Furthermore, when the visitors, for the sake of carrying out visitation, come to some monastery, the abbot and convent of that monastery are immediately to see that the horses, property, and goods of the visitors are guarded with the greatest diligence. But if anything from their property, goods, or horses should happen to be lost or stolen, the abbot and convent of that place themselves, without any contradiction, are to pay the value of the lost goods or property to the visitors without delay; and nevertheless, for such negligence, they are to be punished in chapter at the discretion of the presidents.

If the visitors should happen to be robbed while on the way in carrying out their office.

If, however, which God forbid, the visitors, while on the way to carry out visitation, should be robbed or suffer damage in any respect, the provincial chapter shall compensate them for such loss as is fitting.

Concerning safe conduct for the visitors.

It was further decreed that every abbot who is to be visited shall provide the visitors, according to his ability, safe conduct as far as another monastery to be visited, if he has been asked by the visitors.

No one is to be procurator for more than three.

We also forbid anyone to be procurator for more than three. But if anyone has presumed to be procurator for more, that procuration of his is not to be admitted.

If any convent wishes to send letters to the chapter.

It pleased all those resident in the chapter that, if any convent or monastery of our province has a need to come to the provincial chapter itself, for whatever reason, it should choose from among itself one or two suitable and faithful men, and no more, to present the matter of its delegation diligently. But if they have presumed to send three, let them be punished by their superiors as disobedient.

Concerning the chest and the custodians of the chest.

It was further decreed that, for the common use of the chapter, a chest is to be kept at Nuremberg in the monastery of Saint Giles of the Order of Saint Benedict. From there treasurers are to be designated.

Concerning the mortuary briefs.
