We further decree that individual abbots, or their procurators, when they come to any provincial chapter to be held in the future, are to bring with them briefs containing the names of the deceased brothers of their monasteries who have died between the chapter already held and the chapter to be held, so that they may be commended to the prayers of the fathers.

This concludes the fifth chapter.

Many other things were repeated and decreed in the present chapter which have not been set out here item by item, because they are already contained above once in the same words, and it would be tedious to repeat the same things so often in writing.

The sixth provincial chapter was held at Saint Peter’s in Erfurt in the year of the Lord 1426.

In the year of the Lord 1426, in the fourth indiction, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Pope Martin V, on the twenty-first day of the month of April, which was Jubilate Sunday, the sixth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of Saint Peter in Erfurt. In it these venerable fathers presided: the lord abbots Johannes in Vrauwe, Heinrich of Saint Giles in Brunswick, Georg of Saint Giles in Nuremberg, and Nikolaus in Bretzenhausen.

The old statutes are first commended by common consent of all.

First, we approve, ratify, and renew all and each of the statutes issued in the past chapters, and we will them to have force as expressly confirmed, just as if they had been inserted here.

Sentences of excommunication and censures are here removed.

It pleased the lord presidents and all those resident in the chapter to remove and relax the sentences of excommunication and the censures issued in past chapters, lest they produce a snare for souls. Therefore they said: The penalties and sentences of excommunication, suspension, and interdict pronounced by the presidents in past chapters, lest they bring forth a snare for souls, are removed in the name of God.

we remove, relax, and revoke, and those bound or tied by the same, insofar as lies within us, we absolve in the name of God by apostolic authority through these presents; all statutes, however, remaining safe and continuing in their force.

Concerning the proctors of absentees also. Further, we moderate and mitigate the statute of the fifth chapter, which provides that no one may be proctor for more than three, decreeing that some religious person otherwise suitable may be proctor for four or even five abbots in cases of great necessity.

Let the visitors first reform themselves and their own, and only then visit others. Those appointed by the provincial chapter shall first and before all else visit and reform themselves, their monasteries, and those subject to them, lest, when they direct their eyes to the reformation of others, the sick too should murmur and say, “Physician, heal yourself.” Therefore let them begin first with themselves, and thus confidently visit and reform the monasteries entrusted to them, both of monks and of nuns.

It was further decreed concerning the report of the visitors to the presidents that the visitors, after completing the office of their visitation, shall make a faithful report in chapter to the lord presidents concerning the state of all the monasteries visited by them, both in spiritual and in temporal matters.

An oath is not to be extorted from those being visited. It also pleased us that, without demanding an oath to tell the truth, after first setting forth the word of God, the visitors themselves shall begin and complete their act according to the form prescribed for them in the sacred canons.

Likewise concerning the form of visitation. We also will and ordain that the visitors shall effectively reform, as far as they can, each and every monastery of either sex to be visited by them before they withdraw from the place being visited, according to the rule of our most blessed father Benedict, especially in the three essentials, which are obedience, continence, and poverty, without which no religious life can stand. And where they do not find sound disciplines and ceremonies, they shall establish new ones according to the canonical sanctions and the statutes of the fathers and chapters, which those visited shall be bound to observe without any contradiction.

Concerning the three essentials. We command all and each of the prelates of our province and those subject to the chapter that each of them, immediately after the notification of the present decrees, shall strive in his monastery to correct and reform himself and his monks according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the canonical sanctions, and the statutes of the provincial chapter and of the order, especially in the three essentials, obedience, continence, and poverty; in eating and abstinence from meat; in divine worship and the other monastic disciplines, as far as he can, fearing that terrible and true sentence of our blessed father: let the abbot know that whatever the householder can find of less usefulness in the sheep falls under the fault of the shepherd.

The seventh provincial chapter was celebrated at the Monks’ Mount near Bamberg, in the year of the Lord 1429.

In the year of the Lord 1429, in the seventh indiction, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of lord Martin, pope the fifth, on the tenth day of the month of April, which was the Sunday Misericordia Domini, our seventh provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Saint Michael of the Monks’ Mount near Bamberg. In it the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Georgius in the castle of Saint Peter at Erfurt, Heinrich of Saint Giles at Nuremberg, and Hugo in Alpirsbach, presided.

Concerning the approved statutes of the ancients. First, we approve and renew the old statutes, and we wish all of them, insofar as they were duly and lawfully issued, to be observed inviolably by those subject to our chapter.

That those coming to the provincial chapter shall live communally during those three days. The sacred chapter further decreed that those coming to celebrate the provincial chapter in future times, according to the constitution of blessed memory

... of Innocent III, pope, in Extra, De statu monachorum, chapter In singulis, they shall live the common life and be refreshed together throughout that three-day period. And only two dishes of fish are to be served, one of eggs or fried foods, and two good soups, with cheese added, and some fruits if they can be had.

Concerning lords.

By the authority of the presidents we establish and ordain, with all the fathers present consenting, that each of the presidents shall have full power and authority, acting jointly and severally, to carry out execution and to proceed, according to the tenor of the Benedictine constitutions, against each and every person of either sex who opposes those visiting them, or does not admit them, or impedes them, or otherwise hinders them in any way; and also against those who offend monasteries in persons or goods in any way. And that they shall compel visitors to exact on behalf of the chapter, in accordance with the Benedictina, from the monasteries visited the contribution or the penalties for contumacy from abbots who have neglected to come to the chapter.

Visitors. Concerning the time for completing visitation.

The visitors shall faithfully complete within the year the office of visitation enjoined upon them, and shall make a report about it to the lord presidents as quickly as they can. Rebels are to be denounced by the visitors to one of the presidents.

It was decreed that, if any persons resist the visitors, they are to be denounced to the nearer president, so that by apostolic authority he may proceed against such rebels, and also against those who do not obey the visitors, by ecclesiastical censure according to the measure of their faults and rebellion.

Concerning certain statutes placed in the preceding chapter, which in this one were repeated word for word.

In the next preceding chapter certain statutes were issued, which in this one also were precisely repeated and inserted word for word into the recess, namely: that the visitors should first take care to reform themselves and their own; likewise that, after the word of God has been set forth, they should proceed without exacting an oath; and concerning the full reform to be introduced by them. Likewise, the mandate made to the prelates concerning the reform of themselves and their own. All these are found in the preceding chapter.

The eighth provincial chapter was celebrated at Saint Ulrich’s in Augsburg, in the year of the Lord 1432.

In the year of the Lord 1432, in the tenth indiction, in the second year of the pontificate of lord Eugene IV, pope, on the eleventh day of the month of May, which was Jubilate Sunday, the eighth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Saints Ulrich and Afra in the city of Augsburg. In it the venerable fathers presided: the lord abbots Ortwin of Saint Peter’s at Erfurt, Johannes in Stein, of the diocese of Constance, and Heinrich in Amorbach, of Mainz. In this chapter provision was made concerning persons to be sent for study.

The old statutes.

First, with common consent, they renew and approve what had been approved. We approve, ratify, and renew each and all the statutes issued in the preceding chapters, and we wish them to be inviolably observed by all subject to our chapter, so far as each one is concerned. These statutes, set down several times above, were here again set down.

Finally, in this chapter almost all the statutes of the two immediately preceding chapters were repeated in the same words and inserted into the recess. Therefore, to avoid tedium, it is enough to note them briefly. First, the statute that the fathers coming to the chapter should live together in the refectory throughout those three days, and concerning the number of dishes, as above, chapter 7. Likewise, the statute concerning visitors, that they should first reform themselves and their own; and that, beginning from the word of God, they should fulfill their office without exacting an oath, as above, chapters 6 and 7. A mandate was also given to the abbots that they should take care to reform themselves and their own in three especially substantial matters, concerning abstinence from meats and the other matters issued above in chapters 6 and 7; they are similarly set down here. A statute, moreover, concerning the authority of the lord presidents, as above, chapters 6 and 7, is similarly set down here in the same words.

Concerning the time of visitation.

Moreover, we command these visitors themselves, and under penalty of a sentence of excommunication to be imposed we enjoin, that within the year they shall faithfully and effectively complete the office of visitation enjoined upon them, and shall make a report to the nearer president as quickly as they can.

That mendicants are not to be received into the order.

We forbid all abbots and prelates of our chapter, under penalty of excommunication, to receive anyone from the order of mendicants into obedience; and those already received, who are wandering about, they are to bring back to their monasteries as quickly as possible, as in chapters 2 and 3, and as has often been established in many other places.

Concerning fugitive monks.

Under the same penalty of excommunication we command all abbots and prelates subject to our provincial chapter to gather back their fugitive monks; nor henceforth are they to give anyone permission to stay in parishes or to govern them, unless those parishes are annexed to the monasteries.

What sort of persons abbots ought to be toward their subjects.

Just as the madness of wolves must be driven off by the barking of dogs and the shepherds’ staff, we command all abbots subject to the chapter of our province that, following the example of the good shepherd, Jesus Christ, whose place they are seen to hold in the monasteries, they should kindly foster and prudently defend their monks and subjects, not lording it over the clergy, but becoming an example to the flock.

LXI

In the year of the Lord 1435, in the tenth indiction, in the fifth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Eugenius IV, on the twenty-sixth day of the month of June, which was the Sunday after the Nativity of blessed John the Baptist, the ninth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of the Friars Preachers in Basel, for at that time the general council was being held there. Presiding in it were the venerable fathers and lords, the abbots Ortwin of St. Peter’s at Erfurt, Fridericus of St. Mark’s in Reichenau, Iohannes of St. George’s in Stein, and Heinricus in Faucibus, of the dioceses of Mainz, Constance, and Augsburg.

On the statutes of the earlier chapters.

First, we approve and commend the statutes of the other chapters, and we wish them, as expressed here, to be observed by all.

The statutes of the preceding chapters are repeated here.

In this chapter of the fathers, nearly all the statutes issued in the three preceding chapters were again repeated word for word: first, namely, the statute on those coming to chapter with communal life, and on the number of courses, in the same place, chapters 6, 7, and 8, as it has been set out above exactly. And there it was ordained that the treasurers themselves must provide for the refreshment during the three days of the provincial chapter. Likewise, on the power of the presiding lords, that each of them should have authority jointly and severally to proceed against rebels. On the visitors also, under penalty of excommunication imposed on them, that they faithfully complete their office within the year and make a report as soon as possible to one of the nearer presidents. And that they first visit and reform themselves and their own, and only then proceed to the reform of others. Likewise, that henceforth they are not to receive mendicants into our order, under penalty of excommunication, as above. Under the same penalty it was decreed, as above, that abbots are to seek out their fugitives and are not to give anyone permission to dwell or rule in parishes unless as is permitted above, chapters 7 and 8. Likewise, the statute was repeated as above concerning fugitive monks not to be received to obedience without letters of recommendation. All these things, which I have briefly reviewed, as they stand above in their form word for word, were again issued and enacted as though new.

On the penalty for the contumacious.

It was further decreed that the presidents, and each of them, should compel abbots and others who have not come to chapter in person nor sent lawful procurators with a sufficient mandate to pay double, and also to pay the contributions imposed by the chapter, by ecclesiastical censures according to constitution 12, with appeal removed.

We also command all visitors appointed and to be appointed that, in each monastery which they have visited, they leave a recess or charter of visitation.

On the observance of precepts.

We command all and each of the statutes and mandates written above to be inviolably observed by all, while preserving nevertheless whatever is to be added, decreed, or changed in the holy Council of Basel for the reform of our said order. In the matter of this reform, twelve prelates of the aforesaid order from the said province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg have already been appointed and elected in the said holy council.

The tenth provincial chapter was held in Nuremberg, in which the bull of the Council of Basel was accepted, in the year of the Lord 1439.

In the year of the Lord 1439, in the second indiction, in the ninth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Eugenius IV, on the twenty-sixth day of the month of April, which was Jubilate Sunday, the tenth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of St. Giles at Nuremberg, of the same order. Presiding in it were the venerable fathers and lords, the abbots Hartung of St. Peter’s at Erfurt, Georgius of St. Giles at Nuremberg, Nicolaus of St. Blaise, and Heinricus in Amerbach. In this chapter the bull of the Council of Basel concerning the reform of our order through the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg was presented and accepted. For the execution of this, twelve prelates in the same [unclear]

... in the council from the aforesaid order and province were appointed, as above.

Concerning the consent of all. Concerning the old statutes. C. 9, at the end. With the consent of all the fathers residing in chapter, we approve and renew all and singular the decrees and statutes issued in the provincial chapters held up to now, insofar as they are not contrary to the reform.

Concerning the authority of the presidents. We wish that each of the presidents, severally, shall have full and complete power and authority to carry out execution and to proceed, according to the form and tenor of the constitutions of Lord Pope Benedict XII and the disposition of the common law, against all and singular persons of either sex who have presumed to oppose the visitors, or have not admitted them for visitation, or have hindered them in any way, or have been found contrary to the concluded reform, and who have harmed those monasteries in goods or in persons.

Let the presidents visit the royal monasteries personally, having taken the visitors with them. The holy chapter decreed that each of the presidents must personally visit the exempt and royal monasteries assigned to him, together with the visitors of those monasteries, or one of them. Let the same be done in other monasteries wherever and as often as it shall be necessary.

Concerning the visitors, as above. The statutes issued in the four preceding chapters were again set down in this form and inserted into the recess, concerning the visitors: that within the year they are to begin their office from the word of God, and are as soon as possible to report to the nearest president the condition of those monasteries visited by them; all of which is contained more fully above, chapters 6, 7, and following.

Concerning the bull of the Council of Basel. To the fathers residing in the holy chapter there was shown and read the lead-sealed bull of the Council of Basel concerning the reform of our order throughout the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg. Because of its length I have been unwilling to place it here, but it has been set down separately at folio 34. Given on the tenth day before the kalends of March, in the year of the Lord 1439. The fathers unanimously accept this bull.

With concordant and unanimous vote, no one dissenting, and with mature deliberation, we accept, and, insofar as lies in us, approve the bull of the holy general Council of Basel; and concerning the reform of the monasteries subject to our chapter, we will and command that it be observed in all our monasteries not yet more strictly reformed. Nevertheless, we command all and singular the prelates throughout the aforesaid province of our order that they should take care to reform those subject to them who have not yet been more strictly reformed, according to the same form.

That the bull of the aforesaid reform is to be read publicly in each monastery and in each quarter once in the convent. We also will and command that the form of the aforesaid reform, carefully checked word for word in every monastery, be kept in good and legible script, and that once in every quarter it be read publicly in the daily chapter; and that it be explained in the vernacular to the brothers by the president, or by whomever he shall order, lest anyone be able to excuse himself under pretext of ignorance.

Those coming to the provincial chapter shall live communally. Those coming to the chapter shall likewise take their meals during those three days in one refectory, and there shall be served to them two dishes of fish only, and one of eggs, or fried eggs, and two good pottages, with cheese and some fruits added.

The eleventh provincial chapter was held at Nuremberg for the second time, in the year of the Lord 1441.

In the year of the Lord 1441, on the last day of the month of April, which was the Sunday Misericordia Domini, the eleventh provincial chapter was held at St. Giles in Nuremberg. In it the venerable fathers, the abbots of St. Giles there, of St. Peter’s in Erfurt, of St. Blaise, and of Amorbach, presided.

We again accept the bull of the Council of Basel concerning the reform. With the common assent of all the fathers present and of the procurators of the absent, we receive and again accept the bull of the Council of Basel for the reform to be begun and ...

we will that each abbot have a copy of it in his monastery, and that the superiors of the monasteries should strive effectively to reform those subject to them according to it. Let those already more strictly reformed not wish, under pretext of this form, to relax themselves to a more lenient life. Yet we admonish and exhort in the Lord Jesus those who have thus far begun, in holy religion, the observance of a stricter life, that they persevere in good beginnings and make greater progress from day to day; nor, declining from their purpose under pretext of this norm, should they turn themselves toward more lenient things, since the constitution of this bull was issued as a beginning of regular life for those who up to now have been more negligent, until the good God grants them greater gifts.

The aforesaid bull also commands here that in each monastery it be kept, collated, in good and legible script, and that once in each quarter it be read publicly in the convent, as above in the preceding chapter.

Concerning the proctors of the visitors.

Furthermore, it pleased us, and we have decreed, that the appointed proctors of those absent should observe whether the visitors have fulfilled their visitations, and should report those who are negligent to the nearer presidents, so that, by ecclesiastical censure and other penalties if necessary, they may compel them to fulfill their office.

Let no one be proctor for more than three.

We also forbid anyone henceforth to dare to be proctor for more than three, except because of evident necessity, under a penalty to be imposed by the lord presidents.

Concerning the travel allowance of three florins to be paid to the visitors.

The whole community of the fathers decreed that each abbot who has been visited shall pay his visitors four Rhenish florins for travel allowance, unless the visitors themselves, for good reason, wish to receive less; on this point we burden their consciences.

Let prelates not absent themselves from chapter.

We also earnestly forbid, under the penalties contained in the Benedictina, that prelates who are obliged to come to the provincial chapter should presume henceforth to absent themselves from such a chapter.

Concerning the accounting to be made by the former presidents to the new ones for receipts and expenditures.

We will and ordain that, when their office has expired, the presidents shall make a full and clear account to the new presidents concerning all and several receipts and expenditures on behalf of the chapter.

The twelfth provincial chapter, celebrated at Erfurt at St. Peter’s for the second time, in the year of the Lord 1444.

In the year of the Lord 1444, on the tenth day of the month of May, which was Cantate Sunday, the twelfth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of St. Peter at Erfurt. There presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots of St. Peter there, of St. Gall, of St. Giles at Nuremberg, and of St. Stephen at Würzburg. In it proctors were appointed who should accuse the negligence of the visitors before the presidents.

Concerning the old statutes here renewed and repeated.

In this sacred chapter, as also in the two immediately preceding ones, the bull of the Council of Basel concerning reform was accepted in the same words as above. And it was provided that it should be kept and read in each monastery four times a year, as above in the preceding chapter. And that brothers of the stricter life should not wish, under pretext of this bull, to descend to more lenient things, but should persevere by setting out better, as in the same place. The statute concerning the authority of the presidents over rebels, and concerning the negligence of the visitors to be investigated by proctors, is set down here in precisely the same words as it is found above in the same tenth chapter, with certain other matters.

Royal monasteries are to be visited by the presidents.

Royal monasteries are henceforth to be visited by one of the presidents, with the visitors of that diocese associated with him, as above in chapter ten.

Concerning the monasteries of nuns to be visited.

But also the monasteries of nuns in each diocese are to be visited by the visitors of that diocese; and each monastery visited shall pay its visitors, when they depart, three Rhenish florins for travel allowance.

Concerning the death notices of the dead.

The names of the brothers, sisters, confratres, and all monasteries throughout our province

LXIII

...of the deceased, within the chapter already held and the chapter to be held, they shall henceforth bring to that chapter, so that the debt of brotherhood may be paid for them there. This statute is often repeated in the preceding and following chapters.

The thirteenth provincial chapter, held for the second time in the monastery of Petershausen at Constance, in the year 1447.

In the year of the Lord 1447, on the seventh day of the month of May, which was the Sunday Cantate, the fourteenth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of Petershausen at Constance. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots of Petershausen there, of Saint Giles of Nuremberg, of Saint Stephen of Wuerzburg, and of Saint Gotthard of Hildesheim.

On old statutes here renewed and repeated.

First of all, it receives the oft-mentioned bull of the Council of Basel, and commands in the same words and form as above that it be held and read in every monastery. Several other statutes also were placed here in the recess, though they have been determined several times in the preceding chapters, namely concerning the authority of the lord presidents against rebels; that the visitors of each diocese should visit the monasteries of nuns; and concerning the negligence of visitors to be reported to the presidents by the procurators, along with many others that are fully contained above here and there.

That only the reformed are to be appointed to the offices of the provincial chapter.

As the Lord says in the Gospel: if the blind leads the blind, both fall into the ditch. We establish that, as far as can be done, this rule should be observed in the election of presidents and visitors: that the reformed be appointed to such offices, for one who has neglected first to reform himself can never well instruct others.

On the negligence of visitors.

And because we have learned by experience that some visitors appointed up to now have been negligent and have not taken care to fulfill the office enjoined upon them, therefore we will and command all visitors that they take care to fulfill the office of their visitation with all possible diligence.

Otherwise, according to the tenor of the Benedictine letter, we will and declare that they, and each of them, incur by the very fact the penalties that are incurred by those who do not come to the provincial chapter without having a canonical impediment.

Who are excused from the chapter.

It pleased the fathers that no one henceforth should put forward any excuse for not coming to the chapter except bodily illness, enmities, or evident and plainly established poverty. And only for these reasons are the procuratorial letters of absent abbots to be admitted in chapter.

On wandering monks not to be received.

Wandering monks without commendatory letters from their abbot are not to be kept or received as conventuals, nor are they to be hosted in any monastery beyond three days.

On a monk who has laid violent hands on an abbot.

If any monk, at the devil’s persuasion, has broken out into such audacity that he lays violent hands on an abbot or another brother, such a person is not to be accepted or kept in the province.

On one who wishes to pass over from an unreformed monastery.

If anyone, with pious intention, wishes to pass from an unreformed monastery to a monastery, he shall seek permission from his superior. If the superior refuses, he shall seek it from one of the presidents, who will give him permission to stay there for a time, or even to establish himself there, but with the consent of those receiving him.

On the safe-conduct and travel expenses of visitors.

Every abbot or prelate who has been visited, with the help of his convent, shall conduct his visitors as far as the next monastery to be visited by them. When they wish to depart, he shall not refuse to give them three Rhenish florins for the contribution or collection imposed by the chapter for relieving its burdens, unless the visitors themselves, for a pious reason, have decreed that less should be received.

The fourteenth provincial chapter, held for the second time at Wuerzburg, in the presence of the lord cardinal, in the year of the Lord 1451. [unclear]

LXV

In the year of the Lord 1451, on the twenty-fourth day of the month of May, which was Cantate Sunday, the fourteenth provincial chapter was celebrated at St. Stephen's in Wurzburg, with the most reverend father, lord Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal priest of the title of St. Peter ad Vincula and legate, present and presiding over that chapter. In it the venerable fathers, the lord abbots of St. Giles in Nuremberg, of St. Burkard in Wurzburg, of St. Peter in Erfurt, and of St. Godehard in Hildesheim, presided.

Concerning the old statutes repeated.

Besides those statutes which the aforesaid lord Nicholas, cardinal and legate, issued, the present sacred chapter established certain things, and repeated word for word several things issued in previous chapters, namely:

Concerning safe conduct and the visitors' travel expenses, as above, in the preceding chapter.

Likewise, that the names of deceased brothers are to be announced in the individual chapters, as above, chapter 12. And many other things which it would seem superfluous to insert here in order.

Concerning collations and drinkings not to be held in our monasteries.

It has come to our truthful hearing by report that in certain monasteries, even reformed ones, by a certain special gracious permission of the prelates, collations have customarily been held before compline. Certain brothers now contend that these are to be held daily in certain monasteries as if by right, taking them up on their own authority, to no small prejudice and loss of the purity of reform and of the peace of the same monasteries, with detractions, frivolities, reports of secular business, and also sometimes by extending even to extravagant disputes and at times in the presence of laymen. Therefore we forbid the same collations to be held henceforth without the special grace of those same prelates. We also will that the visitors be specially admonished concerning these things.

Besides these things nothing new was established in this chapter. But the lord cardinal issued certain constitutions for the visitors, some of which are contained here separately.

The fifteenth provincial chapter, celebrated a second time in Seligenstadt, was held in the year of the Lord 1454.

In the year of the Lord 1454, on the twelfth day of the month of May, which was Jubilate Sunday, the fifteenth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, martyrs, in Seligenstadt. In it the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Wolfram of Hirsau, Christian of St. Peter in Erfurt, Ulrich in Wiblingen, and Berthold of St. Stephen in Wurzburg, presided.

They approve the statutes of the lord cardinal.

Following in the footsteps of the lord cardinal and legate, with the sacred chapter approving, we command all and each of the statutes issued and ordained by him for the reform of our order in the immediately preceding provincial chapter celebrated in Wurzburg, and then unanimously accepted by the lord presidents and the whole chapter, to be strictly observed by all, under the penalties and censures contained and expressed in the letters of the said lord cardinal composed concerning this matter.

That the presidents, visitors, and treasurers should arrive before the day of the chapter.

We further will and ordain that, for provincial chapters to be celebrated from now on in the future, the lord presidents, visitors, and treasurers shall arrive on certain preceding days, while also being supported in the meantime at the chapter's expense, to handle the matters that arise and are necessary and suitable for the more useful and speedier celebration and dispatch of the chapter itself.

How visitors are to be received and treated.

We also strictly command all prelates and convents that, if they are required concerning this matter, they are to provide for their visitors safe conduct, at their own expense and according to their ability and knowledge, from the princes of the region and of that place or dominion as far as the next monastery to be visited. They are to receive and treat those visitors with all reverence and humility, charitably; they are diligently to observe their admonitions and ordinances and obey them.

LXVI They shall keep them in faithful security, under penalty of restitution and payment for all and each of the things thus deceitfully or fraudulently lost.

Concerning the household of the visitors.

The visitors, however, shall have with them an honorable household and retinue, and each of them shall be content with four mounts, unless a reasonable cause requires more.

Those who impede visitation incur the sentence of excommunication.

Lest anyone impede so wholesome an office of visitation by any contrivance or pretext, we will that all and every abbots, priors, provosts, and monks who refuse to receive their visitors, or who gainsay them, and who are rebellious and disobedient to them, and who impede the office of visitation by nod, deed, writing, or word, or who arrange, procure, cause, or attempt, by themselves or through another or others, directly or indirectly, that it be impeded by their friends, noble or ignoble, or by any subordinates whatsoever, so that their visitors cannot freely and quietly exercise an office of this kind, shall by that very fact incur the sentence of excommunication. The visitors themselves shall be bound to publish this sentence of excommunication against them and duly have it carried into execution.

Likewise we will that all and every abbots, provosts, priors, convents, and persons who have rejected from themselves this reformation of the lord cardinal legate and of the chapter, previously received and continued for a time, shall incur the sentence of excommunication, unless at least within the time to be fixed for them by their visitors they effectively take it up again and continue it.

Begging under pretext of need is forbidden.

It has come to our ears by a sure report that persons of both sexes of our order go about, not so much compelled by poverty as for the sake of begging, procuring that their begging of this kind be announced from the pulpits, and even begging door to door to the disparagement of the order. We forbid this to be done or to occur henceforth, and we exhort the people of God not to stretch out helping hands to such persons, but to send them back to their monasteries.

Or, if the resources of those monasteries do not suffice, the same brothers or persons of the order shall see to it that petitions of this kind are published and collections conveyed, not by themselves but through secular persons; and they shall seek the necessities of life from neighboring monasteries of the same order. If, after this prohibition of ours, they do not desist from the foregoing, any president may and must proceed against them as disobedient, according to the quality of the offenses.

That permission to wander should not be given to monks.

We have also learned that some abbots of monasteries and prelates do not fear to receive into obedience fugitive monks and others fleeing the reins of discipline, who go about after permission has sometimes even been extorted from their superiors and without proper proof; and that they give an occasion for wandering to those who wish it, to the peril of their souls and the scandal of many. We therefore, desiring to remedy a deadly disease, strictly forbid such things to be done henceforth, under penalty of infamy and incapacity; after warning has first been given, the visitors shall impose this penalty on the prelates who give, and on the monks who receive, permission to wander, with heavier penalties nevertheless to be added if the fault requires it.

Concerning procurators of absent persons.

Let there be a procurator for absent abbots, even three of them, under penalty of suspension from divine services, to be imposed by the presidents then in office, unless an evident cause stands in the way. Whether that cause is sufficient shall be proposed to the presidents.

Concerning ancient statutes here repeated anew.

Consequently, in this chapter very many statutes of past chapters are repeated in form, namely: that abbots should not henceforth withdraw themselves from the chapter, as above, chapter 13; and that all should publicly and everywhere wear the habit fitting to religious life, as above, chapter 1; and also that those visited should pay their visitors three florins for travel expenses, as chapter 4; and certain other things which are set out more fully above in their own places.

C I E S D V N O T M P A G R B U L F H Q W K J X Z Y E S T M P A G R B U L F H Q W K J X Z Y E S T M P A G R B U L F H Q W K J X Z Y E S T M P A G R B U L F H Q W K J X Z Y E S T

LXVII

The sixteenth provincial chapter, held at Erfurt for the third time, in the year of the Lord 1456.

In the year of the Lord 1456, on Jubilate Sunday, the sixteenth chapter was held at Saint Peter's in Erfurt. At it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Berthold of Saint Stephen's at Wuerzburg, John of Saint Michael's at Hildesheim, Ulrich in Blaubeuren, and Rupert of Saint James's at Mainz.

The election of future presidents and visitors belongs to the presidents.

We decree and declare that the election of presidents and visitors succeeding for the time belongs to the presidents, just as constitution 12 of Pope Benedict defines.

That secular persons are not to be allowed to be present at capitular acts.

We will that henceforth no secular person be admitted to capitular deliberations and proceedings; but when some act must be drawn up in public form, then notaries and witnesses who are honorable and worthy of trust are to be called in.

Concerning conformity of habit and tonsure among those coming to the chapter.

We also will and ordain that henceforth the prelates coming to the chapter, and the proctors of absent prelates, should strive for conformity of conduct, especially in habit and tonsure. And those who use birettas are not to wear them bare and openly with the hood of the cowl lowered, as some are accustomed to do, but are to place the hood of the cowl itself under the biretta for the sake of conformity, since this too seems to be a sign of humility. We will this to be firmly observed henceforth in every place, especially by the simple conventual brothers of our order, except during the divine offices.

That the names of abbots and proctors present in the chapter be inserted in the recess regularly.

We have also decreed that henceforth, in the recess of the chapter held for the time, the names of all fathers present and of the proctors of the absent be written down individually.

Concerning not requiring an oath in the act of visitation.

The visitors of the provincial chapter, in the act of their visitation, are not indiscreetly to constrain either prelates or subjects, by oath or otherwise, to disclose or publish hidden matters, especially criminal ones, unless the order of fraternal charity has been observed.

That provostries and priories be visited by the visitors of the provincial chapter.

Some abbots who have provostries, priories, and deaneries subject to themselves or to their monasteries have, as we have learned, hitherto been negligent in visiting them. Therefore we decree that these same provostries, priories, and deaneries are henceforth to be visited by the visitors of the provincial chapter. The abbots, however, to whom they are subject may, if they wish, be present at such visitation. And those so visited are bound for the time to pay only half the contribution.

Monks and nuns ought not to give themselves to disorderly feasting.

It has become known to us that among certain persons of our order there is an abuse of holding in turn, after dinner and also after supper, disorderly and excessive feasts and drinking bouts, mixing with these vain and scurrilous conversations. This abuse we abolish by the present statute, and we prohibit it from being done henceforth, commanding that those who are found transgressors in these matters be duly punished by the visitors with abstinence on bread and water, or otherwise according to the nature of the excess.

And because the aforesaid abuse is said to be fostered by another abuse, altogether more detestable, namely that in certain monasteries they usurp special revenues and have them distributed not through the cellarer, but through whomever they themselves wish, we likewise will that this abuse be wholly abolished, and that all things be brought into common use, and that through the cellarer the necessities be supplied to all according to the Rule.

Concerning the visitations of monasteries of nuns.

The monasteries of nuns of our holy order are to be visited by the visitors of the provincial chapter. These visitors, among other things, while consulting the interests of the same monasteries, should also strive to exclude from them secular girls who are there not for the sake of conversion, but at the request of their parents.

in burdening the monasteries and to the loss of discipline, they are being reared there.

With what caution nuns are to be visited by prelates.

LXVIII

Since the sight of women is dangerous for spiritual men, let the one to whom the care of souls is entrusted take care that he never undertakes the visitation of nuns out of a desire to see them, but only for the sake of necessity; and once that necessity has been dealt with, let him depart quickly. Nor should he presume to enter the enclosures of the monastery unless great necessity or usefulness requires it.

Concerning the appointment of a confessor for nuns.

Let no confessor be appointed for nuns without the consent of at least one president. But if anyone, whether prelate or subject, shall presume to attempt otherwise, let him be punished most severely by the visitors. Entrance into the enclosures of nuns is to be entirely forbidden to the confessor.

That monks are to be received without regard to persons or nobility.

Furthermore, it is reported that there are some monasteries of either sex in our province in which only knights and nobles have customarily been received to profession. From this has come the complete dissolution and abandonment of regular observance, and the total ruin of those monasteries in spiritual and temporal matters. Let the visitors inquire into the reason for this custom; and if privileges are alleged, let them examine them diligently, so that, once the truth has been discovered, such an elevated abuse may be abolished, and henceforth persons otherwise suitable may make profession there indiscriminately according to the rule, without regard to nobility.

No one from a reformed monastery is to be received elsewhere without letters from his abbot.

We forbid anyone to receive in another monastery any monks, converts, or donates who have gone out from a reformed monastery, unless they have the permission of their abbot.

No guest monk is to govern a parish.

Let no guest monk be permitted to govern a parish cure.

The incorrigible are to be referred to the presidents to be corrected.

If any monks or religious are found to be such that they cannot be restrained by their own prelates and visitors, let such persons be reported to the presidents, so that they may make provision concerning them.

Concerning the proclamation of the fathers in chapter.

Because the fathers of the order ought, among other reasons, to come together and be gathered in the Lord for this purpose, that they may celebrate provincial chapters and clear themselves before the presidents concerning their various negligences and faults, the lord presidents decree and establish that henceforth, in the celebration of chapters of this kind, the individual fathers must proclaim themselves concerning their faults, excesses, and negligences with a faithful and humble mind, ready to receive the punishment of the presidents.

Concerning supplying for the negligence of visitors.

If any of the visitors, because of a legitimate impediment, is unable to fulfill the office assigned to him, let him signify this to the nearest president, who will supply his place or will certainly appoint some other one of the prelates to supply it.

That the presidents and visitors should arrive at least four days before the day for celebrating chapter.

We will that the visitors, together with the presidents, hasten to arrive at least four days before the day on which the chapter is to begin, in order to report to the presidents what they have discovered, done, and carried out in their visitations, so that the presidents themselves may be ready, before the assembled fathers, to correct the excesses of the rebellious and disobedient, or also to punish the negligence of those same visitors, if any has been found.

The seventeenth provincial chapter, held at Nuremberg for the third time, in the year of the Lord 1459.

In the year of the Lord 1459, on the Sunday Misericordia Domini, the seventeenth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of St. Giles at Nuremberg. In it presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots George of St. Giles there, Berthold of St. Giles in Brunswick, Eberhard of St. James at Mainz, and Heinrich of Blessed Mary at Ettenmunster.

Concerning the old statutes repeated here.

In this chapter, as in almost all the others, certain old statutes were repeated in form. Of these, first...

The first was that the presidents and visitors should arrive on the Wednesday before the day appointed for beginning the chapter, together with the other matters contained above. And there all who had privileges for receiving only nobles renounced their rights. Nevertheless, with the common consent of all, those same privileges were then entirely abolished.

On the preacher.

The one who is to preach the sermon should arrive before the presidents somewhat before the appointed day, and should submit the sermon itself, in the form in which it is to be delivered, in good time to the correction or alteration of the presidents.

If any of the aforesaid presidents is absent at this arrival.

If it should happen that any of the presidents is absent for any reason, the others shall treat and dispose all matters that are appropriate, with the power of summoning one of the fathers present if need be, until the one arrives who ought to have been present for this preliminary meeting.

On the death of a president.

Concerning the death of any president, or any other kind of deficiency, the bull of Pope Martin V, which is set down above at the beginning of this volume, is to be observed, with this declaration added in this chapter: that the authority of the former presidents lasts until the day of the opening of the chapter, exclusive; and on that day the authority of the new presidents begins.

That schoolboys should not take part in the monks’ choirs by singing.

Since the company of schoolboys and secular clerics in the divine offices forces corruption of maturity upon the minds of religious, the lord presidents decreed that those schoolboys and clerics are to be dismissed to their parishes. But if in some place they cannot be dismissed without notable scandal, the visitors of those monasteries, after hearing the reasons, shall decide how long and in what manner they ought to be tolerated.

The eighteenth provincial chapter, celebrated at Würzburg for the third time, in the year of the Lord 1464.

In the year of the Lord 1464, in the twelfth indiction, on Jubilate Sunday, the eighteenth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of St. Stephen at Würzburg. In it presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Berthold of St. Stephen there, Johannes of St. Michael in Hildesheim, Melchior of St. Ulrich in Augsburg, and Eberhard of Michelsberg. In it it was ordained that serious resistance should be made to those who wish to transfer themselves from the order to the secular state or to the state of secular canons. And against them procurators are to be appointed in the Roman curia.

In difficult and important cases we will and ordain that first the fathers be consulted.

We will and ordain that, in important and difficult cases of the chapter and the order, henceforth during the time of the chapter itself the votes of each of the fathers present be examined in order; and each of them, according to God and his own conscience, shall speak with humility and reverence what he has judged better, when he has been asked.

On the multiplication of constitutions.

Considering that in the earlier chapters many useful statutes were made, from which little profit has so far been found to have followed, because of the negligence of very many, since it is superfluous to establish laws however celebrated if they are not duly entrusted to execution, and lest the multitude of statutes increase the material of transgression, we do not now wish to enact new ones, but we command each person to observe the old constitutions more diligently than hitherto.

The nineteenth provincial chapter, celebrated at Michelsberg for the first time, in the year of the Lord 1467.

In the year of the Lord 1467, in the fifteenth indiction, on the nineteenth day of the month of April, which was Jubilate Sunday, the nineteenth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Michelsberg at Bamberg. In it presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Johannes of Bursfelde, Melchior of Augsburg, Heinrich of St. Michael in Hildesheim, and Johannes in Werden.

On the old statutes repeated again in this chapter.

Many old statutes were repeated again in this chapter; since they are contained above, they are not to be inserted here again. Let us insert only the new ones. On suc-

LXX

It pleased us that, when any one of the presidents or visitors dies, the one who succeeds him in the abbacy should also succeed him in the presidency or visitation, without any new summons from anyone, both in the office and in the dignity of the presidency.

Concerning the feast of the commemoration of Saint Benedict.

We further will that the feast of the translation of our most holy father Benedict, in accordance with the apostolic prohibitions, should no longer be observed; but in place of the translation, the feast of his commemoration should be celebrated in the hours and divine offices, with all the customary ceremonies.

It was also decreed: A new penalty for negligent visitors.

All visitors who do not fulfill the office of visitation enjoined upon them shall be bound, for each monastery not visited, to pay as a penalty three Rhenish florins to the chapter, unless a legitimate cause intervenes.

Concerning the form of a proxy document.

And because negligence often occurs in the proxy documents of absent fathers, when they are not sent in proper form, with ignorance, as we believe, being the cause of this, therefore, to guard against those errors, we unanimously receive and approve this form of a sufficient proxy document inserted here.

Form of the proxy document.

To the reverend fathers in Christ, the lord presidents of the sacred provincial chapter of the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg, of the black monks of the Order of Saint Benedict, to be celebrated in the monastery N., in the diocese N., on the coming Sunday Jubilate: N., called abbot in N., of the same order, in the diocese N., obedience, reverence, and honor.

Venerable fathers and lords: Because, according to the praiseworthy statutes of the fathers, the provincial chapter is coming to be celebrated, to which, as I ought and am bound, I cannot come in person, being prevented by such a cause: let the cause be expressed. Hence it is that I appoint the venerable father, lord N., abbot in N., or the religious brother, a professed monk of our monastery N., as my undoubted proxy, in the best form, with full mandate, to appear in my place in the aforesaid chapter, to treat, vote, conclude, and do every other individual thing that I myself could and ought to do if I were personally present; with power to swear on my soul, if need be, that the cause of my absence alleged above is true. Further, if it should happen that a monetary collection is imposed by this chapter, he is to accept it in my person, and I shall also lawfully pay it when I am required. I promise, under witness of the present letters, that I will hold as ratified and acceptable whatever things shall be established and ordained in the same chapter, and that I will observe them, insofar as I am able, both by myself and by those subject to me. In faith and testimony of all these things, my abbatial seal has been impressed below upon these presents. Given in my aforesaid monastery, in the year, etc.

The twentieth provincial chapter, held for the fourth time at Erfurt, in the year of the Lord 1470.

In the year of the Lord 1470, in the third indiction, on the fifteenth day of the month of May, which was Sunday Jubilate, the twentieth provincial chapter was held at Saint Peter’s in Erfurt, for the fourth time, with the customary protests: that the fathers do not intend to admit excommunicated persons, and that neither they themselves nor the proxies are to depart before the end of the chapter, under penalty of an excommunication to be imposed by sentence.

Presiding at it were the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Gunther, abbot there; Melchior of Saints Afra and Ulrich at Augsburg; Sebald of Saint Giles at Nuremberg; and Paul of Saint Mary at Elchingen. In it it was ordained that the individual acts of each of the preceding chapters should be brought together in one compendium, as has been attempted here in the present compilation.

Concerning the old statutes that were here again renewed.

In the present chapter many statutes of the old chapters were renewed and inserted again into the recess as though anew. Among them are these. First, the form of the proxy document is inserted and confirmed word for word. Likewise, that the presidents of both chapters, together with the visitors, should arrive on the fourth weekday before the appointed day for celebrating the chapter, as above, chapter 17. And concerning negligence to be supplied [unclear].

LXXI

...the negligence of those not arriving on that same Wednesday, as in the same place. Likewise, that no one be made procurator for more than three, as above, chapter 15. And that negligent visitors shall pay three florins for each monastery not visited, as above, chapter 19. Likewise, that provostships and priories are to be visited by the same visitors, with the proper abbot present if he wishes, saving half the procuration, as chapter 16. The same is to be understood concerning reformed and unreformed nuns.

The statute formerly issued in chapters 8 and 9, concerning the recalling of fugitives and not giving a general letter of license to anyone, is again renewed word for word, as above, chapter 15.

That procurators of absentees may take part in capitular deliberations.

It pleased the lord presidents and the chapter that monks who are procurators of absent fathers, having sufficient procuratorial authority, may take part in capitular deliberations, just as they have taken part up to now.

Likewise concerning procurators of absentees.

The procurator of absentees must be fully informed about the visitations of those sending him, if any visitors have been there, and must report all these things to the lord presidents; he must also take upon himself, in place of those sending him, the penances and humiliations, and within a space of two months send the recess of the chapter to those by whom he was sent. But if he does not do this and is found negligent in the aforesaid matters, if he is an abbot he shall be punished by a fine of two florins for each monastery; if he is a simple monk, by suspension from divine offices.

Concerning the propriety and quality of clothing.

We also ordain and enact that abbots and all religious, whatever offices they may have been assigned, both within and outside the monastery, shall wear a decent habit, or a rain-cloak over the scapulars, with cowls sewn on and with covered birettas; and that they go about also with a decent retinue, all ostentation set aside.

If an abbot, in excuse for himself, sends letters of princes to the chapter.

No abbot or prelate may henceforth presume to obtain letters of princes to be sent to the chapter concerning his absence under penalty of three Rhenish florins, to be paid to the chapter without any remission.

What sort of person ought to be elected.

The lord presidents, together with the fathers, enacted concerning an abbot, provost, or prior that no one henceforth is to be elected or postulated as abbot, provost, or prior unless he has remained, without pretense, in observance and regular life for at least the space of a year, and has held and observed it. But if otherwise is done, there shall be done concerning such a man what the lord cardinal legate commanded by his letters to be done in such cases.

Whether a general letter of license should be granted to monks by their prelates.

We most strictly prohibit any prelate of our province or chapter henceforth from granting to his brothers, when they are being sent to any monastery whatever, a general letter of license; nor shall he permit them to use those already granted in this way, but rather, as quickly as possible, he shall prudently revoke what he inconsiderately granted to the peril of souls.

Concerning surreptitious apostolic indults.

We have also salutarily decreed that apostolic indults already obtained, or perhaps to be obtained in the future without the knowledge of the presidents, especially those that tend to the loss of observance and regular discipline, are henceforth not to be used, as being useless and surreptitious.

The twenty-first provincial chapter, held at Nuremberg for the fourth time, celebrated in the year of the Lord 1473.

In the year of the Lord 1473, in the sixth indiction, on Misericordia Domini Sunday, the twenty-first provincial chapter was held at Nuremberg, at St Egidius, for the fourth time. In it the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Theodericus of Bursfelde, Gunther of St Peter in Erfurt, Johannes of St Egidius in Nuremberg, and Johannes of Holy Cross in Werdea, presided.

Which statutes of the old chapters are repeated here.

First, the lord presidents and fathers commanded that all statutes of the preceding chapters, as though they were inserted here word for word, be kept inviolably by all those subject to the chapter.

LXXII

subjects of the chapter. Certain of the same statutes were also again inserted into this recess, which are found above word for word: namely, that the presidents, visitors, and preacher should arrive on the appointed day of the chapter, on Wednesday. Likewise, that if one of the presidents is absent at this arrival, the others, adding to themselves one of the priors if they wish, until he comes, may do everything with full power. Also the decree concerning apostolic indults not to be obtained or used, as is found in the preceding chapter. Similarly, that no one should be procurator for more than three persons; and that the procurators should be fully informed about each matter concerning the visitors, under the penalty stated there, and should transmit the recess to them within two months.

And that statute: that abbots and monks should wear suitable dress in every place. Also that one which forbids any abbot, for his own excuse, to dare to obtain letters of princes for the chapter. Likewise, that prelates should seek out their fugitives, and should henceforth grant no one a general letter of license. And that the visitors should visit provostships, priories, and convents of nuns, with their abbot able to be present if he wishes, as is found there. Also that those visited should pay their visitors three Rhenish florins for travel expenses. And concerning the penalty of three florins imposed on negligent visitors for any monastery not visited. Likewise also this: that the visitors should denounce rebels and disobedient persons to the nearest president, so that they may be punished. These and similar matters, which are contained above word for word, were here repeated again, with the following nevertheless newly added, as seemed good.

Novices are not to be admitted to profession before the completed year of probation.

Seeking as far as we can to forestall future dangers and to comply with regular and legal provision, we strictly forbid any prelate henceforth to receive a novice to profession before the year of his probation has been completed.

Concerning the habit of the lay brothers.

For the pleasing uniformity of all, lay brothers shall wear their cowls open in the front, in the manner of monks.

The twenty-second provincial chapter was celebrated at Michelsberg for the third time, in the year of the Lord 1476.

In the year of the Lord 1476, in the ninth indiction, on Jubilate Sunday, the twenty-second provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Michelsberg near Bamberg for the third time. In it the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Martin in Schwarzach, Hermann of St. James at Mainz, Henry in Blaubeuren, and Johannes of St. Giles in Nuremberg, presided.

The statutes of previous chapters are first approved.

Directing our attention to the things that were established in previous chapters and recesses, we confirm and approve all their constitutions and decrees, and we will that they be held and observed by all, just as if they were expressly inserted here word for word.

Concerning surreptitious apostolic indults not to be used, under penalty of excommunication.

Under penalty of excommunication we command that no one presume to use apostolic indults obtained surreptitiously, tending toward danger to souls and harm to regular observance, whether already obtained or perhaps to be obtained in the future without the knowledge of the presidents, as is also found there.

That absentees, with a procuratorial mandate, should pay four florins for the one whose procurator he is, under penalty of that person’s contumacy, without contradiction, to the chapter henceforth.

Concerning the other statutes placed here.

The statute concerning procurators was also renewed here again word for word: that they should transmit the recess of the chapter to those by whom they were sent, within two months after the chapter has been celebrated, under penalty of two florins if the procurator is an abbot, and of suspension from divine offices if he is a monk, as is found in chapter 20.

The twenty-fourth provincial chapter, celebrated at Nuremberg for the fifth time, in the year of the Lord 1479.

LXXIII

In the year of the Lord 1479, in the twelfth indiction, on the Sunday Misericordia Domini, the twenty-fourth provincial chapter was held at Saint Giles in Nuremberg for the fifth time. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Martin in Schwarzach, Leonhard of Saint Peter in Castello, Bernhard in Hirsau, and Hermann of Saint James in Mainz.

Which statutes of the preceding chapters were here repeated again.

In this holy provincial chapter several statutes were repeated as though anew, although they are known to have been ordained earlier in other chapters of preceding times, with few exceptions, in almost the same words. Among these are the following. First, concerning apostolic indults surreptitiously obtained and not to be used, as above, chapter 20, at the end, but with this clause added: Matters that must be transacted or obtained in the Roman curia for the order, or for monasteries jointly or separately, by the order's proctor residing in the curia for the time being, or with his express consent, all the prelates and monks of our province and order shall cause to be transacted through him.

Likewise, the statute was repeated that those who are visited are to receive and treat their visitors kindly, and are to pay them three Rhenish florins for travel expenses, under the added penalty of triple payment; and that they are to provide them with safe-conduct. And certain other things were also repeated, which nevertheless, because of their penalties and certain particular provisions, we have decided to set out again. The first of these is this.

That a monk is not to be received without letters commendatory from his abbot, under penalty of thirty florins.

We also forbid more strictly, under penalty of thirty Rhenish florins, all prelates and superiors of our order and province henceforth to receive any brother or monk in their monasteries without letters commendatory from that monk's own abbot. Those already received otherwise are to dismiss as soon as possible, under the same penalty, to be paid to the chapter without contradiction as often as they act to the contrary.

That a general license is not to be granted to anyone, under penalty of fifty florins.

We also enjoin the same upon all prelates, that henceforth they are not to grant their monks and professed brethren a general license without the consent of those presiding in the provincial chapter, under penalty of fifty florins, to be paid to the same chapter as often as they transgress this our constitution.

Concerning visitors.

We also strictly enjoin all those subject to our chapter by law or custom not in any way to contrive, either by themselves or through others, with diocesan bishops, princes, or nobles, that the visitors may not freely carry out their office. Nor are they to object that visitors are not to be admitted without the consent of the ordinaries, since they are sent by apostolic authority and visit the monasteries assigned to them in the place of the lord pope, as is found in Extra, De statu monachorum, chapter In singulis, paragraph Ordinentur. Nor are any to impose conditions on the visitors by which they would admit them, or without which they would refuse to admit them, under penalty of thirty florins.

Concerning visitation charters.

Under the same penalty we command all the aforesaid abbots, provosts, priors, deans, monks, and communities to keep diligently, read, preserve, and put into practice the charters, ordinances, and statutes made, or to be made, for them by the visitors.

That an abbot is not to grant property to a monk.

Since private property is always ruinous to monks and the overthrow of all religion, we most strictly forbid all prelates to allow any of their own monks to possess property. For what the supreme pontiff admits that he does not dare to do is judged very rash for an inferior to presume in any way, as we clearly have in Extra, De statu monachorum, Cum ad monasterium, at the end.

The twenty-third provincial chapter, held in Blaubeuren in the year of the Lord 1482.

In the year of the Lord 1482, in the fifteenth indiction, on the Sunday Jubilate, the twenty-fourth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of Saint John the Baptist in Blaubeuren, in the diocese of Constance. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Georg of Saint Stephen in Würzburg...

LXXIII

Likewise, Johannes in Wiblingen, Udalricus of Mönch... [unclear], and Johannes of St. Egidius in Nuremberg.

That the recesses of the provincial chapters from the time of the Council of Constance should be kept in all monasteries and read publicly in the convents.

Lest the statutes and ordinances of the provincial chapters celebrated up to now become unknown to those who are bound to know them, we will and strictly command, under penalty of twenty Rhenish florins, that all and each of the fathers have all recesses of chapters of this kind, from the time of the Council of Constance up to the present, copied and kept in one volume, which they are to bring with them at the time when the chapter is to be celebrated; and that in their convents they see to it that these same recesses are read publicly every quarter. But this statute concerning the reading of the individual recesses would seem too burdensome, as it appears to me. I therefore think it should be understood of an abbreviation, as will be clear below.

Concerning fugitives.

And lest an opportunity be given to monks for wandering here and there, if they were received everywhere as guests, we command all our abbots, under penalty of thirty Rhenish florins, that wherever they find a monk of our province wandering, immediately, if convenience permits, they send him, at the expense of the same monastery, back to the monastery from which he had gone out, to his own abbot; and that abbot shall be bound to receive him when so sent, after paying the expenses to the sender, without objection.

And under the same penalty we forbid all our prelates to admit or lodge any monks or converts turning aside to their monasteries, if they have not first shown letters commendatory, or credentials as they are commonly called; unless perhaps it is for this reason, that they may hold them and send them to their own abbots.

Concerning visitations.

Moreover, because the whole force of regular observance consists in visitations, we therefore forbid all those subject to our chapter to presume in any way to hinder the visitors in their offices; rather, they shall receive and treat them honorably and reverently, and provide for their safe-conduct and for travel-money of three florins, according to the statutes of the preceding chapters, under penalty of twenty florins.

Concerning the form of visitation.

And so that the visitors may be able to observe due order in their visitations, we will and strictly command, under penalty of ten florins, that they take care to fulfill their office according to the tenor of the form of visitation contained in the bull of the lord Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal legate, which he gave to the visitors of our province at that time. And note that this form, contained in the constitutions of the same cardinal concerning visitation, was inserted here word for word into the recess. Since I have placed it separately with the others on folio 42, I judged it superfluous to repeat it again at present in one volume.

The twenty-fifth provincial chapter, celebrated at Augsburg for the second time, in the year of the Lord 1485.

[unclear]

In the year of the Lord 1485, in the third indiction, on the Lord’s Day Jubilate, the twenty-fifth provincial chapter was celebrated for the second time at Saints Afra and Udalricus in Augsburg. In it presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Johannes of St. Egidius in Nuremberg, Johannes of St. Martin in Sponheim, Henricus of Saints Peter and Paul in Weissenburg, and Paulus of Blessed Mary in Elchingen. There the following statutes were made.

That criminal and incorrigible persons should not be expelled but imprisoned.

Although our blessed father Benedict, in the Rule, orders incorrigible monks to be expelled from the monastery, nevertheless we, considering the evident danger that would arise for many from this if it were put into practice, have thought that the statutes should be varied according to the variation of the times. Therefore we strictly forbid all our abbots and prelates to presume to expel or exclude from the monastery their monks, converts, or donates who are guilty of any crime whatever, since such expulsion of incorrigible persons would give them the opportunity to wander and to commit still graver offenses. Rather, they shall thrust such persons, offending so enormously, into prison, to be punished for a longer time according to the nature of the crime committed.

And two offices are to be held in the convents after the chapters have been celebrated.

LXXV

We further establish and ordain that in every monastery of our province, immediately after the chapter has been celebrated, each prelate shall have two offices celebrated conventually on the appropriate days: one for the living, and the other for the dead, with the proper vigils, for the brethren and benefactors of the provincial chapter and of the Order.

On the Initiation of Excommunication.

We also will and decree that those excommunicated, and those hereafter to be excommunicated in provincial chapters for any cause whatever, even for a contribution imposed by the presidents and not paid, shall be announced in their dioceses and monasteries; and that executors shall be appointed for this by the chapter, so that they may not excuse themselves in any way from sentences and censures of this kind, or claim ignorance, until they learn to obey the commands of the presidents.

Visitors shall make charters for the monasteries visited by them, and shall also send these to the presidents at the time of the chapter to be celebrated.

We further command the visitors to leave the charters of their visitations in the monasteries visited by them, according to the ancient statutes and ordinances, and to send copies of them, either personally or through their procurators, to the chapter itself in due time. In these they shall clearly inform the lord presidents concerning the condition of those monasteries in temporal and spiritual matters and with regard to persons, so that the presidents themselves, once the defects have been known, may be able to come as quickly as possible to the aid of such monasteries. But if the condition and necessity of the monasteries visited shall require it, once the visitation has been made the visitors shall immediately transmit copies of the charters to the presidents with suitable notice.

On the Expenses of Monasteries Attempting to Separate Themselves from the Order.

Furthermore, we will and ordain that expenses which the chapter may have had to undergo in any way for monasteries attempting to separate themselves from the Order, or even for recovering those already transferred, once such monasteries have been brought back, shall be paid to the chapter, with due consideration of their respective means.

On the Briefs of the Dead.

We will and ordain that in all future chapters the names of deceased brethren shall be sent by the abbots or their procurators, in schedules, to the chapter itself to be celebrated in due time, so that they may be commended to the prayers of the fathers.

The Twenty-Sixth Provincial Chapter Was Celebrated at Saint James, Mainz, in the Year of the Lord 1487.

In the year of the Lord 1487, in the sixth indiction, on Jubilate Sunday, the twenty-sixth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Saint James near Mainz. In it presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Henry in Wissembourg, Conrad in Wiblingen, Berthold of Saint Gotthard in Hildesheim, and Johannes in Seligenstadt.

On Diffinitors to Be Chosen by the Presidents.

It pleased all of us gathered capitularly that henceforth, in each chapter to be celebrated, the diffinitors shall be chosen by the presidents from among the fathers.

On the Age Required in a Person to Be Received to Profession in the Order.

We further forbid all abbots and prelates of our chapter to receive anyone henceforth to profession in the Order unless that person has reached the required age: a male, namely, having completed fourteen years, and a female twelve years.

On the Age of Brethren to Be Ordained.

We also forbid all the same prelates henceforth to promote their subjects, while under age, to major orders, contrary to the provision of common law and the ordinance of the supreme pontiffs.

On Novices Obliged to Perform the Canonical Hours.

We decree that all professed members and novices of our Order, even those established in no sacred order, are obliged to say the canonical hours every day according to the ordinance of the Rule.

The Twenty-Seventh Provincial Chapter Was Celebrated at Nuremberg for the Sixth Time, in the Year of the Lord 1490.

In the year of the Lord 1490, on the Sunday Misericordia Domini, the twenty-seventh provincial chapter was celebrated at Saint Giles in Nuremberg for the sixth time. In it presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots George of Saint Stephen in Würzburg, Johannes of Saint Giles in Nuremberg, of [unclear]

of Nuremberg, Heinrich in Blaubeuren, and Blasius in Hirsau.

Concerning those who do not admit the visitors.

It has come to our ears by certain and weighty report that some abbots and monks have not only refused to admit their visitors, but, what is more serious, have even shamefully driven them from their houses with reproach and indignation, in manifest contempt of the chapter and canons of the order. Therefore we exhort all and each of the prelates and professed members established anywhere in our province in the order not to presume to attempt such things henceforth, under the penalty more fully expressed in the statutes above; and we wish that penalty to be applied without remission against rebels of this sort by the visitors themselves or by the presidents. Rather, all who are to be visited should meet their visitors cheerfully and reverently, receive them humbly and gladly, and treat them humanely; and, if need be, they should also provide them at their own expense with safe conduct as far as another monastery to be visited by them.

Concerning the visitation documents.

It pleased the fathers that, unless contempt intervenes, in the visitation documents henceforth they should not place words of command or threat under censures, but rather exhortatory or entreating words, by which they may draw the minds of their subjects toward virtues out of love, unless, as we have said, contempt intervenes, or where the matter concerns the transgression of the three substantial vows, or some evident necessity elsewhere compels it.

The twenty-eighth provincial chapter was celebrated in the year of the Lord 1493.

In the year of our Lord 1493, on Jubilate Sunday, the twenty-eighth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul at Hirsau, of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Speyer. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots John in Sponheim, Conrad in Wiblingen, Bartholomew of Holy Cross in Werdea, and Andreas of Monks' Mount near Bamberg,

abbots of monasteries of the dioceses of Mainz, Constance, Augsburg, and Bamberg. In this chapter the statutes of the earlier chapters were newly confirmed, with this one addition, which follows word for word.

Concerning the confession of monks.
