We will and ordain that every monk professed according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, in accordance with the Clementine constitution Ne in agro, De statu monachorum, must and is bound to make confession to his abbot at least once a month concerning matters that arise; and concerning reserved cases, to the abbot as often as he knows himself to have offended in such matters, under the penalties contained in the constitutions of the supreme pontiffs, general councils, or provincial chapters.

It was also established in the same chapter that the abridgment of the recess of the provincial chapters, after it has been printed and presented to the individual monasteries, should thereafter be read publicly at least once every three years.

The first bull of the Council of Constance for celebrating the provincial chapter, in which are recounted the evils that arise from the omission of chapters of this kind, and the benefits arising from their diligent continuation. In the year of the Lord 1416.

The executorial processes of the same bull, in the year as above.

Another bull of the same council concerning the method and form of choosing presidents. In the year 1417.

Another executorial bull of the said council against those rebellious and disobedient to the statutes and ordinances of the fathers of the order. In the year as above.

Another executorial bull of the aforesaid council, in the year as above.

Another executorial bull of the aforesaid council, in the year as above.

The Council of Constance issued executorial bulls against those disobedient and rebellious toward the provincial chapter or its presidents. In the year of the Lord 1420.

A bull of Pope Martin V: that during the time of the chapter others may be deputed and assumed in place of absent presidents; and that the presidents may, for reasons, change the place of the chapter, with extended authority to absolve from all censures and penalties those who submit themselves to regular observance with the mind and intention of continuing such observance. In the year of the Lord 1439. And this privilege is very broad with regard to irregularity, infamy, and other penalties and censures; and it extends only to those who submit themselves to regular observance with the mind and intention of continuing such observance. And it lasts until the express revocation of another general council or of the apostolic see.

The statute of the lord Heinrich, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Eusebius of the most holy Roman Church, Englishman, legate of the apostolic see throughout all Germany and the kingdoms of Hungary and Bohemia, that the father presidents should compel rebels and contemners of the sta[unclear]

of the statutes of the chapter, and to hear any causes whatsoever moved on that account. Done at Frankfurt, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of the most holy father in Christ and our lord, lord Martin, pope, the fifth of that name.

Statute of lord Ludovicus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia of the Roman Church, of Arles, legate de latere deputed to the parts of Germany by the sacred general synod of Basel, lawfully assembled in the Holy Spirit and representing the universal Church: that during the time of the chapter the divine offices may be celebrated even in a place under interdict; and that the fathers, presidents, and visitors may absolve persons subject to the chapter from all censures and penalties, confirm elections, confer the office of benediction, and crown nuns. And this statute has force when those to whom confirmation belongs, after being solemnly required a third time before a public notary and witnesses, with no reasonable cause preventing them, have maliciously refused or neglected to confirm the same election without charge, according to the decrees of the aforesaid synod. Likewise, if those to whom this belongs by right, having been similarly required, have refused or neglected to bless abbots or abbesses, to confer upon them the office of benediction, and to crown nuns, or also to bless them according to the accustomed manner, without charge and according to the decrees just mentioned. Done at Frankfurt, in the year of the Lord 1446.

Penal statutes for the reform of the abbots and brothers of the Order of Saint Benedict of the province of Mainz, issued by lord Nicholas, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter ad Vincula of the Holy Roman Church, legate of the Apostolic See throughout Germany.

Statute of the same: that those entering monasteries of nuns without permission and contrary to the provision of common law incur the sentence of excommunication. Done at Mainz, on the twentieth day of the month of November, in the year of the Lord 1451.

Bull of Pope Pius, which confirms all the statutes of the said lord cardinal. Issued in the year of the Lord 1459, in the first year of his pontificate.

Bull of Sixtus IV, which also confirms all the privileges of his predecessors and of others, under several penalties and censures. Issued in the year of the Lord 1479, in the eighth year of his pontificate.

Privileges of secular princes.

Safe-conduct of Sigismund, king of the Romans, given to the visitors under penalties. Done at Constance, in the year of the Lord 1418.

Confirmation, approval, and admission of the reform and visitation by Albert, king of the Romans. Done in the year 1439.

Safe-conduct granted by the same to the visitors. Done in the year stated above.

A brief and summary recapitulation, or epilogue, of all the matters aforesaid: in what order and manner individuals ought to come together at the provincial chapter.

First rubric.

When any chapter is to be celebrated, those who are officials for the time being, namely the presidents, visitors, treasurers, and the one making the sermon there according to the ordinance of the seventeenth chapter, and certain others, ought to precede the chapter itself by four days, so that they may be present there on Wednesday and may more conveniently inform themselves, both about matters already transacted and about matters to be handled in their offices, and may at last be able to dispatch them more quickly. This should be understood of the presidents of each chapter, namely of the one to be celebrated as well as of the preceding one, as appears above, chapter 20. Concerning the one making the sermon, it has been ordained that his sermon first be examined, so that, if need be, it may be corrected and amended. The rest, however, whether abbots or procurators, ought to present themselves there, so that when the chapter is to be opened, no one may be found absent. Nor is the excuse of anyone to be admitted, except either of one who is ill, or who has deadly enmities, or certainly is so poor that he cannot conveniently present himself at the chapter without danger. Hence no procurator for any absent person without such true and manifest impediments ought ever to be ad-

be admitted. Likewise, no one may obtain letters of princes or nobles concerning his absence, under penalty of three florins. If, however, any one of the officials is absent, the others will nevertheless be able to proceed with the acts, according to the ordinance of chapter 20. But in the event that none of the presidents is present, the others who have assembled for the celebration may, for that occasion, appoint other suitable presidents, by the indult of Pope Martin V, whose bull is included among the acts of the first chapter. By the same indult, those presidents may also change the place of the chapter, together with the extension of the term, for due causes. Likewise, no one there, whether he is an official or not, may leave before the end of the chapter without the presidents’ permission, under the penalty stated above, chapters 3 and 4, and under sentence of excommunication to be imposed, as above, chapter 20. Also, no one coming to the chapter ought to have more than six mounts; if anyone does so, he must, within a month, place in the chest for the common benefit of the chapter three times as much as he is shown to have spent for the rest, as above, chapter 3; and if he has not observed this, at the next following chapter he must be condemned by the presidents to double payment, without any remission. Likewise, each one must contribute there three Rhenish florins, which they must pay either then or within the three-day period during which the visitators happen to be with them, without further delay, under penalty of excommunication; once the term has elapsed, the visitators are most strictly ordered to pronounce this against them, according to chapter 5 of the Benedictine statutes, as above, chapter 1.

How the chapter is to be celebrated, and how the fathers ought to conduct themselves in it. Rubric Two.

Therefore, if the time is at hand for the chapter to be celebrated, which has been appointed always to be celebrated every three years unless, for a certain and reasonable cause, it is extended longer by the presidents, then first, after the Mass and sermon have been held beforehand, and after the fathers have been gathered together in one place in the chapter room, and after the Benedicite has been said, following the reading of the martyrology and the passage from the text of the Rule recited by the reader, a formal protestation is to be made concerning the non-admission of excommunicated persons, as above, chapter 20. Secondly, the place for the future chapter is to be named and announced by the presidents.

That place must not be changed except for a grave and reasonable cause, and only by the presidents, and it can be changed as stated above, chapter 1. Then, according to the ordinance of chapter 17 and certain others, the presidents and the other officials of the future chapter are to be designated, and also the visitators of the monasteries, as well as the one who is to give the sermon and another who is to celebrate the Mass; not, indeed, under their proper names, but only under the names of their offices, so that if anyone should resign or die, or certainly be deposed, then the abbot of the same place would carry out the office enjoined upon him. For although the person changes, nevertheless the dignity, which does not die, always remains. Finally, action is to be taken concerning those matters that are to be corrected in the order, and those that perhaps are newly to be ordered and established for the benefit of the whole order. There one must begin first with those who are present: each of them must state his fault on the mat and voluntarily offer himself for suitable correction. Their visitators must accuse and proclaim them. But those who for that time are procurators of absent persons must undergo disciplines and other suitable penalties not only for themselves, but also for those who appointed them, such as the presidents themselves, according to the report of the visitators or other certain and evident knowledge of any kind, shall justly and reasonably have decreed are to be imposed. Secondly, the absent are to be dealt with, and so, in order, the remaining business pressing upon the order. Lastly, each matter issued and discussed is to be reduced to a certain form and inserted into the charter or recess. Nor may any layman be present at those discussions or be admitted there, except only a public notary and honorable witnesses. But even these must not be admitted indiscriminately; indeed, only when the act itself is now to be reduced into public form. In that form there must also be written the names of all the abbots present and of the procurators of the absent. All who are present must receive a copy of it. But they must send it to the absent persons for whom...

their procurators within two months, under the penalty expressed above in chapter 20. Likewise, in the chapter itself, when great and difficult matters are to be treated, the votes of each one must be carefully sought out; and each person must state his vote according to God and conscience, with humility and purity of intention, and must give the reason moving him.

Furthermore, it has been ordained how those present ought to conduct themselves there in their conversation: namely, that all, both abbots and the procurators of abbots, ought to strive for conformity of manners, especially in habit and tonsure; and no one is henceforth to use a bare biretta, but is to place the hood of the cowl itself under the biretta, as above, chapter 16. Likewise, during the three days over which the chapter continues, all ought to come together to one table, so that they may sit together and be refreshed together. There only two dishes of fish are to be served, one of eggs or fried foods, and two good pottages, with cheese or some fruits added, as above, chapter 7. The treasurers, however, ought to advance the expenses, and then collect them again from the contribution of the individual abbots, as above, chapter 9.

Likewise, there also the abbots and the procurators of abbots ought to present notices in which the names of the dead from the next preceding chapter are contained, so that in chapter they may be absolved, that is, by way of prayer, and prayers may be made for them. The form of these notices is as follows: Brother N., priest or levite, died on such a day in that place, etc., as above, chapter 4.

Concerning the presidents. Rubric Three.

The presidents who are to preside in the future chapter must, according to the ordinance of chapter 16, which was drawn from the constitutions of Benedict XII, be chosen by the presidents of the preceding chapter; and, according to the ordinance of chapter 13, only from among the reformed. Further, in that same future chapter over which they preside, they must choose, just as their predecessors did, all the officials of the chapter, namely the presidents, visitors, etc., and do the other things contained in the constitutions of the aforementioned Benedict XII. For they have authority in chapter to preside, to hear, inquire into, and discuss faults, and to impose penalties and penances according to the measure of the faults; to compel negligent visitors, under ecclesiastical censures, to execute faithfully the office enjoined upon them; to determine, in certain cases, an increase of the subsidy or travel allowance that is owed to the visitors by the monasteries visited by them, beyond three florins; to make ordinances concerning brothers to be sent to study; and to license brothers who, with pious intention, desire to pass from an unreformed monastery to a reformed one.

Against those who do not appear in chapter, and against all who hinder, oppose, or refuse to admit reformations and visitations, or in any other way act contrary to them, and also against those who do not obey the visitors, and against those who harm monasteries in goods, persons, etc., they have authority to proceed by censures, their authority applying jointly and severally. They also have authority, and are bound, to visit exempt and royal monasteries in person together with the visitors. Likewise, they have authority from Martin V to change, for certain reasons, the place appointed for holding the chapter, even with a prorogation of the term. The same aforementioned pope also grants that, if anyone elected president is unwilling to accept the office or cannot conveniently be present, then the other presidents, with the consent of the greater part of those making up the chapter, or, if none of the presidents is present, the others assembled for the celebration of the chapter, may choose and appoint other suitable persons as presidents for those occasions.

Concerning the chest and the keepers of the chest. Rubric Four.

A common chest is recognized as always necessary for the benefit of the chapter, so that in it may be placed the monetary contributions, the penalties for contumacy or for any other fault of the abbots, and also the other things that are received, either by the visitors or by the treasurers, as pertaining to the necessity or benefit of the chapter. But it is also necessary that this chest be kept in a safe and suitable place under trustworthy custodians, who are called treasurers. They have full power to exact penalties, under censures, from those who have incurred penalties, and likewise to absolve any who may perhaps have been excommunicated on account of the aforesaid matters. Therefore, in the fifth chapter of the monasteries

For this reason, in chapter 5 the monastery of St. Giles in Nuremberg was appointed as the place where the chest is now kept, and from there the treasurers were designated, who now have their office set out above. They must also provide the midday meal for three days at the provincial chapter, as above, chapter 9. And they must come to the chapter itself according to the ordinance set out above under the first rubric.

Concerning proctors. Rubric 5.

There are two kinds of proctors. Some are general, belonging to the whole chapter; it is their duty to see to it that the visitors carry out the office entrusted to them energetically and faithfully, indeed to compel them by censures if need be, and to report their negligence to those presiding, as above, chapter 13 and certain following chapters.

Others are special proctors, who are substituted for certain abbots unable to come to the chapter. Enough has been said above, in chapter 20 and in very many other places, such as chapters 4, 6, 11, 13, 17, and 18, about these proctors and the abbots substituting them: namely, how one proctor is not to undertake the cases of more than three abbots, except for the cases there expressed; and that they are not to be admitted unless an effective bodily oath has first been taken; and likewise many other matters that can be seen there. A form of procuration, for the sake of those ignorant of it, has also been inserted in the recess of the nineteenth chapter. It is as follows.

To the reverend fathers in Christ, the lord presidents of the sacred provincial chapter of the province of Mainz and diocese of Bamberg, of the black monks of the Order of Saint Benedict, to be held in the monastery N. of the diocese N. on the coming Sunday Iubilate, N., humble abbot of the monastery N. of the Order of Saint Benedict of the province of Mainz, offers whatever reverence and honor he can.

Reverend fathers and lords, since according to the praiseworthy institutes of the fathers a provincial chapter is coming to be held, to which I both ought and am bound to come in person, but because I am so hindered by such a cause that I cannot conveniently appear in person, therefore I constitute the reverend lord abbot N. as my envoy and true proctor, in the best form, with full mandate in my stead in the said provincial chapter,

to appear, promise, conclude, and do all things that I myself could and ought to do if I were personally present, with power to swear on my soul, if need be, that the cause alleged for my absence is true. Moreover, if a monetary collection should happen to be imposed by the chapter, he is to accept it in my person, and I promise that I will lawfully pay it if I am required. By the testimony of these present letters, I promise that whatever shall be duly and lawfully ordained in the same chapter I will hold ratified and acceptable, and will observe it, as far as I can, both for myself and for those committed to me. In witness of all these things my abbatial seal has been impressed on these presents. Given in the year of the Lord etc.

Concerning visitors. Rubric 6.

Visitors of monasteries and visitors of visitors must be elected by those presiding in the provincial chapter, as above, chapter 16, and only from reformed houses, as above, chapter 13. They are bound to know each and every thing that has been done and ordained in every chapter from the first to the last, so that, by first observing most strictly in themselves the law that they wish and ought to impose on others, they may at length require it more effectively from others and bind them to it, and may be able and empowered to punish transgressors, as they ought, with fitting vengeance, under the strictest account to be rendered in the dread judgment to come.

After they have come from the chapter, these visitors must begin their visitations within a year, under penalty of thirty florins, as in chapter 4, or of three florins for each monastery to be visited, as in chapter 20, indeed also under sentence of excommunication to be imposed, as in chapter 8, unless they are excused by reason of hostility, illness, or some other legitimate cause, as in chapter 13. And they must faithfully complete the work under virtue of holy obedience, keeping God before their eyes, to whom they will render a strict account, so that before they leave the monasteries they effectively reform, as far as lies in them, whatever is in those houses, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the canonical sanctions, and the statutes of the provincial chapter and of the order, especially in the three substantial matters, which are obedience, continence, and poverty. And where they do not find disciplines and ceremonies [unclear].

...valid; they ought to establish those disciplines and ceremonies which they have received as given to them by the chapter, as above, chapter 6, and from there they ought to make a report to the presidents concerning the first matters.

Likewise, in whatever diocese they have been appointed to visit monasteries of men, they ought also to visit the monasteries of nuns in it, just as do the others to whom care of them has been committed. Nevertheless, they must take care never to visit them out of desire to see them, since the sight of them is dangerous; and when they have finished there, they ought to withdraw at once, etc., 16.

They ought likewise to visit provostships, priories, and deaneries that are subject to certain monasteries, admitting, however, the abbots to whom they are subject, if they wish to be present. And those visited in such places shall pay half the collection.

They ought to perform the act of visitation itself according to the form prescribed to them by the presidents of the provincial chapter, without exacting an oath, after first setting forth the word of God, etc., 6. Nor ought they to constrain anyone by oath, or otherwise indiscreetly, to reveal and publish hidden offenses, unless the order of fraternal correction has been observed.

They may also visit again a monastery previously visited by them, if they see that this is expedient, but not for that reason exact procuration again and as often. Likewise, they can impose penalties, and ought to do so according to the requirement of the faults; and they may exact penalties instituted either by the provincial chapter or otherwise by anyone, both corporal and monetary. But the money which they receive, whether tributary or penal, they ought to send to the guardians of the chest, so that it may be deposited by them in the chest.

Likewise, for contumacy or rebellion and disobedience they can pronounce sentences of excommunication, and absolve from an imposed penalty after suitable satisfaction has first been promised. Likewise, if they find any rebels and resisters whom they cannot correct by themselves, they ought to denounce them to the neighboring president, so that he, with the assistance of such persons brought in, may proceed through ecclesiastical censure according to the measure of the fault. For all those are also excommunicated by the very fact who in any way either impede visitations from being carried out or abandon a reformation once begun, unless within the time to be set by the visitors they attempt to begin it again. Likewise, they ought to provide the record to every monastery visited by them. To these things, therefore, the visitors themselves are bound under obedience and the penalties noted above. If they have been negligent, whether in many matters or in few, they ought to be compelled by the presidents and procurators of the chapter, through ecclesiastical censure or another penalty, not to neglect the office entrusted to them.

Yet, lest they be compelled to do labor without reward and, contrary to apostolic tradition, to serve as soldiers at their own expense, it has been ordained that each monastery visited by them ought to give them three Rhenish florins for travel expenses. It has been committed to their consciences either to remit or even to increase those same florins for good reason.

Likewise, the visited monasteries are to guard their horses and other goods with the utmost diligence. And if, which God forbid, anything from their goods should happen to be lost or carried off, before all else the abbot and convent of such a monastery must pay without delay the value of the goods or things lost, without contradiction; and nevertheless they are to be punished for negligence by a penalty to be moderated by the presidents. And the same abbot must also provide safe-conduct for the visitors. If the visitors have been despoiled or harmed, he must likewise provide safe-conduct. The visitation is not to have six mounts, neither in the act of visitation nor in coming to chapter.

Concerning the Act of Visitation. Rubric Seven.

In the act of visitation, the eye of consideration of the fathers making the visitation must be directed chiefly to four things. First, namely, to the sites of the monasteries, as the more visible things. Second, to the persons dwelling within the sites of the monasteries. Third, to the conduct and discipline of the persons. Fourth and last, to the divine worship itself. If one considers the first of these diligently, it at once shows what should probably be thought concerning the second; and again...

and again, the second in some respect concerning the third, and so on.

Concerning the Places of Monasteries. Rubric Eight.

The Apostle says: “What is spiritual is not first, but what is natural.” Therefore, first, as has been said, one must consider external things, that is, places, as bodily matters. Places are of three kinds. Some are necessary, such as the oratory, cloister, refectory, dormitory, infirmary, bath, storehouse, cellar, a place for guests with the abbot’s house, kitchen, and the porter’s cell with the chapter room. If any of these places is lacking, it must be built within a year, by virtue of holy obedience, or repaired if it has fallen down; and those who are negligent must actually be punished by the visitors, as above, chapter 3.

Some places, however, are matters of well-being, such as a garden, bakery, mill, workshop for binding books, and the like. Others are superfluous, harmful and contrary to the regular norm, such as wandering, secluded, and suspicious lodgings belonging to certain houses. These must either be utterly destroyed or converted to some other, better use of the monastery, under the same obedience as above.

The oratory, which is first among the necessary places, must be furnished with lights, altars, and ornaments that are clean, pure, and decent; the choir with seats, pulpits, and chant books; the sacristy with chalices, corporals, missal books, sacred treasures, and vestments and ornaments pertaining to the divine office and ministries, as is said in chapter 1, where these words are also added: “We will,” it says, “that within a month provision be made for clean, decent, and secure vessels and a place in which the Eucharist is to be reserved.” The same statute has provisions there and in the following sections concerning the baptistery. Books, with the other ornaments, are to be kept under careful custody. These things are to be understood and observed concerning treasures and seals, and certain following chapters likewise wish the same. Therefore the visitors must diligently attend to each of these matters concerning the oratory.

And concerning these things they must consider: what revenues, offerings, and so forth pertain to the oratory and sacristy; likewise, in what manner, whether simoniacally or not; likewise, under what appearance of vice property is possessed; and so concerning the other matters. And in the same way a similar ordinance applies to the other officials, such as the abbot, cellarer, and so forth: whether every year they render an account, and in what manner.

For it is prescribed in the above-mentioned third chapter, and also in the first, by virtue of holy obedience and under penalty of excommunication to be imposed by the visitors, that every abbot shall hand over to the visitors in writing a distinct account of the ancient and present state of his monastery, and that all officials shall present to them a faithful account of receipts and distributions. Likewise, inventories are to be made; places are not to be leased out except according to the Benedictine constitution, which must also be observed in receiving spoils from benefices and in loans and sales to be made. Transgressors must be punished severely, even beyond the penalties contained in the aforesaid constitutions. These things concern the oratory. The rest concerning the other places will appear below in the section on the discipline of persons.

Concerning the Persons Who Dwell Within Monasteries. Rubric 9.

The persons who dwell within monasteries, if they are not professed, must be not only necessary and useful, but also respectable and free from suspicion. Therefore all who are superfluous, disreputable, and suspicious must be removed far from the boundaries of the monasteries. Those, however, who are already professed or soon to be professed must be considered very carefully, both according to the quantity of their number and according to the quality of their condition. For everywhere the number of monks once established ought, if resources suffice, to be preserved whole, or at least as many as can conveniently be supported, as above, chapter 1, and in certain following chapters; through them the divine worship may be performed perfectly and laudably. From them sufficient and necessary officials are to be appointed according to the disposition of the Rule: namely, abbot, prior, deans, cellarer, porter, infirmarian, and so concerning the rest. And especially some suitable men...

who are to instruct the young sufficiently in the elementary sciences, according to the form of the statutes of Benedict XII, as above, chapter 1 and 3. And some are to be brought from reformed houses elsewhere, if the monastery itself has not previously been well reformed.

Likewise, not only nobles are to be received, nor only Scots, but according to the rule one sort as well as another: the freeborn as well as one converted from servile status, the poor man who has nothing at all as well as the rich, powerful, and very well supplied man, as above, in the same chapter, and commonly in many others, as 16 and 17. Nor should anything be demanded from them, nor should any of them promise anything for his reception, whether through himself or through others, nor otherwise promise that he will give anything, except what, without agreement, he himself or his parents may wish or have wished by free will to offer at the altar, or otherwise to the monastery or to God. And those received in this way, when the year of probation has elapsed, are to make profession and promise stability according to the rule, as above, chapter 2. Without that probation, too, no one is to be received into obedientiaries: neither one recently coming from the world, nor one arriving from another monastery with letters or without letters, as above, chapters 8, 13, 15, etc.

Also, henceforth brothers should not be received without the permission of their superiors, nor be permitted to wander. If any have been received up to now, even by authority of the Apostolic See or with otherwise sufficient permission, they should nevertheless all be recalled within two months, namely, and instructed according to the statutes of our order, under penalty of excommunication and suspension, as above, chapters 1 and 2. Or they should even be sent back to their own monasteries, if they were received without sufficient permission and authority, under the same penalty, as above, chapter 8. Fugitive or wandering monks should not be received without letters of commendation from their abbots or from the nearer president; nor should they even be lodged except for three days, as above, chapters 8 and 12, under the same penalty. Likewise, no one should be received or permitted to remain in the province if he has laid, or had laid, violent hands either on a monk or on an abbot, as above, chapter 12, under the same penalty.

Likewise, concerning persons it must further be considered whether all are present; whether some are sick or in prison; whether some are fugitives and not recalled, or dismissed with general permissions, which henceforth should not be done; whether some are in priories or provostships; whether some are in study or in another unreformed monastery, even with a special mandate. For no one should be sent from a reformed house to an unreformed one except for the sake of reform. In all these matters, and likewise in the following ones as also in the preceding ones, the visitors must both show and exercise exact diligence according to the mandate of those presiding, in virtue of holy obedience, as above, chapter 1.

Concerning the discipline of persons dwelling within monasteries. Rubric 10.

The discipline of monks is to be weighed and considered in many respects, both according to the rule and also according to the statutes of the fathers. First, however, concerning the exterior things of a person, namely tonsure and clothing: by whom garments are supplied to the brothers; whether by a common wardrobe-keeper, or whether indeed they have them through friends or from some property of their own; and whether provision is made for each equally, or differently, without illness or another reasonable cause. Likewise, whether the garments are according to the statutes of the fathers: only such as are necessary, namely, and religious both in material and in form.

Second, concerning food and fasting: whether all, except the sick, are fed in the refectory without eating meat; whether there is a reader at table and ministers who, according to the rule, enter on Sunday with a blessing. For it should not be permitted that individual monks, or any of them, have special youths or servants as ministers, as it has been found to happen in certain monasteries. Nor should anyone obtain anything for himself through himself, through labors, through friends, or through any others whatever, or receive anything even not obtained in advance but offered freely without permission; rather, he should expect everything from the father of the monastery. And if the eating of meat is at times granted to some for cause, this should be done only on certain days and only in the infirmary, where no layperson should be admitted. But on the road, or outside the monastery, no healthy person should eat meat, just as neither should he within the monastery. Likewise, whether alms are given from what is surplus. And whether the ministers perform their washings on Saturday at the Mandatum.

Likewise, concerning fasting: whether the fast both of the church whether he duly observes both the ecclesiastical and the regular fast; when and how, and with whom, dispensation is made for a second meal in the refectory; when also they use oil, and when eggs or butter; how in Advent, and how in Lent.

Third, concerning nocturnal rest and silence: namely, whether all sleep in one dormitory, girded and clothed; whether each sleeps in a separate bed, or two in one bed, which ought not to be done; whether seniors are mixed with juniors; whether the dormitory is closed, and when; whether the prior has keys to all cells; whether they sleep in woolens; whether the cells are sufficiently latticed, as they ought to be, under penalty of excommunication latae sententiae; whether the beds are frequently inspected because of private property; whether silence is kept in the dormitory, oratory, cloister, and refectory after Compline, and in chapter and at other times and places, in the manner and form set down in the Rule.

Fourth, concerning subjects: whether they are obedient; whether they are proprietors, possessing anything whatever from offerings, Mass stipends, labors, offices, or any other sources whatsoever; whether there is a report of incontinence concerning anyone.

Fifth, concerning shaving and bathing: when, how, and with what discipline they have them; and, concerning the sick, how they are provided for; whether they have an infirmarian and cellarer who are diligent and fear God; whether the sisters and the others in the convent, and also they themselves, are provided with suitable food; whether they have appropriate comforts at the proper time; and whether the young are instructed by competent masters in morals and ceremonies, and also in the elementary sciences; and by whom, whether by monks or seculars; and whether any are at study.

Sixth, how they conduct themselves toward one another: whether humbly and charitably; and whether, after a disturbance has arisen, they seek reconciliation according to the Rule.

Seventh, how they conduct themselves toward outsiders and strangers: whether perhaps they are too familiar with them, or whether, because of them, or also because of relatives, friends, or parents, it often happens that they leave the monastery. Likewise, conversely, whether they receive guests who come to them with all kindness, to lodging and to table, with the prescribed washing of feet and reading of the divine law.

Eighth, how they conduct themselves when leaving the monastery: whether they leave with permission, and whose permission; whether with a companion, and what sort; with how many horses and servants, and what sort; whether with a blessing both when going out and when coming in; whether also with fitting habit and books of hours, and so forth concerning the other matters about which above, chapter 1, and below in the following rubric.

Ninth, concerning individual persons, a particular consideration and inquiry must be made. First, concerning the abbot: whether before election he had been reformed, or at least had remained in reform for a year; whether afterward he continued the reform; whether he attended chapter and paid the contribution; whether he gives an accounting each year; and whether he handed over in writing the state of his monastery to the former visitors; and whether he obeyed them in all their ordinances; whether he alienated, pawned, or handed over the goods of the monastery to a friend; how he confers benefices; how he orders offices, whether with counsel or according to his own opinion; whether he has priories, provostships, or churches annexed to the monastery; how he confers them, and on whom. Likewise, whether each year he receives an account from them and holds a chapter; whether he frequents choir or devotes himself to hunting; and so concerning the other matters that are noted above in various places about the abbot, and will still be touched on below in certain rubrics. And so also one must proceed in like manner with the prior, cellarer, custodian, vestiarian, and the other officials, with each according to the requirement of his office. Likewise with the porter: whether he is old and mature, joining the others for refectory, dormitory, etc. Likewise whether they permit women to enter or to live inside; whether the brothers frequently go out; and so concerning the other matters. All these things are set out more clearly in the recesses of the first and third chapters, and also of other chapters, and in the method of visiting, folio xiii, as well as in the bull of lord Nicholas, the legate often mentioned, whose points are given below in the final rubric.

Tenth, concerning the daily chapter: whether they practice it daily whether it is practiced with exposition of the Rule and correction of faults?

On the propriety of outward habit. From chapter 1. Rubric 11.

We ordain and establish that all are to wear large and broad tonsures, so that the circle of them does not exceed the space of two transverse fingers; and that they conduct themselves properly in clothing, habits, and footwear, according to the Clementine Ne in agro and the constitution of the aforesaid Pope Benedict.

Concerning the form and propriety of garments: namely, that the brothers are to wear tunics and garments next beneath the outer habit, of black, brown, or white color, according to the custom usually observed among them; round, ankle-length, not slit, nor marked by any other deformity; having broad sleeves extending to the wrist, in no way buttoned or knotted, yet not so broad that their width above the wrist, with the thumb raised, can be stretched out. Nor should they extend around the elbow-opening, as is the abuse of certain persons, farther than so that the arm can easily be turned and inserted within.

They are to be content with almuces of skins in place of hoods. Yet with the abbot’s permission they may use decent hoods in places where they are accustomed to wear them, slit over the shoulders for a length of at least four transverse fingers.

For linings in garments they are not to wear sendal, or miniver, or other precious materials, but are to use only the skins of lambs or young lambs for the said linings, or at least other non-precious cloths; nor are the linings to appear in any way above the collar or at the ends of the garments or sleeves. Furthermore, when they have to go outside the monastery they may wear a frock, cowl, or cloak, and beneath the cloak, if they wear it, a cowl or scapular. The lay brothers are to use a cowl within the monastery, cut open on both sides, and outside the monastery; and the boys are to use a scapular with a hood attached to it both within and outside the monastery.

But because some use the aforesaid habits more ample and long, while others use them less so, for that reason we have thought fit to insert in the present statutes the breadth and length of the aforesaid garments, which we wish to be observed.

And first, beginning with the hood of the frock, we ordain that its breadth is not to reach the elbow-opening by the thickness of two transverse fingers, nor may it be narrower or so short that it does not extend as far as the middle of the elbow and of the upper bone near the shoulder. The said hood, however, is to extend behind at least as far as the belt, but may not extend beyond it by as much as four fingers. The length of the sleeves is to extend one cubit beyond the hand, and their width is not to exceed another cubit and a half. Yet below it is to be so broad that steps may easily be taken within it. And what has been said about the frock we wish also to be understood of the cowl, the sleeves being excepted, since it has none.

Within the monastery, in places where there are twelve monks, all are to use the frock. But in other places where there is not so large a congregation, they may use cowls; and if they wear these, no one is to use the frock, except only the president of the monastery and the first after him, whom we wish always to wear the frock. Yet in duties, namely in the divine office beneath the alb, and when riding beneath the cloak, they may use a scapular, which is to have at least the breadth of half a cubit.

They are not to use linen sheets and canopies, but are to wear either a woolen or a linen garment in place of the aforesaid shirts. And they are to wear boots or shoes, or high laced shoes, so that their height covers on the leg a space of four fingers above the ankle. If they have been negligent in any of the aforesaid matters, or if within three months after they have come to their monasteries, as stated above, they have not complied, then, beyond the penalties imposed by law, we wish them to be punished by their superior in religion, or, if they have no superior, by the aforesaid visitors, in such a way that it may serve as an example to the rest.

On divine worship. Rubric 12.

The office in divine worship, both day and night, at the hours

at the appropriate hours according to the Rule, devoutly, slowly, and deliberately, not by rushing through or abbreviating it. Nothing is to be preferred to this work; but as soon as the signal has been heard, leaving behind everything that was in their hands, all must hasten to it with due gravity, lest levity find fuel there, as above, chapters 1 and 3.

For this reason also the signal for Matins, which must be held at midnight, as above, chapter 1, and for Prime, and for Vespers, must be prolonged for at least a quarter of an hour, where above and in several of the following chapters. And lest, because of a shortage of persons, some might be able to excuse themselves for performing this worship less perfectly, it has been ordained above, chapter 3, that everywhere as many monks must be kept and received as can conveniently be supported from the goods of the monastery; and those negligent in these matters must be punished most severely.

The abbots and the others must also celebrate, confess, and communicate as is contained in the constitutions of Benedict XII concerning the celebration of Masses. And all who according to law and the Benedictine sanctions ought to have been constituted in orders must be promoted to orders within the year, as above, chapter 1, and in the following chapters.

This too must be considered by the visitors: whether there are any churches annexed to the monastery, and whether any Masses are to be performed within or outside the monastery; how many they are, how they were founded and received, how they are performed, and by whom. Likewise the same must be done concerning anniversaries and other foundations or votive actions. And finally concerning readings, manual labors, and also meditations, whether they are regularly applied to them.

Concerning Monasteries of Nuns. Rubric 13.

Those things which have been said concerning monasteries of men must also be observed in monasteries of nuns, insofar as they pertain to the articles relevant to them, as above, chapter 1 and following. Nor should secular girls who are not there for the sake of conversion be permitted there, as above, chapter 16. They must be under perpetual enclosure, as above, chapter 1, and as is contained in the constitution of Boniface which begins Periculoso, De statu monachorum, book 6. These women the visitors and others to whom care of them has been committed must never, out of a desire to see them,

visit, as was touched on above in the rubric concerning visitors; nor should they enter their enclosures unless great necessity or utility requires it, as above, chapter 16. The confessor of the same women is also wholly forbidden entry of this kind, in the same chapter. Nor should anyone be appointed their confessor without the consent of at least one president.

Concerning the Method and Form of Reforming Monasteries, according to the tenor of the bull of lord Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal priest of the Roman church of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, and legate from the side for Germany. Rubric 14.

First, that the prelates of the monasteries to be visited be so instructed that, by fitting habit and tonsure, by uprightness of life, gravity of conduct, the word of teaching, and the example of holiness, they may preside laudably and fruitfully over their subjects. They are to correct and amend the excesses of individuals according to the Rule and the statutes of the order, without any dissimulation. They are to recall all their fugitive brothers and absent monks, within a term to be established for them by the visitors for this purpose, except those who preside over annexed parishes. And no one is to be permitted to use damnable private property; rather, all things are to be brought into common use.

Against the incontinent, both prelates and subjects, let stricter discipline and censures proceed, so that not only the vices of public incontinence may be punished worthily, but also every occasion from which suspicion of incontinence could arise may be removed from their midst.

The three substantial points of the Rule are especially to be preserved most completely by all, so that no dispensation or contrary custom may ever avail anyone against them. Silence is to be kept in the oratory, refectory, and cloister, etc. Likewise the brothers are to be refreshed under table reading, which is to continue until the end of the meal. The eating of meat is to be most strictly forbidden to all healthy persons in every place and time.

Likewise all are to sleep in the dormitory, as far as possibility permits, girded with belts or cords, upon mats, mattresses, or blankets. They are not to use linen shirts and sheets. Due care is to be applied concerning the enclosure of monasteries

With regard to the enclosure of the monasteries, he shall apply due vigilance. Entrance into the precincts of the monastery is not to be open to women, even those not suspected. Nor is it lawful for any religious, except officials, to leave the precincts of his monastery without the special permission of his superior.

All who are healthy shall observe the fasts, both those instituted by the rule and those instituted by the Church. They shall perform the divine office, both by day and by night, fittingly and distinctly, as is proper, at the appropriate hours. When this has been completed, they shall apply themselves to reading or to manual labor, according to the requirement of the time and of their business, and according to the direction of the aforesaid rule.

Books are to be supplied to the brothers at the appointed time. They shall inspect each brother’s beds, on account of private possessions. He shall observe the chapter of faults daily; in it, after the readings of the martyrology and the rule have first been made, he shall proceed, if there is need, to the exposition of the rule and to the examination and correction of faults.

He shall also see to it that the brothers appointed for this do not neglect, at the proper times, confession, communion, and celebration. He shall provide diligently for the monks concerning food and drink according to the disposition of the rule. Suitable places in the monasteries themselves are also to be assigned both for sick brothers and, for the time being, for guests who arrive; to all of these care and humanity shall be shown according to the disposition of the aforesaid rule. They shall lead guests to prayer; a reading shall be read to them for edification, and he shall wash their feet.

With the utmost diligence he shall take care that monasteries are not burdened with unbearable loads of debts, and that their goods are not dispersed or alienated, in accordance with the sanctions of Benedict XII and other apostolic sanctions, and the oaths sworn by abbots at their confirmation and blessing; alienated goods, if there are any, they shall carefully recover.

Abbots, provosts, priors, or rectors shall diligently protect and preserve the rights of those monasteries. They shall use their fruits, revenues, and proceeds for the common benefits of the monasteries. And each year they shall give a lawful account of their revenues and of the state of their temporal goods. They shall abstain from superfluous and unbecoming riding-horses, and from hunting dogs and birds. Nor shall any religious within the precincts of the monastery

presume in any way to have weapons or to contract confraternity.

These and other things handed down by the holy fathers and by canonical and regular institutions, according as the character of the time and the condition of persons requires and as seems salutary to the visitors, they shall renew by establishing them in monasteries and places that have fallen away from regular observance, for the introduction of holy reform. And they shall take care to commit them to due execution, causing all and each of these things to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, by our authority which, through the present letters, we commit to them.

Thus, at the instance of the reverend father in Christ, the lord abbot of the monastery at Saint Giles in Nuremberg, a prelate of the aforementioned order, whose wish he greatly desires to satisfy, Georg Stuchs of Sulzbach, citizen of Nuremberg, with his craft as leader and fortune as companion, brought to its preconceived and intended end the present volume: divided and arranged in brief form into the form of visiting the monasteries of both nuns and monks of the Order of Saint Benedict throughout the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg; into the manner of celebrating a provincial chapter of the same every three years; into an abridgment of the recess of each provincial chapter celebrated from the year of grace 1417 up to the present; into a summary of the privileges granted to the aforesaid order; and into an epilogue briefly expressing the foregoing matters.

In the year of the incarnation of the intelligible divine Word, from the Holy Spirit and from Mary ever virgin, 1493, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of the month of October. May the most blessed Benedict aid us in attaining the clear intellectual and most blessed vision of him. Amen.
